title: The CSO Handbook
text:
The CSO Handbook
One contract, three languages — reproducible analytics in R, Python, and Stata.
Download the handbook (PDF)
This handbook documents the cso-toolkit contract. Start with the Introduction, then read the part that matches your role.

title: Foreword
text:
Every number UNICEF publishes about children is, in the end, a claim that someone can check. A coverage rate, a stunting estimate, a count of children out of school — each is only as credible as our ability to say where it came from and to produce it again. In official statistics, “again” is often the hard word. The same indicator, recomputed by a second analyst in a second language, can come out a different number, and reconstructing why can take longer than the original analysis did. I have spent enough of my career re-deriving a number someone else had already published — once in R, once in Stata, arriving at two answers and no way to choose between them — to take this problem personally. That gap between published and reproducible is the problem this toolkit exists to close.
cso-toolkit is the Chief Statistician Office’s answer: one contract, expressed identically in R, Python, and Stata. It fixes one way to read, write, compare, and merge data; one way to call external sources; one way to aggregate, version-sync, and scaffold a project — so that an analytics product can be re-run by someone other than its author and yield the same numbers. The contract is not advice. It is enforced at every wrapped call site: a provenance sidecar — a small companion file, written beside every output, that records exactly where the numbers came from; an automatic check that the rows are uniquely identified by the key you declare; and a producer / reviewer split that makes the network physically unreachable to a reviewer, rather than trusting them not to reach for it. Those three guarantees turn “trust me” into “check me.”
One design choice deserves dwelling on — it is the institutional case for this book: we vendor the toolkit rather than install it. A consumer repository copies the helpers into its own tree and keeps them under version control alongside the analysis they serve. This is, on the surface, the less fashionable option — package managers exist precisely to spare us from copying code. But UNICEF’s statistical files are meant to outlive the environment that produced them. A figure citing dw_<sector>.csv in 2026 must reproduce identically when a reviewer re-runs it years later, working from the canonical deposit and the vendored helpers alone — no network, no upstream package drift, no ambient version skew silently changing a rounding rule. Vintage permanence is not a feature we add on top; it is the reason the toolkit is shaped the way it is. This matters more for us than for most: the numbers in these files set corporate-scorecard targets and inform what national budgets prioritise for children, and when a government acts on a UNICEF estimate, that estimate has to still mean the same thing the year someone audits the decision — long after the software that produced it has moved three versions on. Vendoring is how a statistical office that publishes for the long record protects that record from the churn of the software underneath it.
This handbook is deliberately scoped to the contract itself, not to any one warehouse that uses it. Its companion, the DW-Production handbook, documents the child-data warehouse — the operational store of signed-off sector files. This book documents the reusable machinery beneath that and any future repository that publishes signed-off data: how the wrappers behave, what the sidecars promise, how the roles are enforced, and how a new repo adopts and stays in sync. The two are complementary by design. Read together, they describe both what UNICEF Data & Analytics produces and how it guarantees the producing.
The twelve named authors are the members of UNICEF Data & Analytics’ Database Managers Working Group — the colleagues whose shared, hard-won operating practice the toolkit encodes. This is genuinely collective work: the toolkit is the written-down form of how this group already agreed to handle data, and authorship is credited to the group as a whole rather than parcelled out by sector or function. The other eight editors are the unit chiefs of UNICEF Data & Analytics, who reviewed the handbook in that editorial capacity; I chair the editorial group as Chief Statistician. The Working Group did this on top of full workloads, and what they wrote down is not a wish-list — it is the practice they had already fought their way to, sector by sector. I am grateful to all of them, and a little in awe of the discipline it represents.
A note on how the book was made, in keeping with our own standard of provenance: parts of it were drafted with generative-AI assistance. The AI did not author the book. It produced drafts that the named authors and editors reviewed, edited, and checked against the cso-toolkit codebase, and we take full responsibility for every methodological claim, factual statement, and code example in it. The handbook text is released under CC BY 4.0; the toolkit code under r/, python/, and stata/ is MIT-licensed — attribute each part under its own terms.
The toolkit is young, and so is this book. The coverage is honestly uneven across the three languages today, and the handbook says so wherever that is true rather than papering over it. What is already settled is the principle: one contract, enforced, reproducible, and built to last longer than the tools it runs on. The toolkit will get more even — full parity across R, Python, and Stata, and more deposits adopting the contract — because the teams adopting it will hold it to that. That is the expectation I would set: do not treat the contract as a constraint to satisfy, but as the floor you build above.
João Pedro Azevedo
Chief Statistician and Deputy Director, Data and Analytics, UNICEF
Chair of Editors

title: Preface
text:
What this handbook is
This handbook documents cso-toolkit: the UNICEF Chief Statistician Office’s reusable, cross-language contract for reproducible analytics. The toolkit encodes one way to read, write, compare, and merge data; one way to call external APIs; and one way to aggregate, version-sync, and scaffold projects — and it does so identically in R, Python, and Stata. Every call routes through wrappers that enforce a provenance sidecar on each output, an isid uniqueness check on stated keys, and a producer / reviewer mode contract. The promise these mechanisms add up to is simple: an analytics product can be re-run by someone other than its original author and yield the same numbers.
The toolkit is vendored, not network-installed. Its source files are copied into each consumer’s own repository rather than pulled from a package index at run time. That choice is deliberate and it is the spine of the whole design: a publication that cites a deposited file today should reproduce identical numbers years later from the deposit and the vendored helpers alone — no live network, no upstream package drift, no ambient version skew. The handbook returns to that idea throughout.

title: Preface
text:
What this handbook is not
This is not a tutorial on R, Python, or Stata, and it is not a statistics text. It assumes you can already write a script in at least one of the three languages and that you understand the analytical work your sector or team does. Its subject is narrower and more specific: the contract — the shared conventions and the wrappers that enforce them — and nothing beyond what the code in the repository actually implements. Where a capability exists in one language but not another, the book says so plainly rather than describing an aspiration; the cross-language coverage matrix in Appendix A is the source of truth when the prose and the code seem to disagree.
It is also not the warehouse handbook. The companion DW-Production handbook documents UNICEF’s child-data warehouse — the operational store of signed-off dw_<sector> files that the public data products draw from. This book is complementary to that one: DW-Production documents a particular warehouse and its sector pipelines; this book documents the reusable contract itself, for any consumer that adopts it. DW-Production is the toolkit’s first and largest adopter, but it is not the only one the toolkit is built to serve.

title: Preface
text:
Who this handbook is for
The book is written for several audiences at once, and most readers will live in one or two parts of it rather than reading front to back:

Database managers (producers) who run sector pipelines, pull upstream APIs, and deposit canonical files. The contract — the roles, the mode that governs network access, the provenance sidecars — is your daily working environment, and Part I describes it.
Reviewers who re-run a pipeline from pre-deposited inputs and compare the result against the canonical deposit. The same mode contract governs your work, with the network deliberately unreachable; Part I explains why that constraint is enforced rather than merely advised.
Publishers who move signed-off deposits into downstream products. The role boundaries in Part I tell you where the toolkit’s guarantees end and the publication infrastructure begins.
Peer-institution adopters — maintainers of other deposit-bearing repositories who want to vendor the toolkit into their own codebase and keep it in sync. Part III is written for you, and it assumes the role and mode concepts from Part I.

Analysts and sector teams who simply need to read, write, and aggregate data the CSO way are served by Part II, which is the reference for that daily work in all three languages.

title: Preface
text:
How to read it
The handbook is organised into six parts and a set of appendices.

Part I — The Contract motivates the toolkit and lays out its shape (one contract, three language siblings, many consumer repositories, one canonical deposit), then defines the three roles, the session-level mode that governs network access, and the two cross-cutting mechanisms — provenance sidecars and the standard error envelope — that make the toolkit trustworthy.
Part II — Using the Helpers is the daily reference, one chapter per capability family: reading and writing data, external APIs, and aggregation, with R, Python and Stata side by side.
Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository is for adopters: starting a repository or adopting the toolkit in an existing one, profiles and the mode switch, vendoring and updates, checks and CI, and working with AI coding agents.
Part IV — Maintaining the Toolkit is for the toolkit’s maintainers and contributors: versioning and the release discipline, how the three languages are certified to agree, and how to contribute a change.
Parts V and VI document the microdata archive (datalib) and the wider ecosystem of shared code.
Appendices collect the dense reference material: the coverage matrix (A), the provenance sidecar schema (B), the error taxonomy (C), a function reference (D), a glossary (E), and curated third-party functions (F).

If you are new, read the architecture and roles chapters in Part I, then the reading-and-writing chapter in Part II. Those three give you enough to use the toolkit safely. If you are here to start a repository or adopt the toolkit in an existing one, begin with “Starting a repository” in Part III, keeping the roles chapter to hand.

title: About the authors
text:
How authorship is framed
The DW-Production handbook attributes work per sector and per file, because that book documents a warehouse whose pipelines split cleanly along sector lines. That model does not transfer to the toolkit. cso-toolkit is a single shared contract, not a collection of sector pipelines; its value is precisely that one helper behaves the same for every sector and every consumer. We therefore credit the authors collectively rather than carving the toolkit into per-person slices.
The collective credit is deliberate, not a placeholder for finer-grained attribution. The toolkit is the written form of a working practice the named authors hold in common: no single helper “belongs” to one of them, and the contract’s worth lies in its uniformity rather than in who wrote which line. Splitting it into per-person modules would misdescribe how the work was actually done.






Editor to finalize. If, before release, the team decides to surface finer-grained credit (for example, by opening the repository’s commit history to multiple named authors, or by adding a CONTRIBUTORS file), this section should point readers there. As currently maintained, the repository does not carry a per-author commit ledger, so this page does not claim one.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
Consumer and adopter repositories
This toolkit exists to be vendored into other repositories — copied into a consumer’s own codebase rather than installed over the network — so that each consumer’s pipelines run against a pinned, drift-free copy of the contract. We thank the teams maintaining the repositories that adopt and exercise it:

DW-Production — the operational copy of the UNICEF child-data warehouse, and the toolkit’s first and primary consumer. Its sector pipelines are where the contract is stress-tested in daily use. The companion DW-Production handbook documents that warehouse; this handbook documents the reusable contract those pipelines depend on. The two are complementary.
Future deposit-bearing repositories (editor-to-finalize: confirm which adopters to name at release — e.g. UNPD-Population, datalib) that vendor the toolkit to gain the same provenance, uniqueness, and producer/reviewer guarantees.

Adoption feedback from these consumers — bug reports, coverage-gap requests, and onboarding friction — has shaped the toolkit’s API and is the reason its asymmetries between languages are documented honestly rather than papered over.

title: Acknowledgements
text:
Methodological lineage
The toolkit does not invent a measurement methodology; it serves one. It is the reusable contract that makes the analytics behind UNICEF’s flagship statistical products reproducible, as those products are derived through the warehouse it serves. The practices it encodes build on:

UNICEF’s MICS programme and its long history of country-led survey methodology
WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for WASH measurement
WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC)
The UN Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME)
UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS) for education indicators
World Bank’s DIME Data Handbook as the genre exemplar this handbook follows, and the DIME Wiki community for ongoing reproducibility reference

The toolkit’s contribution is upstream of these: it is the plumbing — provenance sidecars, the isid uniqueness check, mode-aware path routing, and the vendoring model — that lets the numbers feeding these products be re-derived years later from a canonical deposit alone.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.1 What cso-toolkit is
cso-toolkit is the shared, cross-language contract that the UNICEF Chief Statistician Office (CSO) uses to make its analytics reproducible. The CSO runs a data warehouse: a shared store of signed-off statistical files, named dw_<sector>.<ext> (one per sector — education, water and sanitation, immunisation, and so on), that UNICEF’s public data products draw from. The repository that holds the operational copy of that warehouse is DW-Production. The toolkit is what lets anyone, not just the file’s original author, re-run a sector’s pipeline and reproduce those files exactly.
Download the handbook (PDF)
It does this by encoding one way to read, write, compare, and merge data; one way to call external APIs; one way to aggregate, version-sync, and scaffold projects — and it does so identically in R, Python, and Stata. Every call routes through wrappers that enforce provenance sidecars (a .provenance.json file written next to every output, recording who made it, when, and from what), a uniqueness check (isid — that rows are unique on a stated key), and a producer / reviewer mode contract, so that any analytics product can be re-run by someone other than its original author and yield the same numbers. This handbook documents that contract.
cso-toolkit (the repository unicef-drp/cso-toolkit, currently v0.12.0) is a set of small helpers that enforce one way of doing each task, grouped into five capability families. Part III gives each family its own chapter.
These families look miscellaneous, but one idea ties them together: vintage permanence. A vintage is a dated snapshot of upstream data — the data as it stood when a release was cut. Vintage permanence is the guarantee that a publication citing dw_<sector>.csv in 2026 will, years later, produce identical numbers when re-run by a reviewer who has only the canonical deposit and the vendored helpers — no network access, no upstream package drift, no ambient dplyr version skew. Everything in the toolkit serves that goal.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
IO — dw_save, dw_use, dw_compare, dw_merge, dw_isid, dw_verify_z, dw_stage, dw_root, dw_fetch_inputs, dw_check_deposit, dw_read_provenance, dw_provenance_diff: uniform file IO with auto-dispatch by extension, an isid uniqueness check, an automatic provenance sidecar on writes, a Z: drive mirror on canonical writes (a canonical write being the final, signed-off dw_<sector> file that downstream products cite, as opposed to an intermediate working file), an integrity check on canonical reads, fetch-and-verify of inputs kept out of Git against the deposit, and a run-level comparison of two outputs from their sidecars.
External API — dw_api_fetch, dw_api_cached, dw_api_inventory: a mode-aware wrapper around external data sources (UIS, SDMX, World Bank, ILO, UNSD-SDG, GitHub-raw, generic HTTP/JSON, flat CSV at a URL) with a deposit-side cache.
Aggregation — aggregate_data_v2, apply_time_window, generate_agg_footnote, dw_nestweight, dw_pop, dw_regions (the earlier aggregate_data is kept for back-compat): weighted aggregation with population and country coverage, latest-observation time windowing, survey-weight redistribution, and population / region lookups.
Vintage sync — cso_toolkit_check, cso_toolkit_diff, cso_toolkit_pull, cso_toolkit_sync: consumer-side helpers that compare the locally vendored copy of the toolkit (its source files copied into the consumer’s own repository rather than installed over the network) against the latest upstream release and refresh it on demand.
Scaffolding and contract auditing — create_research_project, create_official_stats_project, create_profile, create_sector_script, review_profile, test_scripts: project scaffolds plus a static auditor that flags raw IO/API calls that should have gone through the toolkit.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 One contract, three languages
The defining commitment of cso-toolkit is cross-language parity: the same command names and the same behaviour across R, Python, and Stata. A dw_save in R looks and behaves like a dw_save in Python, which looks and behaves like dw_save in Stata. The same provenance sidecar schema, the same mode-aware path routing, and the same three-part error envelope ([cso_toolkit.<func>] WHAT / Why / Fix) hold across all three siblings.

RPythonStata


df <- tibble::tibble(REF_AREA = c("AGO", "BFA"), OBS_VALUE = c(0.5, 0.7))
dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = "REF_AREA",
        metadata = list(title = "Education indicators", vintage = "2026-05"))


df = pd.DataFrame({"REF_AREA": ["AGO", "BFA"], "OBS_VALUE": [0.5, 0.7]})
dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        isid=["REF_AREA"],
        metadata={"title": "Education indicators", "vintage": "2026-05"})


use "input.dta", clear
dw_save, filename("dw_ed_edu.dta")  ///
    path("$teamsWrkData/ed")        ///
    idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR)      ///
    title("Education indicators")   ///
    vintage("2026-05")



The kind argument in the examples names which tier of the warehouse a file belongs to: kind = "wrk" is a working (intermediate) output, written to scratch and freely re-runnable; a canonical write is the final deposit that downstream products cite, and the toolkit guards it with the Z: drive mirror and the reviewer-mode write lock described below. The examples deliberately use the working tier, which is the common case during a pipeline run.
That parity is the ideal, and most of this handbook is organised around it. But the parity is not yet complete. The current gaps:

Stata has no external-API wrapper — the API contract (dw_api_fetch and friends) exists only in R and Python. Stata also has no Parquet support; pipelines that need Parquet route through R or Python on the producer side and deposit a .dta for Stata consumption.
dw_fetch_inputs, dw_check_deposit, dw_read_provenance and dw_provenance_diff are R and Python (#152); Stata routes via R or Python.
dw_merge and dw_verify_z are R + Python only. Stata folds the uniqueness check into dw_save (via its idvars() option) rather than exposing a standalone dw_isid.
The demographics family: dw_pop ships in R and Python; dw_regions is R-only, and neither has a Stata sibling (a scope decision: Stata pipelines aggregate natively; see Appendix A).
Reference documentation is asymmetric. R has Roxygen-complete reference pages and a pkgdown site; Python has hand-written references rather than autogenerated, pkgdown-style docs.

The cross-language coverage matrix in Appendix A is the authoritative, function-by-function record of what exists where. Wherever this book shows code, it shows all three siblings side by side; where a language is missing a capability, it is marked, not faked.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 The roles this toolkit serves
cso-toolkit divides everyone who touches the data warehouse into three roles, each with a strict capability boundary the toolkit enforces at every wrapped call site:








Role
What they do
Network access




PRODUCER (Database Manager, DBM)
Runs the sector pipeline, pulls upstream APIs, deposits the final dw_<sector>.<ext> into the canonical warehouse, and writes a submission template (a pre-deposit checklist documenting the deposit).
Yes — dw_apis_allowed = TRUE.


REVIEWER (Database Reviewer, DBR)
Re-runs the pipeline from pre-deposited inputs, compares against the canonical deposit, files issues. Writes only to a sandbox.
No — every API call site raises a mode-lock error.


PUBLISHER (Database Publisher, DBP)
Pulls signed-off deposits into data.unicef.org, SDMX, and downstream products.
N/A (infrastructure outside this repo).



The mode is not a per-call argument but a session property. It is read once at profile-load time (dw_mode) and then enforced automatically everywhere. A reviewer does not have to remember to avoid the network; the toolkit makes the network unreachable for them. This is why we say the contract is enforced, not merely conventional.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.4 Who this handbook is for
This book is written for several audiences at once:

Analysts and sector teams working in R, Python, or Stata who need to read, write, and aggregate warehouse data the CSO way. You will spend most of your time in Part II (using the helpers).
Database managers (producers) and reviewers who operate the producer / reviewer / publisher mode contract day to day. Part I explains the roles and what the provenance sidecars and error envelopes guarantee; Part III shows how the mode is wired into a repository.
Repo adopters — maintainers of DW-Production and of future deposit-bearing repositories such as UNPD-Population and datalib — who want to vendor the toolkit into their own codebase and keep it in sync. Part III is your section; Part IV is for those who maintain the toolkit itself.
LLM and coding-agent developers — building assistants that turn documentation, existing sector-specific helpers, and legacy code into the standard functions this toolkit supports; or orchestrators that compose the toolkit’s deterministic functions as trusted building blocks. The handbook is written to be precise enough for a machine to follow — see § How coding agents should use this handbook.

You do not need to read the book front to back. Use the part that matches your role and follow the cross-references to adjacent chapters.

title: 1  Introduction
section: 1.5 How coding agents should use this handbook
text:
1.5 How coding agents should use this handbook
A growing share of code — across software generally, and increasingly in official statistics — is written or reviewed with LLM assistance. Part of the toolkit’s value is that it imposes a minimum common architecture — a minimum set of guardrails — on that code: no matter who (or what) writes a script, routing it through the wrappers guarantees the same provenance sidecars, the same isid uniqueness check, the same mode-aware role enforcement, and the same error envelope. Those guardrails do not depend on the author’s discipline — which makes LLM-assisted code safer to integrate: they enforce provenance, uniqueness, and role boundaries regardless of who wrote the code, but they do not certify that the numbers are correct. That remains the reviewer’s job.
But that safety is structural; it is not a transfer of responsibility. LLM assistance does not dilute accountability — it concentrates it. Code now gets produced and checked at machine speed and scale. That means the people who lead, review, and publish the results must vouch for more output, generated faster by a process whose plausible-looking errors are easy to miss. The toolkit shrinks the surface they have to police; it does not sign off in their place. The named producer, reviewer, and publisher remain accountable for every number (see § The roles this toolkit serves) — and the higher the degree of automation, the higher the bar for the human scrutiny that accountability demands.
For an LLM or an agentic orchestrator, that implies:

Map onto the toolkit’s functions; don’t reinvent them. When porting documentation or a sector’s bespoke helpers, translate them into dw_save, dw_api_fetch, aggregate_data_v2, and the rest — the verified, reproducible primitives — not equivalent ad-hoc logic.
Compose, don’t regenerate. An orchestrator calls the deterministic functions as building blocks; the LLM handles orchestration and glue, not the contract’s enforced behaviour. The determinism is the point.
Operate within the human’s role and session. An agent runs under the session’s dw_mode — in reviewer mode the network is unreachable — and must not flip the mode or reach for the allow_canonical_write / producer-bootstrap escape hatches on its own; those exist for explicit human action. The agent gets no role of its own; accountability stays with the named producer, reviewer, or publisher.
Never fabricate values, provenance, or coverage. Read and cite the provenance sidecar; surface gaps from the coverage matrix (Appendix A) rather than faking parity.
Treat the contract as binding. Code that bypasses the wrappers is flagged by the contract auditor (Checks and CI); generate code that passes it.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.6 How to navigate this book
The handbook is organised into six parts and a set of appendices.

Part I — The Contract motivates the toolkit and lays out its architecture (one contract, three language siblings, many consumer repositories, one canonical deposit), then defines the three roles, the session-level mode contract, and the two mechanisms that make the toolkit trustworthy: provenance sidecars and the standard error envelope.
Part II — Using the Helpers is the reference for daily work, one chapter per capability family: reading and writing data, external APIs, and aggregation. Each presents R, Python and Stata together; which language has which function is shown on one line under each function, from the coverage matrix.
Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository is for the people who start or adopt a repository: creating one (or adopting the toolkit in an existing one), profiles and the mode switch, vendoring and updates, checks and CI with check records and the contract auditor, and working with AI coding agents.
Part IV — Maintaining the Toolkit is for the toolkit’s own maintainers and contributors: versioning and the release discipline, how the three languages are certified to agree, and how to contribute a change.
Part V — The Microdata Archive (datalib) documents the survey-microdata archive, its IHSN folder grammar, and the datalib_* API and conformance suite.
Part VI — The Ecosystem sets out the three tiers of shared code and documents unicefData.
Appendices collect the dense reference material: the cross-language coverage matrix (A), the provenance sidecar schema (B), the error taxonomy (C), a full function reference (D), a glossary (E), and curated third-party functions (F). How the three languages are certified to agree is a chapter of its own in Part IV.

If you are brand new, read the architecture and roles chapters in Part I, then the reading-and-writing chapter in Part II. Those three pages give you enough to use the toolkit safely.
If you are here to start a repository or adopt the toolkit in an existing one, read Starting a repository in Part III first; it assumes the role and mode concepts from Part I, so keep the roles chapter to hand.






This handbook documents the toolkit as it actually exists in the repository, including its current asymmetries between languages. Where this book describes a capability as present in one language but not another, that reflects the real state of the code, not an aspiration. Treat the coverage matrix in Appendix A as the source of truth when in doubt.

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.1 The problem: analytics that cannot be re-run
A 2026 analysis must re-run identically in 2028. That single requirement, call it the reproducibility floor, is the reason cso-toolkit exists. Everything else in this book follows from it.
The toolkit is the shared, cross-language contract that the UNICEF Chief Statistician Office (CSO), within the Office of Strategy and Evidence (OSE), uses to read, write, compare and merge data; to call external APIs; to aggregate; and to keep copied-in (“vendored”) helper code in sync. In practice it is one input/output (IO) contract, one external-API contract and one mode contract, a session-level switch that decides whether a run may touch the network, implemented three times (R, Python, Stata) and shipped by copying rather than installing.
The first half of this chapter sets out the problem and the design choices it forces. The second half describes the shape that delivers on them: four layers, from the contract down to the deposit it protects, and the wider ecosystem of shared code around it.
A statistical office publishes numbers, and those numbers carry a promise: that they are not an accident of the machine, the week, or the analyst who happened to produce them. A figure cited in a 2026 publication, say an education indicator deposited as dw_ed.csv, must produce the same number two years later when a different person re-runs the pipeline.
That promise is surprisingly hard to keep. Three things routinely break it:
These are not hypothetical. An internal cross-sector audit (23 May 2026) found four regional-metadata CSV files being read independently across five sectors, each with no shared vintage record: four chances for the same kind of file to disagree, and nothing recording which copy any run actually used.
The toolkit’s answer is to route every data touch-point through a wrapper that applies the same discipline everywhere: one way to read and write that records provenance automatically, one way to call an external API that can be frozen and replayed, and one session-level contract that decides whether the network may be touched at all. The repository README states the goal directly: the toolkit exists “to facilitate the reproducibility and scalability of analytics developed by the UNICEF Chief Statistician Office.”
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
Upstream drift. The external source changes between the original run and the re-run. An SDMX (the statistical data-exchange standard) dataflow is revised, a World Bank indicator is re-based, a UIS (UNESCO Institute for Statistics) endpoint returns a slightly different shape. The re-run pulls live data and quietly produces different numbers.
Ambient version skew. The original analyst had one version of dplyr (or pandas, or a Stata .ado); the reviewer has another. A default changes, a sort becomes unstable, a join behaves differently. Nothing errors; the answer just shifts.
Untracked provenance. Nobody recorded what was read, from where, with what schema, by whom and when. When the numbers disagree there is no artefact to point at and no way to tell which run is wrong.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.2 The reproducibility floor
A floor is a guarantee you inherit, not a feature you opt into. Any codebase that vendors the helpers gets it: you do not have to remember to record provenance, wire up a cache, or police whether a reviewer accidentally hit the network. The wrappers do it.
The floor rests on three primitives that recur throughout the book:

Provenance sidecars. Every write through dw_save() emits a .provenance.json sidecar by default, recording a content hash of the file, its schema, the user, a timestamp and any metadata you pass. When two runs disagree, the sidecars tell you which input changed. Provenance sidecars and the error envelope explains the idea; Appendix B lists the fields.
A frozen deposit you can replay. External API calls go through dw_api_fetch(), which caches each response in the deposit. A re-run reads the cache rather than the live source, so upstream drift cannot leak into a reviewer’s numbers. See The external-API contract.
Uniqueness and integrity checks. Writes assert that the identifier columns you name are unique, and reads of the canonical deposit compare it with its Z: mirror. Silent duplication and silent corruption are caught at the call site, not three steps downstream.

Routing every call through a wrapper is not ceremony. The README is emphatic that the contract is enforced “at every wrapped call site, not by convention”. Convention is what fails when someone is in a hurry; an enforced contract does not.
The floor needs one more idea to hold: someone must be allowed to touch the live network and someone must be forbidden from it, and the toolkit must enforce the difference. So it distinguishes roles by what they may do, and makes the distinction a session-level mode, dw_mode, set once in your profile rather than passed to each call:

The producer (the Database Manager) runs the pipeline, pulls upstream APIs through the cache, and deposits the canonical artefacts, the official version of record that other people read and trust. The producer is the only role with network access.
The reviewer re-runs the pipeline from the frozen deposit, compares against it, and files issues. In reviewer mode a wrapped API call reads the frozen cache or stops with an error; it never reaches out, so a reviewer cannot “fix” a discrepancy by quietly pulling fresh data. That is what makes the re-run a real check.
The publisher takes signed-off deposits on to data.unicef.org, SDMX and other products, largely outside the toolkit’s boundary.

The producer’s run is the run of record; the reviewer’s run, with the network sealed off, is the proof that it reproduces. Roles and the mode contract defines the roles and how the mode enforces them, and Profiles and the mode switch shows how you set it.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.3 Vendoring, not installing
If a 2026 analysis must re-run identically in 2028, the helper code itself must be the same in 2028 as it was in 2026. A toolkit installed over the network (devtools::install_github(), pip install, net install) gives you whatever version the network serves at session start, which is upstream drift applied to your own tools. So repositories do not install the toolkit; they vendor it. They copy the helper files into their own 00_functions/ folder, commit them to their own history, and record the release they copied in a small manifest, .toolkit_manifest.yml. Every commit then shows exactly which helper code was in effect; updates happen only when a producer reads the release notes and chooses to refresh; a reviewer with no network can still re-run everything; and the same copy-and-pin model works for Stata, which a package model would serve poorly. On UNICEF laptops it has a further, blunt advantage: copying files into a project folder works where AppLocker blocks a network installer. Vendoring and updates sets out these reasons in full and covers the manifest, the development install and the update flow.






Vendoring trades a little convenience for a hard guarantee. You take on the small chore of an explicit refresh; in return, the helper code can never drift out from under a published result. For a statistical office, that trade is the whole point.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.4 Scaling across sectors and projects
The CSO is not one pipeline but many: education, water and sanitation, nutrition, health, poverty, immunisation and more. The toolkit’s users extend beyond DW-Production (the cross-sector deposit pipeline) to other repositories that will deposit canonical data, such as UNPD-Population and datalib. Without a shared contract each of them would re-invent the same primitives, and each re-invention is a new chance to drift, as the five-sector regional-metadata duplication showed.
A single vendored toolkit changes the economics. The same helpers, templates and audit functions go into every codebase, so a new sector or project “inherits the reproducibility floor for free instead of re-inventing it”. Adding the next sector is a vendoring step, not a re-implementation. The idea also gates the toolkit’s v1.0.0: that release waits until the education pilot lands and a second sector vendors the helpers without modification, proof that the contract generalises rather than being bent to one team’s habits. Versioning and releases describes the gate.
Scale is also why the contract spans three languages. Sectors work in R, Python and Stata, and the next sections show how one contract serves all three.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.5 The four layers
The shape that delivers the floor can be read in one sentence: the toolkit encodes a contract once; three language siblings implement it; consumer repositories vendor one sibling into their own code; and everything they produce lands in a single canonical deposit that the contract keeps reproducible.








Layer
What it is
Where it lives




The toolkit
One contract, expressed as five capability families
unicef-drp/cso-toolkit


Language siblings
Three idiomatic implementations of that contract
r/R/, python/src/, stata/src/


Consumer repositories
Codebases that vendor the helpers and use the contract
DW-Production, the sector pipelines, CCRI (the Children’s Climate Risk Index) and geospatial work


Canonical deposit
The frozen store every producer writes and every reviewer reads
The Teams folder 060.DW-MASTER/, its Z: drive mirror, and downstream Helix and SDMX



Dependence runs one way. The toolkit knows nothing about any consumer. The siblings know nothing about each other: they agree on the contract, never on shared code. A consumer depends on a pinned release of one sibling. The deposit depends on nothing; it is the inert artefact at the end of the flow, and that inertness is the point, because a reviewer can read it without re-running anything upstream.
Three names in the last row recur. The Z: drive is a network-mapped mirror of the Teams deposit, so that scripts can address the canonical store through a stable drive letter rather than a synced-folder path. Helix is UNICEF’s internal data platform. SDMX (Statistical Data and Metadata eXchange) is the exchange standard through which signed-off artefacts reach data.unicef.org. Helix and SDMX are downstream of the toolkit, not part of it: the architecture’s job ends when the deposit is written.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.6 The toolkit: five capability families
The helpers fall into five families. Each is the single sanctioned way to do its job inside a CSO analytics product, not a grab-bag of utilities. This section says what each family is for and where it is documented; Appendix D gives every signature, and Appendix A records which language has which function.

2.6.1 IO
One way to read, write, compare and join data. dw_save() and dw_use() choose the reader or writer from the file extension, and the chapter linked below lists the formats each language handles. Every write checks that the identifier columns you name are unique and leaves a provenance sidecar. Paths follow the session’s mode: a producer’s write is copied to the Teams deposit and its Z: mirror, while a reviewer writes to a local sandbox and is stopped if a path points at the deposit. The same family fills a gitignored inputs folder from the deposit and checks it, compares a new output with a reference, and tells you whether a run reproduced the previous one. See The IO contract.


2.6.2 External API
One mode-aware wrapper around a set of named external sources (UIS, SDMX, the World Bank, ILO, the UNSD SDG API, pinned GitHub files, plain HTTP and CSV at a URL). A producer fetches live and caches the response under _apis/<api>/<cache_key>.<ext> in the deposit, with its own sidecar; a reviewer reads only from that cache. The external-API contract lists the sources, generated from the code, and the arguments each takes.


2.6.3 Vintage sync
The consumer-side half of vendoring. These helpers read your .toolkit_manifest.yml, find the latest release, show its release notes since the release you pinned, compare your vendored files with it, and refresh them when you ask. They never update anything on their own. Reaching GitHub for a release and changing the vendored files are a producer’s acts, so in reviewer mode the helpers only make offline checks. See Vendoring and updates.


2.6.4 Aggregation and survey weights
The arithmetic that turns country rows into regional and global figures: weighted means, sums and proportions with population and country coverage and a coverage threshold; the latest observation per country within a year window; the matching coverage footnote; redistribution of survey weights over missing nested observations; and the population denominators and regional groupings the aggregators consume. See Aggregation.


2.6.5 Scaffolding and audit
The helpers that set a repository up and keep it honest. They create a new research or official-statistics repository with its checks, hooks, tests and agent files; write a profile with the standard building blocks (user identification, configuration load, mode resolution, a reproducibility seed, the no-API guard); write sector run-scripts; review an existing profile against the same blocks; and audit a folder of scripts for raw file-IO or API calls that should go through the wrappers. See Starting a repository, Profiles and the mode switch and Checks and CI.


2.6.6 The error envelope cuts across all five
One behaviour belongs to no family because it belongs to all of them. Every error the toolkit raises, in any language, has the same shape: a [cso_toolkit.<function>] prefix, what went wrong, why the rule exists, and a numbered fix. The fixed prefix lets a consumer find every site that hits a given error class with one search, and the fixed shape lets tests assert on it. Provenance sidecars and the error envelope explains the design; Appendix C catalogues the messages.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.7 Three languages, one contract
The toolkit ships three implementations: R under r/R/, Python under python/src/ and Stata under stata/src/. The word that matters is siblings, not ports and not bindings. They are not generated from a common source and do not call one another at run time. They are independent code that agrees on a contract: the same function names, the same .provenance.json schema, the same mode-aware path routing, the same error-envelope shape.
The contract is defined by behaviour, not by shared code. A dw_save in any sibling enforces uniqueness on the identifier columns, writes a sidecar with the same JSON schema, and refuses a reviewer’s write to the canonical deposit. Given the same inputs it produces the same numbers, which is what reproducibility cares about. Here is the same write in each language:

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("REF_AREA", "INDICATOR"),
        metadata = list(title = "Education indicators", vintage = "2026-05"))


dw_save(df, name="dw_ed.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        isid=["REF_AREA", "INDICATOR"],
        metadata={"title": "Education indicators", "vintage": "2026-05"})


dw_save, filename("dw_ed") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
    idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR)                       ///
    title("Education indicators")                    ///
    vintage("2026-05")



Each sibling stays idiomatic. R and Python take a logical store (name, sector, kind) and resolve the path from the mode; Stata takes comma options in the usual Stata way (dw_save, filename(...) path(...), not a using form) and an explicit path built from the profile’s globals. The contract is in what the calls do, not in how they are spelled.
Equal support in all three languages is the pledge, and two devices keep the pledge honest. Appendix A, generated from the code, records for every function whether each language has it, has it in a documented narrower scope, or does not need it, and each function’s chapter carries the same information as a one-line badge. The conformance harness under conformance/ runs the same cases in R, Python and Stata and compares the results; sh tools/certify records a parity certificate (How the three languages stay in step). A repository vendors one sibling and gets whatever that sibling implements, so before choosing a language for a new pipeline, check the matrix rather than assuming every name works everywhere.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.8 Consumer repositories
A consumer repository vendors the sibling for its language into 00_functions/ and pins the release in .toolkit_manifest.yml. DW-Production is the first consumer, and the sector pipelines (education, water and sanitation, nutrition, HIV/AIDS, child poverty, immunisation and the rest) consume through it. The CCRI and geospatial work uses the Python sibling directly. Future repositories, such as UNPD-Population and datalib, are expected to vendor the same way.
The architectural fact is that the dependency from consumer to toolkit is a copy plus a pin, not a live link. That is what lets a consumer be re-run identically years later, and what lets the vintage-sync family detect, without ever forcing, that a consumer has fallen behind the latest release. Starting a repository walks through adopting the toolkit in a new or existing repository.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.9 The canonical deposit
Everything the consumers produce in producer mode flows to one place. Physically it is the Teams folder 060.DW-MASTER/, carbon-copied to the Z: drive mirror, and from there published downstream to Helix, the SDMX endpoints and data.unicef.org. Architecturally it is the immutable record that closes the reproducibility loop: the producer writes it, the reviewer reads it frozen and never re-runs anything upstream of it, and the publisher takes signed-off copies to the outside world.
The deposit is where the contract’s parts meet. The IO family writes artefacts there with their sidecars and mirrors. The API family caches upstream pulls there, so they too become part of the frozen record. And the mode contract draws its hard line at this boundary: a producer may write canonical paths, while a reviewer’s writes are forced into a sandbox. Because the deposit can be read without being recomputed, the numbers it holds stay reproducible.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.10 Reading the architecture diagram
The README’s “Architecture at a glance” diagram (a Mermaid flowchart) draws the four layers in one picture: external sources at the top, the toolkit and its families, the three siblings, the consumers, and the canonical deposit. It uses two line styles.

Solid arrows are the normal producing flow: external sources into the API family in producer mode, the siblings into the consumers, and consumers depositing into the canonical store. The arrow from the siblings to the consumers is the vendoring edge, and it is the one labelled with a file, .toolkit_manifest.yml, the pin that the vintage-sync family watches.
Dashed arrows mark the two reproducibility relationships, and there are exactly two. The one from the toolkit to the siblings, “language-parallel implementations”, is the one-contract, three-implementations relationship. The one from the deposit back to the consumers, “reviewer reads (frozen)”, is the reviewer’s path: reading the deposit without recomputing it.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.11 The wider ecosystem: three tiers
The toolkit is not the only shared code a CSO pipeline touches, and this book’s authority is not the same for all of it. The shared code falls into three tiers, and the tier decides both who maintains the code and what the book asserts about it:

(i) The toolkit. The dw_* contract and its three siblings, everything this chapter describes. The book is normative here: it is the documentation.
(ii) UNICEF-supported packages. Full packages with their own repositories and release lines, maintained by CSO staff: unicefData as a full member, datalib as a provisional one, and a mapping and boundaries capability under evaluation. Membership follows published criteria, not reputation. The book documents how these packages fit together and points to each package’s own documentation; it never re-documents their functions.
(iii) Third-party functions. External packages used inside production pipelines. The book asserts only that a named version behaved as described on a stated date in a stated pipeline; Appendix F holds the rules and the list.

The UNICEF analytics ecosystem: three tiers in Part VI sets out the tiers in full, with the membership gate and what “supported” does and does not promise.

2.11.1 Configuration across the tiers
The tiers do not yet share a configuration contract, and the divergence is deliberate until a common design is agreed. The toolkit reads your block of ~/.config/user_config.yml through the generated profile and dw_load_config. datalib reads a datalib: block from its own configuration file; dw_load_config skips such a block without adopting its keys, so sharing a file is safe for the toolkit. unicefData is configured through environment variables and reads no user file at all. If you work across tiers, treat the three as separate namespaces. Profiles and the mode switch covers the toolkit’s file; the ecosystem chapter covers the other two.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together
text:
2.12 What this buys you
Pulling it together: the toolkit gives the CSO a reproducibility floor (provenance, frozen replay and integrity checks, enforced at the call site); a vendoring model that pins helper code to a release so published results never drift; and one contract in three languages that lets new sectors and repositories inherit all of it instead of rebuilding it. The producer and reviewer split turns “we wrote it down” into “we can prove it re-runs”.
Hold the four layers (toolkit, siblings, consumers, deposit) as the frame for the rest of the book. The rest of Part I sets out the contract they carry: the roles and the mode, then provenance and the error envelope. Part II gives each user-facing family its own chapter. Part III covers how a repository joins the architecture and stays in sync, and Part IV is for the toolkit’s maintainers.
crumbs: 2  Why a toolkit, and how it fits together

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
text:
3.1 The three roles
DW-Production is a relay. Upstream agencies publish their statistics; a Database Manager refreshes caches and produces deposited indicators; an auditor reproduces those outputs and files findings; and a publisher pushes approved data packages to UNICEF’s data warehouse and the public pages that draw on it. Each runner touches a different part of the filesystem and carries a different obligation. The toolkit names the three runners PRODUCER, REVIEWER and PUBLISHER, and it does not rely on discipline alone to keep them apart: a session in reviewer mode is prevented in code from writing canonical artefacts (the single authoritative copy of the data everyone downstream trusts) and from calling live APIs.
This chapter sets out the three roles, what each may read and write, how the dw_mode session setting turns those policies into mechanical guarantees, and the second setting beside it: the project’s collaboration model.
Two terms recur. A deposit is a finished data package a producer places in the canonical store. A deposit is blessed once it has passed the producer’s pre-deposit checklist and the reviewer’s compare report; only blessed deposits may be published.
Each role has a short acronym used in the repository’s internal documentation; this chapter uses the plain names.
All three use the same helpers (dw_save, dw_use, dw_api_fetch, dw_compare and the rest) and the same path globals, derived from the user’s profile. What differs is the slice of the filesystem each may read and write, and whether it may reach the network at all.

text:
Role
Acronym
Plain meaning




PRODUCER
DBM (Database Manager)
Owns the deposit. Refreshes upstream caches and produces the deposited indicator outputs.


REVIEWER
DBR (Database Reviewer)
Reproduces and validates. Audits, finds bugs, gathers sector-lead sign-off.

Pushes blessed deposits into the canonical UNICEF data warehouse and downstream surfaces.

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
section: 3.2 What each role may read and write
text:
3.2 What each role may read and write










Role
Reads from
Writes to
API calls
Owns




PRODUCER
upstream APIs + the canonical deposit (060.DW-MASTER)
the canonical deposit (Teams, and the Z: mirror automatically)
yes
refreshing cached upstream data; producing the deposited outputs


REVIEWER
the canonical deposit (read only) + own sandbox
the sandbox only (sandboxRoot, per user)
no, forbidden by the reviewer-mode guard
reproducibility validation; sector-lead sign-off; finding bugs


PUBLISHER
the blessed work-data deposit (013_wrkdata)
the data warehouse: Helix, SDMX endpoints, data.unicef.org, SoWC tables
reads warehouse endpoints only
publication into the warehouse and downstream surfaces



The deposit folders are numbered by lifecycle stage under one root, 060.DW-MASTER/01_dw_prep: 011_rawdata holds upstream pulls, including the _apis/ cache, and 013_wrkdata holds finished, promoted deposits. The numbering is a sequence (raw input becomes work data), not a count. The full path table for each mode is in Profiles and the mode switch.
Three things follow. Only the producer touches upstream: reviewers read the frozen caches the producer deposited. The reviewer reads canonical but writes sandbox: its reads fall back to the deposit (with a Z: integrity check), and an attempted canonical write fails. And the publisher consumes only blessed outputs from 013_wrkdata, never raw or staging paths.

3.2.1 What each role must not do
The same boundaries, seen from the other side:







Role
Forbidden




PRODUCER
skip the pre-deposit checklist; deposit without a compare-vs-prior-vintage report; deposit without sector-lead sign-off on non-trivial deltas


REVIEWER
write to canonical paths; call external APIs; modify caches in the deposit


PUBLISHER
promote outputs that have not passed the producer’s checklist and the reviewer’s compare; publish without a provenance chain back to the original API fetches; roll back without amending the source



The producer’s prohibitions are procedural: enforced by checklist and review, not by code. The reviewer’s are mechanical: enforced by dw_mode, as the next section shows. The publisher’s are mostly procedural, with one mechanical exception: dw_publish refuses reviewer-mode calls (see The publisher and dw_publish).

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
text:
3.3 The data flow
A single indicator moves through the relay like this:
External APIs                 (UIS · SDMX · WB · ILO · UNSD)
  │  PRODUCER: dw_api_fetch(refresh = TRUE)
  ▼
API cache  ── 011_rawdata/_apis ───────────────────────────┐
  │                                                          │ REVIEWER: dw_api_cached
  ▼                                                          │ (cache reads only, no live calls)
Sector pipeline  ◄─────────────────────────────────────────┘
  │  PRODUCER: dw_save(isid = ...)            REVIEWER: writes routed to sandbox
  ▼                                                   │
Canonical deposit ── 013_wrkdata ── carbon copy ──► Z: mirror (integrity check)
  │  │  ▲                                               ▲
  │  │  └── REVIEWER: dw_use (read only) ───────────────┘
  │  │            │
  │  │            ▼
  │  │     Compare report ──► Issues filed to PRODUCER / sector lead
  │  │
  └──┴── PUBLISHER ──► Helix · SDMX endpoints · data.unicef.org · SoWC / SI tables
The reviewer’s arrows are read only; the publisher’s fan out from the blessed 013_wrkdata deposit. The diagram shows why enforcement matters: the reviewer’s pipeline runs the same scripts as the producer’s, so the only thing between an audit run and a corrupted deposit is the mode contract redirecting every write.

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
text:
3.4 How dw_mode enforces the boundaries
The producer/reviewer split is one session-level setting, dw_mode, which each person sets to producer or reviewer in their own ~/.config/user_config.yml. It has no default, because defaulting either way is unsafe. From it the profile derives the path globals: the working globals (teamsWrkData, teamsRawData) point at the deposit for a producer and at the sandbox for a reviewer, the *Canonical aliases always point at the deposit, and dw_apis_allowed is true only for a producer. So the same scripts write to the deposit in one mode and to the sandbox in the other. How the mode is set and resolved, and the derivation, are in Profiles and the mode switch.
Routing paths at the profile is the first layer. The write and fetch helpers then check the mode again at the call site, so a script that builds a canonical path by hand, or calls the network directly, is still stopped. Two guards do this work.

3.4.1 Guard 1: reviewer mode forbids canonical and Z: writes (dw_save)

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.
When dw_save is asked to write under the canonical deposit or under the Z: mirror, and the session is in reviewer mode, it refuses. The single escape hatch is allow_canonical_write, meant for a Database Manager’s bootstrap, never for routine reviewer work.

RPythonStata


# Reviewer-mode session. This canonical path raises an error.
dw_save(df, file.path(teamsWrkDataCanonical, "dw_im.csv"), isid = c("iso3", "year"))
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to canonical (Teams) deposit: .../dw_im.csv
#>  Reviewer sessions must keep canonical / Z: deposits read-only to preserve vintage permanence; writes go to the local repo sandbox.
#>  Fix:
#>  1. Resolve a sandbox path instead (the profile's `teamsWrkData` should point there in reviewer mode), OR
#>  2. If this is a deliberate Database Manager bootstrap, pass `allow_canonical_write = TRUE`.

# Producer bootstrap (rare): explicit opt-in bypasses the guard.
dw_save(df, canonical_path, isid = c("iso3", "year"), allow_canonical_write = TRUE)


# Reviewer-mode session. This canonical path raises PermissionError,
# with the same Why and Fix as in R.
dw_save(df, os.path.join(teams_wrk_data_canonical, "dw_im.csv"), isid=["iso3", "year"])
# PermissionError: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to
#   canonical (Teams) deposit: .../dw_im.csv

dw_save(df, canonical_path, isid=["iso3", "year"], allow_canonical_write=True)


* In reviewer mode $teamsWrkData points at the sandbox, so this lands there:
dw_save , filename("dw_im.dta") path("$teamsWrkData") idvars(iso3 year)

* A path under $teamsWrkDataCanonical, $teamsRawDataCanonical or $dwZDrive
* stops with error 459:
*   [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to canonical (Teams)
*   deposit [<root>]. Pass -allow_canonical_write- to override (DBM bootstraps only).
dw_save , filename("dw_im.dta") path("$teamsWrkDataCanonical") ///
    idvars(iso3 year) allow_canonical_write



R and Python guard a few more roots than Stata does; the exact list is in Appendix C.






In R and Python the same guard also runs a producer-side pre-flight: in producer mode, a non-canonical (sandbox) write needs at least one of the Teams or Z: mirrors to be reachable, so a deposit never ends up living only on the producer’s laptop. Producer outputs are redundant by design. Every producer write fans out to both mirrors when they are available, and the Z: carbon copy is what later lets a reviewer check that Teams equals Z:.





3.4.2 Guard 2: reviewer mode forbids live API calls (dw_require_no_api)

Languages: Stata. R: defined by the generated profile; Python: defined by the generated profile. See the coverage matrix.
The second guard sits at every entry point that would reach the network. There are two of them:

dw_api_fetch reads the cache first. Only when there is no cache (or the producer passed refresh = TRUE) does it check dw_apis_allowed, before any HTTP request; in reviewer mode it stops with the [cso_toolkit.dw_api] envelope. A reviewer reads the frozen cache with dw_api_cached instead.
dw_require_no_api is the explicit assertion for any script that reaches a remote without going through dw_api_fetch. Call it at the top of such a script. In a Stata pipeline it is the only check there is, so call it before every network operation.


RPythonStata


# At the top of a script that calls a remote directly
# (dw_require_no_api is defined by the generated profile):
dw_require_no_api(context = "ed/06_pull_uis")
#> Error: [X] External API access is forbidden in reviewer mode. Context: ed/06_pull_uis

# dw_api_fetch with no cache, in reviewer mode:
dw_api_fetch("uis", cache_key = "uis_entrance_age_primary")
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls.
#>   Call:   dw_api_fetch('uis', cache_key='uis_entrance_age_primary')
#>   Reason: cache missing at .../_apis/uis/uis_entrance_age_primary.csv
#>   Fix:
#>     1. The expected workflow is that a Database Manager has already populated the cache under teamsRawDataCanonical/_apis/. Verify the cache file exists at the path above.
#>     2. If you ARE the producer, switch modes: set dw_mode: producer in user_config.yml and re-source the profile.

# Read the frozen cache instead:
dw_api_cached("uis", cache_key = "uis_entrance_age_primary")


dw_require_no_api(context="ed/06_pull_uis")   # defined by the generated profile
# PermissionError: [X] External API access is forbidden in reviewer mode. Context: ed/06_pull_uis

# dw_api_fetch with no cache raises PermissionError with the same envelope
# as R; only fix 2 differs: _state.configure(dw_mode="producer", dw_apis_allowed=True)
dw_api_cached("uis", cache_key="uis_entrance_age_primary")


* Assert the contract just before a live network call:
dw_require_no_api , context("ed/06_pull_uis")
* Reviewer mode aborts with error 459:
*   [cso_toolkit.dw_require_no_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls
*     (context: ed/06_pull_uis).
*   Why: reviewer sessions must read frozen producer caches to preserve
*     vintage permanence; any live API call breaks provenance.
*   Fix: switch the call to dw_use() against the frozen cache, or
*     re-run in producer mode.



All of these block in reviewer mode and pass silently for a producer. dw_api_fetch and the Stata dw_require_no_api raise the toolkit’s full envelope; the profile-defined R and Python dw_require_no_api prints a one-line [X] message, since it is the profile’s helper rather than the package’s (Profiles and the mode switch shows its definition).






The Stata guard has a subtlety: an unset mode passes. It blocks only when $dw_mode is "reviewer"; "producer" and any empty or unknown value pass silently. This is deliberate, since a stray script never falsely blocks a producer, but it means the profile must set dw_mode correctly. The no-default rule closes the gap: an unconfigured session stops when the profile loads (dw_load_config stops with error 459), before it ever reaches a guard.
