title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
text:
3.6 The publisher and dw_publish

Languages: R. Python: Planned (#15); Stata: n/a (API-side capability). See the coverage matrix.
PRODUCER and REVIEWER are fully wired into the mode contract; PUBLISHER only partly. One piece of the role is code: dw_publish(path, indicator, vintage, sector, endpoint = "helix", dry_run = TRUE). Where dw_save writes a file to the Teams folder and its Z: mirror, dw_publish submits a file that already exists to Helix through its API; calling the canonical write “publish” confuses the two.
It already enforces the call-site contract: a reviewer-mode call stops before any I/O ([cso_toolkit.dw_publish] Reviewer mode forbids API submissions to 'helix'.); path, indicator, vintage and sector must each be a single non-empty string; the artefact must exist on disk; and the endpoint allowlist admits only "helix".
What it does not yet do is submit. It is a dry-run stub: dry_run = TRUE validates the call and returns status = "dry_run" with the payload a live submission would send, including the file’s sha256; dry_run = FALSE stops with an envelope pointing at issue #15, where the Helix endpoint contract is being negotiated with sector leads. The publisher’s transport (to Helix, SDMX, the data portal and the SoWC tables) and its other boundaries are still enforced by procedure and review: a contract honoured mostly by hand, with the mechanical version arriving one helper at a time.
crumbs: 3  Roles and the mode contract

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
section: 3.7 Collaboration model: single- and multi-producer projects
text:
3.7 Collaboration model: single- and multi-producer projects
Everything above assumes one producer per deposit. Co-authored research projects do not work like that: several people produce code and results, and who produces and who reviews changes over time. JP produces while Karen reviews, and a month later they swap. The toolkit handles this with a second setting beside dw_mode rather than inside it.

3.7.1 Modes are per session; the collaboration model is per project

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.










Setting
Question
Where it lives
Who sets it
Values




dw_mode
Is this session producing or reviewing?
~/.config/user_config.yml (personal, never committed)
each person, as often as their role changes
producer, reviewer


collaboration
How many people may produce in this project?
cso_project.yml at the repository root (committed)
the project, in one reviewed commit
single-producer, multi-producer



A missing cso_project.yml means single-producer, so existing projects need no change. The file is short (template: templates/cso_project.yml):
schema: cso_project/1
collaboration: multi-producer
collaboration_since: 2026-11-20
members:          # optional, informational
  - jpazevedo
  - kbarnes
The toolkit finds it by walking up from the root you pass, the profile’s rootFolder or the working directory, and stops at the repository root, so a repository without the file never picks up a parent folder’s. The model is resolved once per session and dw_collaboration() returns it. A new repository chooses its model when it is created (Starting a repository).


3.7.2 Why not a third mode or a new role
The obvious alternative was a third session mode (say, co-producer) or a fourth role. It was rejected because a mode cannot be coordinated. Modes are per person, set in a file nobody else sees. If the number of producers were a mode, two co-authors could run under different rules on the same outputs, and a producer session that knew nothing of the other producer would overwrite their work without a trace. The number of producers is a fact about the project, so it belongs in the repository: the same for everyone, changed in one reviewed commit, with a history. Modes keep their meaning.


3.7.3 What multi-producer changes
Only dw_save() behaves differently, and only for an output that already exists and has a provenance sidecar. Reviewer sessions write to their sandbox and are not affected.

Out-of-band change. If the file’s SHA-256 no longer matches the sha256 in its sidecar, someone changed it without dw_save(); replacing it would discard a change nobody recorded, so dw_save() stops. A text output that differs only in line endings (a Windows clone with core.autocrlf=true checks tracked files out with CRLF) is not a change: dw_save() prints a note instead. output/** -text in .gitattributes, which the scaffolders write, keeps tracked outputs byte-exact.
Concurrent write. If the sidecar says another user wrote the file after this session started, two producers may be writing the same output at once, and one would silently overwrite the other, so dw_save() stops. The exception is an output whose file and sidecar are committed and unmodified in git: that write reached this session through a pull or merge, so this one builds on it. Outputs outside git, such as deposits, keep the check.
Otherwise it writes. When the previous writer was someone else, it prints a note, not an error. Handing the producer role back and forth is normal; a guard that fired on every handover would teach people to override it without reading it.

Either stop can be overridden with takeover = TRUE once you have checked what happened, and the override is recorded in the new sidecar. Every sidecar written in a multi-producer project also records its lineage (the previous writer’s hash, user and time, and the git branch and commit); the fields are in Appendix B. Single-producer sidecars are unchanged.
The API cache follows the same rule. An existing cache is read, never replaced, unless the producer passes refresh = TRUE; in a multi-producer project a refresh over another user’s fetch says so and keeps the previous fetch (metadata.previous_fetch) in the new provenance.

RPythonStata


dw_collaboration()
#> [1] "multi-producer"

# Karen changed the file by hand after her last dw_save():
dw_save(df, path = "outputs/table2.csv", overwrite = TRUE, force = TRUE)
#> Error: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to replace outputs/table2.csv.
#>  Why (out-of-band change): the file's SHA-256 (5e1f0c...) no longer matches its
#>  provenance sidecar (a07c9b...): someone changed it without dw_save(), so
#>  replacing it now would discard a change nobody recorded.
#>  Fix:
#>  1. Reconcile first: sync or pull the other change, check the file's history
#>     (git log, the sidecar's user and written_at), and re-run, OR
#>  2. If you have checked it and mean to replace it, pass `takeover = TRUE`;
#>     the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.

dw_save(df, path = "outputs/table2.csv", overwrite = TRUE, force = TRUE,
        takeover = TRUE)


dw_collaboration()
# 'multi-producer'

dw_save(df, path="outputs/table2.csv", overwrite=True)
# PermissionError: [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to
#   replace outputs/table2.csv.
#   Why (out-of-band change): ...
#   Fix: ... pass `takeover=True`; the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.

dw_save(df, path="outputs/table2.csv", overwrite=True, takeover=True)


* The same guards, through Stata's Python integration (Stata 16+):
dw_collaboration                       // $dw_collaboration_model, once per session
dw_save, filename(table2) path("outputs") idvars(iso3 year)
* [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Multi-producer project: refusing to replace ...
*   Fix: ... pass -takeover-; the takeover is recorded in the new sidecar.
dw_save, filename(table2) path("outputs") idvars(iso3 year) takeover
* Without Python a multi-producer write stops unless -takeover- is passed.





3.7.4 How to switch, and why switching midway is safe

Languages: R, Python. Stata: No: switch from R or Python (one reviewed PR). See the coverage matrix.
Switch with dw_set_collaboration(), never by editing the file alone, and commit the result as one pull request that a co-author reviews:

RPython


dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", root = rootFolder,
                     members = c("jpazevedo", "kbarnes"))
#> [cso_toolkit.dw_set_collaboration] wrote .../cso_project.yml: collaboration = multi-producer
#> [cso_toolkit.dw_set_collaboration] baselined 37 of 37 provenance sidecar(s) under ...


dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", root=root_folder,
                     members=["jpazevedo", "kbarnes"])



The call writes cso_project.yml and adds a baseline object (collaboration, at, by) to every existing *.provenance.json under the root, inserted as text so sha256 and every other field keep their bytes. It refuses to run in reviewer mode, because it writes, and a second call changes nothing. Switching back is the same call with the other value.
The switch is a non-event for three reasons:

No mixed rules. The setting is in the repository, so every collaborator moves to the new rules at the same commit, when they pull it.
No flood of alarms. The baseline marks artefacts produced before the switch as project-owned, so the first multi-producer write over each is quiet instead of reporting a change of producer.
No lineage gap. The baseline leaves sha256 untouched, so the first multi-producer write records it as previous_sha256, and the chain starts from the last single-producer state of each file.



3.7.5 A worked example: two co-authors who swap roles
JP and Karen co-author a paper in one repository. Until now JP has produced every table; Karen has reviewed.

The switch. Karen will produce the robustness tables, so JP runs dw_set_collaboration("multi-producer", ...) in a producer session and opens a pull request with cso_project.yml and the baselined sidecars. Karen reviews and merges it.
Karen produces. She sets her own dw_mode to producer, pulls and re-runs 03_robustness.R. Her first write over table3.csv, last written by JP, is quiet because the sidecar carries a baseline; the new sidecar records JP’s hash as previous_sha256.
JP reviews. He sets his dw_mode to reviewer and reproduces her tables in his sandbox. No guard is involved.
They overlap by accident. Both run 02_main.R in producer mode on the shared folder. Karen’s run finishes first, so when JP’s reaches dw_save() for table2.csv the sidecar shows a write after his session started, and it stops. JP pulls, compares, and either re-runs or passes takeover = TRUE, which is recorded.
The roles swap back. A month later JP’s first write over a table Karen last wrote prints a note (“last written by kbarnes; your write follows theirs in its lineage”) and proceeds.

Neither changed the project setting again: who produces is a session matter; how many may produce was settled once, in review. A new co-author needs only their personal block in user_config.yml, with dw_mode: reviewer until they start producing; the project file decides the rest, and they could not override it there if they tried.
crumbs: 3  Roles and the mode contract

title: 3  Roles and the mode contract
text:
3.8 Why this matters
The point of the relay is reproducibility with permanence. A reviewer must run the producer’s exact scripts and get the producer’s exact numbers, which means reading the same frozen caches (each a vintage: the data as they stood when the producer pulled them), never a fresher pull from a live API that has moved on. And the reviewer must do so without any risk of overwriting the deposit under audit. The API guard keeps the reviewer on frozen vintages; the dw_save guard keeps the reviewer’s output in a sandbox. Set dw_mode once, and the same code base behaves as a producer or as a reviewer, without editing a single sector script.
crumbs: 3  Roles and the mode contract

title: 4  Provenance sidecars and the error envelope
text:
4.1 The provenance sidecar
Two small conventions make cso-toolkit outputs trustworthy and its failures readable. The provenance sidecar is a small JSON file written next to every data artefact, recording who wrote it, when, in what mode and with what content hash. The error envelope is a fixed three-part shape that every deliberate error and warning in the toolkit follows, so a failure reads like an instruction rather than a stack trace. Both hold in R, Python and Stata. This chapter explains why each exists and what it guarantees. The fields of the sidecar are listed in Appendix B, and the messages the toolkit raises are catalogued in Appendix C.
Whenever you write a data file through dw_save (The IO contract), the toolkit also writes <path>.provenance.json beside it: write dw_ed_edu.csv and you also get dw_ed_edu.csv.provenance.json. The sidecar is a receipt about the data, readable by a person and by a program, that travels with the artefact into the canonical Teams folder and its Z: mirror.
crumbs: 4  Provenance sidecars and the error envelope

title: 4  Provenance sidecars and the error envelope
text:
4.1.1 Why a sidecar at all
The toolkit exists so that someone other than the author can reproduce an analysis (Why a toolkit, and how it fits together). Reproducibility is not only being able to re-run a pipeline; it is also being able to trust a frozen artefact two years after it was deposited. A reviewer who opens dw_ed_edu.csv from the deposit needs answers the file itself cannot give. Who produced it? In which session mode, producer or reviewer (Roles and the mode contract)? Has it been altered since it was written? What shape was it, and which inputs fed it? The sidecar answers these without touching the data file’s own schema.
The toolkit keeps this record beside the file rather than inside it (as Stata’s char _dta[] or a Parquet key-value footer would). A sidecar wins on three counts:

It works for every format. The same scheme serves CSV, Parquet, DTA, XLSX, JSON and YAML.
It never changes the artefact’s bytes. A content hash of the data file stays stable however rich the metadata grows.
It is easy to review. A sidecar diffs cleanly in a pull request and can be dropped when unwanted.



4.1.2 What it guarantees
The hash describes the bytes on disk. The sidecar is written after the primary file lands, and its sha256 is computed by reading that file back, not from the object in memory. That makes the hash an integrity anchor. Re-hash the file later and compare: a match means the bytes are the ones that were written; a mismatch means someone changed the file outside the toolkit. The toolkit uses this anchor itself. dw_use compares the Teams copy of a canonical file with its Z: mirror on every read, and dw_verify_z does the same on demand (The IO contract). In a multi-producer project, dw_save refuses to replace a file whose bytes no longer match its sidecar (Roles and the mode contract).
Each copy carries its own receipt. When a producer write fans out to the Teams and Z: mirrors, the sidecar is copied with it, so every copy of the artefact can be checked on its own.
Two runs can be compared without reading the data. If the caller records the inputs in the sidecar’s metadata (one record per input file with its SHA-256, which is what dw_fetch_inputs returns), then two sidecars of the same output show whether a new run reproduced the old one: same inputs and the same output hash, or which inputs changed, or (the case that warns) the same inputs but a different output, which only the code or the environment can explain. dw_read_provenance and dw_provenance_diff do this (The IO contract).
The record lives in git while the data stay out. Data live in the deposit; the sidecars that say which bytes each result came from are committed. A reviewer can then tell from the repository alone what produced a result (Checks and CI).
A sidecar never costs you the data. If the metadata hold a value that cannot be written as JSON (an R Date, a NumPy scalar), the sidecar write emits a warning and the primary file stays. The sidecar is metadata about the asset; the asset is what matters. You can also turn the sidecar off for one call (provenance = FALSE; nosidecar in Stata).


4.1.3 Two shapes, one intent
The sidecar dw_save writes describes a write event: the file, its format, its schema, its writer and its hash. When dw_use downloads an allowlisted URL and freezes it for reviewers (a producer-only step; see The external-API contract), it writes a sidecar of a different shape that describes a fetch event: the URL, the hash, the size, and who fetched it and when. Both use the .provenance.json extension and the same hashing, but their keys differ, so do not read one with a parser written for the other.
Stata writes the same sidecar with the same intent, but one difference matters. Stata records the file’s sha256 only through its Python integration (Stata 16+). It always records its native datasignature as well, and without Python that is the only hash. A datasignature is a checksum of the dataset’s values, not of the file’s bytes, so it can never be compared with an R or Python sha256. Appendix B sets out this and the smaller Stata differences field by field.

title: 4  Provenance sidecars and the error envelope
text:
4.2 The error envelope
The toolkit’s second convention governs failure. Every deliberate stop() in R, every raise in Python and every error message in Stata follows one shape:
[cso_toolkit.<fn>] WHAT happened
  Why it happened / why the rule exists.
  Fix:
    1. The first concrete remedy, OR
    2. An alternative remedy / escape hatch.
The bracketed prefix names the function that raised: [cso_toolkit.dw_save], [cso_toolkit.dw_use], [cso_toolkit.dw_api]. The body says why the rule exists rather than restating the symptom. The Fix: block lists what to do next, often ending with the deliberate escape hatch for when you really do mean to do the forbidden thing.

4.2.1 Why one shape
One shape on every error buys three things.

Searchability. The prefix is a stable token you can grep. To find every place in a consumer project that can trip the reviewer-mode write guard, search for [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids. The library’s errors become an index.
Actionability. Because Fix: is mandatory, an error never leaves you knowing what broke without knowing how to proceed. The escape hatch (allow_canonical_write = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE, takeover = TRUE, switching dw_mode) appears at the point of failure, not in a manual.
Triage. A failure prefixed [cso_toolkit.*] is a decision the toolkit made on purpose, usually the contract doing its job rather than a bug. An unprefixed error is something leaking from arrow, haven, pandas or the operating system.



4.2.2 Reading one
The reviewer-mode write refusal, shown in full in Roles and the mode contract, is the envelope at its fullest, and every clause does work. The prefix names dw_save. The WHAT line names the rule and the offending path. The Why line gives the reason the rule exists, vintage permanence: a deposited vintage must never change under the people who rely on it. The Fix block gives the ordinary remedy first (write to your sandbox) and the deliberate override second (allow_canonical_write = TRUE, for a Database Manager’s bootstrap). The numbered options are ranked the same way everywhere: option 1 is the expected remedy, and a later option is usually the escape hatch.


4.2.3 Warnings wear it too
The shape is not kept for fatal errors. Non-fatal warnings use it too, including the ones the sidecar machinery emits. A sidecar that cannot be written warns with [cso_toolkit.dw_save] Provenance sidecar write failed for <path>, says the primary file is unaffected, and tells you how to make the metadata serialisable. A reviewer whose canonical and Z: locations are unreachable, and who falls back to a repository-local copy, gets a [cso_toolkit.dw_use] warning that the fallback breaks provenance and that Teams or Z: should be re-mounted before the output is relied on. The envelope makes even a soft degradation legible.


4.2.4 A tested invariant
The envelope is not only a style guide. The R test suite asserts it with an expect_envelope() helper, which checks for the [cso_toolkit.<fn>] prefix and a Fix: block on each raise the tests trigger; a raise that loses either fails the suite. Python has a script that checks the same on its raise paths, run by hand. Stata keeps the prefix everywhere, but the body is fuller in some commands than others: dw_require_no_api prints the full WHAT / Why / Fix, while the dw_save reviewer-mode refusal fits on one line that names the rule and the -allow_canonical_write- override. Stata’s adherence is kept by convention and review. Consumer repositories assert their own errors the same way (Checks and CI); the details of each test are in Appendix C.

title: 4  Provenance sidecars and the error envelope
section: 4.3 How the two conventions reinforce each other
text:
4.3 How the two conventions reinforce each other
The sidecar and the envelope are two halves of one reproducibility contract. The sidecar makes a successful write describe itself and be checkable afterwards: who, when, in which mode, with what hash and what shape. The envelope makes an unsuccessful operation explain itself at the moment it happens: which function, which rule, why, and how to proceed.
They also lean on each other. Several of the toolkit’s stops are decisions taken by reading a sidecar: the multi-producer guards in dw_save, which compare a file’s bytes with its recorded sha256 and its writer with the current session; the dw_stage stop when a reviewer’s staged copy no longer matches the hash archived beside it; and the warning from dw_provenance_diff when the same inputs gave a different output. Each of those reaches you as an envelope whose Fix points back at the record (check the sidecar’s user and written_at, re-run, or override and have the override recorded in the new sidecar). The sidecar supplies the evidence; the envelope turns it into a decision you can act on.
Together they ensure that a cso-toolkit artefact is never a bare file of unknown origin and a cso-toolkit failure is never a bare exception of unknown cause, in whichever of the three languages a consumer repository uses.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.1 Terms this chapter uses
Every analytics pipeline begins and ends with reading and writing files. In a shared statistical repository an unguarded read_csv or to_csv is a liability: it can silently overwrite a published deposit, leave a producer’s only copy on a laptop, read a stale file with no provenance, or let a duplicate-keyed table into the warehouse. The IO contract is the toolkit’s answer. It is a small family of paired read and write helpers, chiefly dw_save and dw_use, that wrap ordinary language-native IO with three layers of discipline: dispatch on the file extension, path routing that depends on the session mode, and a uniqueness and integrity check at the call site.
The same function names and the same behaviour hold across the languages, so a sector that runs partly in R and partly in Stata uses one mental model on both sides. Where the languages differ in a default, an argument or a format, this chapter says so. Which helper exists in which language is shown in the line under each heading and, in full, in the coverage matrix.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
A canonical deposit is the permanent, published copy of a dataset. Downstream work and external users depend on it, so once it is written for a vintage it must not change.
Deposits live in two shared stores. Teams is the SharePoint-synced library that holds the canonical area; Z: is a network drive that mirrors it byte for byte. The toolkit treats a path under either as canonical.
The session mode is producer (you write new deposits) or reviewer (you read them and write only to a local sandbox). It is set once per session in user_config.yml, never per call; Profiles and the mode switch explains how, and how the profile derives the path globals the helpers resolve through.
The kind argument picks one of three data roots: wrk (working outputs, the global teamsWrkData), raw (inputs, teamsRawData) or meta (metadata, dwMetaData). It defaults to wrk.
An error envelope is the toolkit’s structured failure message: WHAT failed, WHY, and HOW to fix it. Warnings use the same shape. See Provenance sidecars and the error envelope and the error taxonomy.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.2 Auto-dispatch by extension
dw_save and dw_use choose their writer or reader from the file extension. You never name a format; the suffix decides. Switching an output from CSV to parquet is a change to the file name, not to the code.









Extension
R writer / reader
Python writer / reader
Stata




.csv / .tsv / .txt
data.table::fwrite / fread
to_csv / read_csv
.csv read only


.csv.gz / .tsv.gz
fwrite(compress = "gzip")
to_csv(compression="gzip")
—


.xlsx
writexl (or openxlsx for a Workbook) / readxl
openpyxl via pandas
read only


.dta
haven::write_dta / read_dta
to_stata / read_stata
read and write


.rds (R) / .pkl, .pickle (Python)
saveRDS / readRDS
pickle.dump / load
—


.RData / .rda
save() / load()
—
—


.parquet
arrow::write_parquet / read_parquet
to_parquet / read_parquet
—


.json
jsonlite
json / to_json
—


.yml / .yaml
yaml
PyYAML
—



R’s .rds and Python’s .pkl play the same role, a fast native object dump. An .xlsx write takes a data frame, a named list or dict of data frames (one sheet each) or a pre-built workbook; in R, dw_use(..., sheet = NULL) reads every sheet into a named list.






WarningStata reads .dta, .csv and .xlsx, and writes .dta



Parquet, RDS and JSON do not dispatch on the Stata side. A pipeline that needs them routes that step through R or Python and hands Stata a .dta (or .csv). This is a design boundary: keeping the .ado helpers free of external binaries is what keeps them working under AppLocker, the Windows policy on UNICEF laptops that blocks unsigned executables.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.3 Writing: dw_save

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.
dw_save resolves a path, optionally checks that the rows are unique, writes the file, emits a provenance sidecar and, in producer mode, copies the result to the redundant mirrors. It takes a literal path, or, more usefully, a name that it resolves through the mode-aware roots, so the same script lands in the canonical deposit in producer mode and in the local sandbox in reviewer mode with no change to the call. name is the file name, sector the sector folder ("ed", "nt", …), kind the data root, and an optional vintage adds a subfolder between sector and file.

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, path = "out.csv")
dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk")


dw_save(df, path="out.csv")
dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk")


dw_save , filename("dw_ed_edu") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR)



Stata’s calling convention differs. It takes path() and filename() explicitly (a trailing .dta in the file name is dropped and added back), the folder must already exist (create it with dw_mkdir; otherwise error 601), and idvars() is required, so the uniqueness check is never optional. The R and Python name / sector / kind style is resolved by dw_resolve_path, described below.

5.3.1 The uniqueness check: isid
Pass a key tuple and dw_save checks that the declared columns uniquely identify every row before writing anything. Duplicates stop the call with their count and a sample of up to five offending rows, and the table never reaches disk. This is the toolkit’s main guard against a silently double-counted series.

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
                 "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "RESIDENCE", "TIME_PERIOD"))


dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        isid=["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
              "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "RESIDENCE", "TIME_PERIOD"])


dw_save , filename("dw_ed_edu") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
    idvars(DATAFLOW REF_AREA INDICATOR SEX WEALTH_QUINTILE RESIDENCE TIME_PERIOD)



Stata uses its built-in isid, which also fails when a key variable has missing values; R and Python check duplicates only. The same check is available on its own as dw_isid.


5.3.2 Metadata and the provenance sidecar
Every successful write emits a companion <path>.provenance.json recording who wrote the file, when, in which mode, its hash and shape, and the keys checked. Appendix B lists the fields and the few that differ by language; Provenance sidecars and the error envelope explains why the sidecar exists. What you control at the call site is the descriptive metadata, which makes the sidecar self-describing:

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        metadata = list(
          title    = "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
          producer = "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
          sources  = c("UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"),
          contact  = "@karavan88",
          vintage  = "2026-05"
        ))


dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        metadata={
          "title": "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
          "producer": "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.py",
          "sources": ["UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"],
          "vintage": "2026-05",
        })


dw_save , filename("dw_ed_edu") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
    idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR)                          ///
    title("Education indicators")                       ///
    producer("01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/example.do")      ///
    sources("UIS bulk SDG_092025")                      ///
    contact("@karavan88")                               ///
    vintage("2026-05")



In R and Python metadata is a named list or dict and may hold a data frame, such as the input manifest from dw_fetch_inputs, which is written as an array of rows. Stata has dedicated title(), producer(), sources(), contact() and vintage() options, and takes any other fields as semicolon-separated pairs: metadata("key1 value1; key2 value2"). To skip the sidecar, pass provenance = FALSE (R, Python) or nosidecar (Stata).


5.3.3 Mode-aware write routing
Reviewer mode refuses to write to a canonical deposit. A write whose resolved path lands under a canonical Teams root or under the Z: drive stops with an envelope (R stop(), Python PermissionError, Stata error 459), so a published vintage stays permanent. A Database Manager who must seed the deposit from a reviewer session passes allow_canonical_write = TRUE (Python True, Stata the allow_canonical_write option). Roles and the mode contract shows this guard and its message as the first of the two places where the mode is enforced.
Producer mode copies every deposit. A producer’s output must never live only on the producer’s laptop. In R and Python, each successful producer write is copied, with its sidecar, to the Teams canonical equivalent and the Z: equivalent of the path, whichever the profile makes available. When the primary is already in the canonical deposit (the usual case, since a producer’s working roots are the canonical roots), only the Z: copy is needed. Before writing to a non-canonical path, dw_save checks that at least one mirror is configured and stops if neither is, because the deposit would not be recoverable. A mirror copy that fails after the primary write is a warning tagged “Teams mirror” or “Z: mirror”; it does not roll back the primary. Stata’s dw_save writes only the primary .dta and its sidecar.
A legacy mirror_to_z argument is still accepted by R and Python but ignored with a deprecation warning: mirroring is automatic.
In a project set to collaboration: multi-producer, dw_save also refuses to replace an output that was changed outside dw_save or written by another user after your session started, unless you pass takeover. Roles and the mode contract describes the collaboration model and these guards.


5.3.4 The overwrite gate
dw_save will not silently replace an existing deposit, and the default depends on the language:

R. overwrite = NULL (the default) resolves to TRUE in reviewer mode, because the sandbox is gitignored and safe to re-run, and to FALSE in producer mode or when no mode is set.
Python. overwrite=False in every mode, so a reviewer re-run also needs overwrite=True.
Stata. No overwrite option: save, replace always replaces the primary, and the canonical deposits are protected by the reviewer-mode guard instead.

When the gate is closed, it checks every destination the write will touch (the primary and, for a producer, the Teams and Z: mirrors) and stops if any already exists (Python raises FileExistsError). Pass overwrite = TRUE to replace.
R adds one more stage. Overwriting an existing producer deposit counts as destructive even with overwrite = TRUE: interactively dw_save asks [y/N]; non-interactively it stops unless you also pass force = TRUE for a deliberate automated re-deposit.


5.3.5 Other writing behaviours

Atomic writes. R and Python write to a .tmp sibling and rename it into place, so a crash never leaves a half-written file under the final name. R retries the rename a few times, because OneDrive sync or a virus scan can hold the destination briefly; a file open in Excel still makes it fail. R and Python create missing folders. Stata writes with save, replace into a folder that must exist, and runs compress first unless you pass nocompress.
Compression. For CSV, TSV and TXT, compress = TRUE appends .gz and gzips the file. A path that already ends in .gz turns compression on by itself, so you cannot ask for .gz and get an uncompressed file.
CSV dialect (R). dialect = "base" writes through utils::write.table and reproduces the bytes of legacy utils::write.csv() output, for sector scripts that depend on them; the default "fwrite" uses data.table. "base" cannot be combined with compress = TRUE and says so.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.4 Reading: dw_use

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.
dw_use is the read counterpart: the same path resolution and the same extension dispatch. R returns a tibble by default (as = "data.frame" or as = "data.table" changes that); Python returns a pandas DataFrame for tabular formats; Stata loads the dataset into memory, replacing the one there.

RPythonStata


edu <- dw_use(name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk")
edu <- dw_use(path = "C:/path/to/file.parquet")


edu = dw_use(name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk")
edu = dw_use(path="/path/to/file.parquet")


dw_use , filename("dw_ed_edu") path("$teamsWrkData/ed")



In Stata a file name without an extension is read as .dta, and path() may be left out when filename() is a full path. Stata reads a .csv with every column as text and then converts each column that is wholly numeric, one column at a time, so one stray value leaves only its own column as a string.

5.4.1 Mode-aware read routing
Reads branch on the mode too, in the opposite direction: the goal is provenance, not protection.

Producer mode, or no mode (local first). Read the literal path. If it is missing and fallback_canonical is on (the default), swap the working root for its canonical one (teamsRawData for teamsRawDataCanonical, and so on) and read the canonical copy.
Reviewer mode (network first). Read the Teams canonical equivalent, then the Z: mirror, then the local copy. The local step warns, because a reviewer reading a local copy is reading bytes of unverified provenance. If the file is in none of the three places, dw_use stops and points the reviewer at the sector producer. fallback_canonical = FALSE (Stata nofallback_canonical) disables the local step so the read fails fast.



5.4.2 Remote URLs: fetched once, then frozen

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (no remote-URL reads in Stata). See the coverage matrix.
dw_use also accepts an http(s) URL, under two rules. The URL must match a pattern in the profile’s dw_url_allowlist; an empty or unset list allows none. And the file is downloaded only once: the first read saves it under the frozen-cache root with its own provenance sidecar, and every later read uses that copy. The root is the profile’s dw_frozen_root, or <githubFolder>/_frozen, or _frozen in the working directory, in that order. Commit the frozen file and its sidecar so later runs are deterministic. A reviewer never downloads: a missing frozen copy stops with an envelope that says a producer must freeze it first.

RPython


# In the profile:
dw_url_allowlist <- c(dw_default_unicef_allowlist(),
                      "^https://yourorg\\.github\\.io/")
dw_frozen_root   <- file.path(githubFolder, "_frozen")

# In a script:
codes <- dw_use("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/unicef-drp/<repo>/main/codes.csv")


_state.configure(dw_url_allowlist=[*dw_default_unicef_allowlist(),
                                   r"^https://yourorg\.github\.io/"])
codes = dw_use("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/unicef-drp/<repo>/main/codes.csv")



dw_default_unicef_allowlist() returns the patterns for UNICEF DRP repositories on GitHub. Live API calls are a different mechanism, covered in The external-API contract.


5.4.3 Column subsetting: strict and lenient
dw_use accepts cols to restrict the read. Whether a requested column that is missing from the file is an error depends on the format:









Format
R
Python
Stata




.parquet, .dta
error
error
.dta: error


.csv
warns and skips it
error
cols() ignored


.xlsx
keeps the columns present
keeps the columns present
cols() ignored



R adds cols_lenient = TRUE, which means “select if present”. It reads only the file’s schema (parquet metadata, or a header-only read of .dta, .csv or .xlsx), keeps the requested columns that exist, and reads all columns with a warning if none do. This gives sector scripts the intent of dplyr::any_of() inside dw_use, where calling any_of() directly fails under tidyselect 1.2.0 and later.

RPythonStata


# Strict (default): errors if a requested column is missing
df <- dw_use(path = parquet_path, cols = c("REF_AREA", "OBS_VALUE"))

# Lenient: keep only the requested columns the file has
df <- dw_use(path = parquet_path,
             cols = c("REF_AREA", "OBS_VALUE", "MAYBE_PRESENT_COL"),
             cols_lenient = TRUE)


df = dw_use(path=parquet_path, cols=["REF_AREA", "OBS_VALUE"])


dw_use , filename("dw_ed_edu.dta") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
    cols(REF_AREA OBS_VALUE)





5.4.4 The Z: integrity check
When a read resolves to a canonical file and Z: is available, dw_use compares the Teams copy with its Z: mirror. By default this is a fast size check; a mismatch warns, and the read still completes with the Teams data. verify_z = "sha256" compares hashes instead, and verify_z = FALSE (Stata verify_z(off)) skips the check. Stata’s deep check compares datasignature values and works only for .dta.
Stata’s dw_use also compares the datasignature recorded in a .dta file’s sidecar with the data it has just loaded. A mismatch prints a note and the read completes; the outcome is returned in r(prov_status).

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.5 The resolver and lower-level helpers

5.5.1 dw_isid: the uniqueness check on its own

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Embedded in dw_save (no standalone command). See the coverage matrix.
The check dw_save runs is callable by itself, to validate an in-memory frame mid-pipeline:

RPython


dw_isid(df, keys = c("REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"))


dw_isid(df, keys=["REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"])



On failure it stops with the duplicate count and up to five offending rows. It also catches a key column that does not exist in the data.


5.5.2 dw_verify_z: the Z: mirror check

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (integrity via datasignature inside dw_use). See the coverage matrix.
dw_verify_z(path, compare = "size") returns a status rather than stopping, so the caller decides what a mismatch means: match_size, size_mismatch, match_sha256, sha256_mismatch, z_missing or no_z_mirror (and, in R, verify_unavailable when the hash cannot be computed). It is the building block behind dw_use’s automatic check.


5.5.3 dw_root and dw_resolve_path: building paths

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
dw_root("wrk" | "raw" | "meta") returns one of the three data roots, already resolved for the current mode, so a sector script can build paths without knowing whether it runs as producer or reviewer:
final_path <- file.path(dw_root("wrk"), "nt", "2025", "dw_nut.csv")
When the profile has not set the root, R returns NA and Python returns None.

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Internal to dw_use / dw_save. See the coverage matrix.
dw_resolve_path(name =, sector =, kind =, vintage =) is the full path builder that dw_save and dw_use call internally. It also accepts path = relative to the root. It stops with an envelope when the root’s global is not set, which usually means the profile has not been sourced.


5.5.4 dw_stage: reviewer sandbox staging

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (a Stata reviewer reads canonical inputs in place). See the coverage matrix.
dw_stage is an opt-in reviewer helper that copies a canonical input into the local sandbox once and hash-guards the copy with a <path>.staged.json sidecar. Outside reviewer mode it does nothing. Its lifecycle has five states:

First stage. The sandbox copy is missing: copy from the first available source (Z: before Teams), re-hash the copy against the source (one retry, then stop), and archive the hash.
Clean later run. The sandbox copy matches its archived hash: skip the copy and return the sandbox path.
Sandbox drift. The staged copy was changed out of band: stop with the SANDBOX DRIFT envelope.
Forced re-stage. overwrite = TRUE re-copies, re-checks and re-archives unconditionally.
Upstream changed. The canonical source has moved on: warn, but do not refresh, because rolling canonical inputs forward is the reviewer’s decision.

When both Z: and Teams hold the file, they are hash-compared before either is used; if they disagree, staging stops with a canonical-integrity error.
One known limit is tracked in open issue #226: in a reviewer session whose teamsFolder is not redirected to a sandbox, dw_stage can target the canonical folder itself. The standard profiles always redirect it.
You rarely call dw_stage directly; dw_use calls it, per call or for the session:

RPython


df <- dw_use(name = "dw_nut.csv", sector = "nt", kind = "wrk", stage = TRUE)

# For the session, in the profile:
#   dw_autostage <- TRUE


df = dw_use(name="dw_nut.csv", sector="nt", kind="wrk", stage=True)

# For the session:
#   _state.configure(dw_autostage=True)



dw_use(..., stage = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE) passes overwrite on to force a re-stage. Staging never applies to URLs. R and Python write the same sidecar, so a file staged in one verifies in the other. The .staged.json sidecar is kept separate from dw_save’s .provenance.json, so a file both written and staged carries both; dw_stage refuses a .staged.json whose type is not dw_stage.


5.5.5 dw_fetch_inputs and dw_check_deposit: inputs kept out of Git

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python (#152). See the coverage matrix.
Some pipelines keep their raw inputs out of Git (Consult-tool exports, licensed microdata, large deliveries) in a gitignored folder of the repository. The copy that makes such a run reproducible is the one in the deposit, so the toolkit treats the deposit as the source of truth. The local folder mirrors a deposit folder: <repo>/<rel_dir> corresponds to <teamsFolderCanonical>/<rel_dir> on Teams and <dwZDrive>/<rel_dir> on Z:. Pass teams_root or z_root to use other roots.
dw_fetch_inputs runs at the top of such a pipeline. It:

lists the input files matching pattern, locally and in the deposit folder on Teams and Z:, and stops when Teams and Z: hold different versions of a file (the rule dw_stage applies);
copies deposit-only files into the local folder, Z: preferred, each copy SHA-256-checked and moved into place by an atomic rename, or, with copy = FALSE, returns the deposit paths to read in place;
with gitkeep = TRUE (the default), creates the local folder and every local or deposit subfolder with an empty .gitkeep, so the layout stays visible although the data are gitignored (the .gitignore needs !<rel_dir>/**/ and !<rel_dir>/**/.gitkeep exceptions); .gitkeep files are never inputs;
finishes with dw_check_deposit, so a local file missing from the deposit, or different from it, stops the run.

It returns the input manifest: one row per input with file, path (what to read), sha256, origin (local, copied from Z:, copied from Teams, read from Z: or read from Teams) and the Teams and Z: status.

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python (#152). See the coverage matrix.
dw_check_deposit(paths, local_root, rel_dir) can also be called on its own. A file passes when an identical copy exists on Teams or Z: and no existing copy differs, so an unmounted Z: is fine when Teams matches. stop_on_fail = FALSE returns the per-file report (match, differs, missing, no access) instead of stopping. Both functions only read the deposit and write only under the local folder, so they behave the same in producer and reviewer sessions.

RPython


rel <- "02_consultations/023_targets/inputs"
manifest <- dw_fetch_inputs(
  local_root = file.path(projectFolder, rel),
  rel_dir    = rel,
  pattern    = "_20(23|24|25)\\.(csv|txt)$"
)
inputs <- lapply(manifest$path, readr::read_csv)


import pandas as pd
from cso_toolkit import dw_fetch_inputs

rel = "02_consultations/023_targets/inputs"
manifest = dw_fetch_inputs(
    local_root=f"{project_folder}/{rel}",
    rel_dir=rel,
    pattern=r"_20(23|24|25)\.(csv|txt)$",
)
inputs = [pd.read_csv(p) for p in manifest["path"]]



A Stata pipeline runs the fetch once from R or Python and then reads the fetched files from the local folder with dw_use.
Record the manifest in the outputs’ sidecars, with dw_save(..., metadata = list(inputs = manifest[, c("file", "sha256", "origin")])), so each output names the exact inputs it was built from; dw_provenance_diff (below) reads that record back.

title: 5  The IO contract
text:
5.6 Comparing and joining

5.6.1 dw_compare: what changed since the last deposit

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.
dw_compare keys two datasets on by and classifies rows as added (in current, not in reference), removed (the reverse) and changed (in both, with a differing value column). Numeric columns compare within a tolerance. R and Python treat the missing-value spellings "", "NA", "N/A", "NULL" and "." as equal; Stata compares strings exactly. R and Python return a list with a one-row summary and the added, removed and changed frames, and with write_report_to also write a CSV per part.

RPythonStata


report <- dw_compare(
  current   = dw_use(name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk"),
  reference = dw_use(path = file.path(teamsWrkDataCanonical, "ed/dw_ed_edu.csv")),
  by         = c("DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
                 "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "TIME_PERIOD"),
  value_cols = c("OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"),
  numeric_value_cols = "OBS_VALUE",
  write_report_to = file.path(tempdir(), "ed_compare")
)
report$summary


report = dw_compare(
    current=dw_use(name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk"),
    reference=dw_use(path=ref_path),
    by=["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
        "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "TIME_PERIOD"],
    value_cols=["OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"],
    numeric_value_cols=["OBS_VALUE"],
)
report["summary"]


* compares two .dta files on disk
dw_compare , current("dw_ed_edu.dta") reference("ref_dw_ed_edu.dta") ///
    idvars(DATAFLOW REF_AREA INDICATOR SEX WEALTH_QUINTILE TIME_PERIOD) ///
    valuevars(OBS_VALUE) tol(0.00001) label("ed_dw_edu")



The languages differ in four ways:

Arguments. R and Python take value_cols and numeric_value_cols; Stata takes valuevars() and decides numeric or string comparison from each variable’s storage type.
Tolerance. The default is 1e-5 in R and Python and 1e-8 in Stata, so set tol explicitly when it matters.
A first deposit. R treats a missing or unreadable reference as empty, with a warning, so every current row reports as added. Python raises FileNotFoundError for a missing reference path (pass an empty DataFrame for a first deposit), and Stata stops with error 601.
Output. Stata prints a console summary and, with report(), writes a short Markdown file of row counts and per-column change counts, sized for a publication-gate check.

When the counts are not enough. diagnose = TRUE adds a profile, also available on its own as dw_diff_profile(cmp, by, numeric_value_cols).

Languages: R, Python. Stata: No: r(col_changed) gives the per-column counts (#111). See the coverage matrix.
It turns “36,334 changed” into a diagnosis: which value columns differ, most first; how far each numeric column moved where it changed (absolute and relative q50, q90, q99 and max); and which key values the changed, added and removed rows concentrate on. It prints these and, with write_report_to, also writes <label>_profile.txt. In DW-Production’s ed sector this showed that an alarming mismatch was a population-weight difference, not an aggregation regression: the top column was POP_COVERAGE, every changed row was a regional aggregate, and the median relative drift was 0.01%. Stata returns the per-column counts in r(col_changed).
report <- dw_compare(result, canonical_path, by = key,
                     numeric_value_cols = "OBS_VALUE", diagnose = TRUE)
report$profile$columns     # column, n_changed
report$profile$magnitude   # abs_/rel_ q50, q90, q99, max per numeric column
report$profile$keys        # key, value, n, pct among the changed rows
Never compare a file with itself. In reviewer mode dw_use reads a sandbox path network-first from the canonical deposit, so dw_compare(sandbox_path, canonical_path) would read the deposit on both sides and report a false “0 changed”. When both arguments resolve to the same file, dw_compare stops with an envelope (#111); Stata compares the literal paths. Pass the new output as an in-memory data frame instead.


5.6.2 dw_read_provenance and dw_provenance_diff: did this run reproduce the last one?

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python (#152). See the coverage matrix.

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python (#152). See the coverage matrix.
dw_compare says which records moved. dw_provenance_diff answers the question before it, from the dw_save sidecars alone and without reading any data: did the new run reproduce the previous one? dw_read_provenance reads an output’s sidecar (or returns NULL / None when there is none); read the previous one before the new run overwrites the output. dw_provenance_diff then compares the inputs through the metadata$inputs record (file and sha256 per input, the shape of the dw_fetch_inputs manifest) and the outputs through sha256, and returns a status:

reproduced: the same inputs and a byte-identical output;
inputs_changed: input files were added, removed or changed; the three lists are returned;
output_changed: the same inputs but a different output, which only the code or the environment can explain; it warns with an envelope;
first_run: there is no previous sidecar;
no_input_record: a sidecar has no input record, so only the output hashes are compared.


RPython


previous <- dw_read_provenance(out_csv)      # NULL on the first run
dw_save(result, path = out_csv, isid = key,
        metadata = list(inputs = manifest[, c("file", "sha256", "origin")]))
run <- dw_provenance_diff(previous, out_csv)
run$status                                   # e.g. "reproduced"


previous = dw_read_provenance(out_csv)       # None on the first run
dw_save(result, path=out_csv, isid=key,
        metadata={"inputs": manifest[["file", "sha256", "origin"]]})
run = dw_provenance_diff(previous, out_csv)
run["status"]                                # e.g. "reproduced"



Stata sidecars record sha256 when Stata’s Python integration is available, so dw_provenance_diff can compare Stata outputs too. It never stops on a difference; only a missing or invalid current sidecar is an error. The status is yours to act on: log it, fail a CI job on output_changed, or follow up with dw_compare.


5.6.3 dw_merge: a join that checks its cardinality

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
dw_merge is a left join that checks its cardinality. You declare how as m:1 (the default), 1:1, 1:m or m:m, and the helper warns when the duplication of the keys on either side differs from what you declared, in either direction. That catches the silent fan-out that turns a clean join into a row explosion. using can be a data frame or a path, which is read with dw_use.

RPython


enriched <- dw_merge(
  edu_sdg_uis,
  using = file.path(teamsRawData, "ed/metadata/regions.csv"),
  by    = "ISO3",
  how   = "m:1"
)


enriched = dw_merge(
    edu_sdg_uis,
    using=os.path.join(_state.teamsRawData, "ed/metadata/regions.csv"),
    by=["ISO3"],
    how="m:1",
)



Stata’s own merge m:1 already takes the cardinality, and stops rather than warns when the data disagree.

title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.1 Why a wrapper at all
A reproducible analysis must re-run today and produce the numbers it produced last month, even if a statistical agency has since revised its figures, renamed an indicator or gone down for maintenance. Most analytics code reaches for live data with bare calls to jsonlite::fromJSON(), rsdmx::readSDMX(), wbstats::wb_data(), httr::GET(), requests.get() or wbgapi. Each such call depends silently on the network and on whatever the server happens to serve at that moment. The external-API contract removes that dependency. It gives every consumer of cso-toolkit one mode-aware wrapper that fetches once, freezes the result to a provenance-stamped cache, and reads from the frozen copy thereafter.
Two session modes govern the network. A producer session may hit the live API and populate the cache; a reviewer session reads the frozen cache and may not touch the network at all. The Database Manager, the producer who owns the deposit, decides when each cache is refreshed. Roles and the mode contract defines the roles; this chapter shows how the API wrapper enforces them.
A direct API call ties together three concerns that belong apart: what you want (an indicator, a codelist, a flow), how you reach it (the package, the URL shape, the authentication), and when it was last retrieved. The wrapper separates them. You name the source with a short api = string and the result with a stable cache_key. The wrapper picks the right package, builds the URL, writes the result to disk and records where it came from. A sector script stops being a tangle of bespoke HTTP and becomes a list of named fetches. In DW-Production, fourteen hand-coded SDMX codelist requests became a small manifest table and one loop over dw_api_fetch(api = "sdmx_codelist", ...).

title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.2 The three entry points
dw_api_fetch(api, cache_key, ...) does the work. It checks the cache first; on a miss it either fetches live (producer) or stops (reviewer). Besides api and cache_key it takes refresh, ext, metadata and takeover (the last only matters in multi-producer projects), and passes every other argument to the fetcher for that source.

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python. See the coverage matrix.
dw_api_cached(api, cache_key, ext = "csv") reads a cache and never touches the network, whatever the mode. It reads only the canonical root (teamsRawDataCanonical), never the reviewer sandbox. Its ext defaults to "csv", not to the source’s default format, so a cache stored as RDS or pickle needs ext = "rds" (R) or ext="pkl" (Python). A missing cache stops in R and raises FileNotFoundError in Python; the message says that an ext mismatch is a common cause.

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python. See the coverage matrix.
dw_api_inventory(api = NULL) lists what has been cached, so the Database Manager can audit freshness (see Auditing what is cached below).

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python. See the coverage matrix.

RPython


# Fetch (or read the cache): one named source, one stable cache key.
entrance_age_primary <- dw_api_fetch(
  api       = "uis",
  endpoint  = "indicators",
  params    = list(indicator = "299905"),
  cache_key = "uis_entrance_age_primary"
)

# Cache-only read; never hits the network, stops if absent.
lp <- dw_api_cached(api = "wb", cache_key = "wb_learning_poverty_primary")

# What is already cached?
dw_api_inventory("wb")


from cso_toolkit import dw_api_fetch, dw_api_cached, dw_api_inventory

entrance_age_primary = dw_api_fetch(
    api="uis",
    endpoint="indicators",
    params={"indicator": "299905"},
    cache_key="uis_entrance_age_primary",
)

# Raises FileNotFoundError if no cache exists.
lp = dw_api_cached(api="wb", cache_key="wb_learning_poverty_primary")

dw_api_inventory("wb")

title: 6  The external-API contract
section: 6.3 The mode contract, applied to the network
text:
6.3 The mode contract, applied to the network
dw_api_fetch has no mode = argument. The session decides. Before it reaches the network the wrapper tests dw_apis_allowed, which the profile sets to true exactly when dw_mode is producer; Profiles and the mode switch shows where both come from. A standalone Python example that skips the profile has to set dw_apis_allowed=True itself, as the worked example below does.








Session
Cache state
Action




Producer
cache present, refresh = FALSE
reads the cache


Producer
cache missing or refresh = TRUE
hits the live API, writes the cache through dw_save, returns the result


Reviewer
cache present, refresh = FALSE
reads the cache


Reviewer
cache missing or refresh = TRUE
stops with the [cso_toolkit.dw_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls. envelope (stop() in R, PermissionError in Python)



The cache lookup has two tiers. On a call without refresh, the wrapper looks in the producer sandbox (teamsRawData) first and then in the canonical deposit (teamsRawDataCanonical), so a reviewer reads the frozen deposit even when no sandbox copy exists. The IO contract introduces both roots.
refresh = TRUE is the producer’s way to re-pull a source on purpose. It skips the lookup, fetches live and replaces the existing cache; the wrapper passes the overwrite confirmation to dw_save for you. In a reviewer session the same call stops, and the envelope’s Reason line still reads cache missing at <path>, even when the cache is there: it is the refresh that was refused. In a multi-producer project, a refresh that replaces another user’s fetch says so and keeps that fetch’s sha256, user and fetched_at as metadata.previous_fetch in the new sidecar (Appendix B).
The lockout message names the call, the path it expected and two ways forward: check that the Database Manager has populated the canonical cache, or, if you are the producer, switch the session to producer mode. A script that reaches a remote outside the wrapper should call the reviewer gate dw_require_no_api() first; it is described in Profiles and the mode switch.

The two languages differ in what happens to extra arguments. R passes them through ... to the underlying call (httr::GET(), readr::read_csv(), rsdmx::readSDMX() and so on). title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.5 The cache and its provenance
Every fetch writes two files, at a fixed place keyed by api and cache_key:
<rawdata>/_apis/<api>/<cache_key>.<ext>
<rawdata>/_apis/<api>/<cache_key>.<ext>.provenance.json
The cache_key is the file name, so make it readable snake_case that carries the distinguishing parameters: wb_learning_poverty_primary or sdmx_codelist_UNICEF_CL_RESIDENCE_1_0, not a hash. The wrapper writes the cache through dw_save and reads it back through dw_use, so the cache inherits the mode-aware write path, the Z: mirror when the drive is mapped, and the standard .provenance.json sidecar (The IO contract; fields in Appendix B).
To the sidecar’s standard fields, dw_api_fetch adds a metadata block that records how the cache was obtained:
"metadata": {
  "api": "sdmx_codelist",
  "cache_key": "sdmx_codelist_UNICEF_CL_RESIDENCE_1_0",
  "fetched_at": "2026-05-25T14:23:11+0000",
  "elapsed_secs": 0.412,
  "refresh_flag": false,
  "fetch_args": {"agency": "UNICEF", "codelist": "CL_RESIDENCE", "version": "1.0"}
}
fetch_args lets a reviewer, or a later producer, see exactly which parameters produced the frozen result. fetched_at and elapsed_secs give its age and its cost, and refresh_flag says whether it was a first fetch or a deliberate re-pull. Whatever you pass as metadata = is merged on top, which is how a load-bearing fetch carries a reason, a ticket or a vintage into the sidecar.
The two languages treat credentials differently. Python replaces the value of any fetch_args key whose name looks sensitive (it contains token, auth, password, secret, api_key, headers, cookie, bearer or a similar substring) with "<redacted>" before the sidecar is written. R stores fetch_args as passed, so a credential you pass through ... in R ends up in the sidecar.
Caches never expire on their own. A refresh is always an explicit refresh = TRUE, and the Database Manager owns the cadence for each cache.
A CSV cache is an ordinary CSV file, so a Stata script reads it like any other, with dw_use:
dw_use, filename("wb_learning_poverty_primary.csv") path("$teamsRawData/_apis/wb")

title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.6 Auditing what is cached
dw_api_inventory walks teamsRawDataCanonical/_apis/, skips the sidecars, and returns one row per cache file with the columns api, cache_key, ext, size_bytes, mtime and fetched_at. It takes fetched_at from the sidecar’s metadata (falling back to written_at), so stale caches stand out. It lists the canonical root only, and returns an empty frame when nothing is cached there.

RPython


dw_api_inventory()
#   api cache_key                   ext size_bytes mtime               fetched_at
# 1 wb  wb_learning_poverty_primary csv 142136     2026-05-23 16:42:31 2026-05-23T16:42:31+0000


inv = dw_api_inventory()
# DataFrame columns: api / cache_key / ext / size_bytes / mtime / fetched_at

title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.7 When a live fetch fails
A live fetch can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with your code. In Python every fetcher goes through one HTTP helper that turns a timeout into TimeoutError, a connection failure into ConnectionError and an HTTP error status into RuntimeError. Each message carries the method, the URL and a fix; the status error adds the code and the first 300 characters of the response body. R fetchers raise the underlying package’s error (for example from httr::stop_for_status()), without the [cso_toolkit.*] prefix. Appendix C shows the messages and how to tell a blocked call from a failed one.






WarningAPI failures are about the network, not your cache_key



A timeout or a 403 can only happen on a live fetch: in producer mode, on a cache miss or with refresh = TRUE. A reviewer never sees one, because a reviewer never reaches the network. A recurring burst of 403s from the UNICEF SDMX endpoint is an upstream rate limit, not a wrapper bug. Retry later or from a different network, then commit the frozen cache.

title: 6  The external-API contract
text:
6.8 Migrating a sector script
Adopt the contract one call at a time:

Find each raw API call: fromJSON, readSDMX, wbstats::wb_data and httr::GET/POST in R; requests.get, httpx.get, sdmx.Client and wbgapi calls in Python.
Pick the matching api = value from the tables above.
Choose a stable, descriptive snake_case cache_key that carries the distinguishing parameters. It becomes the file name.
Replace the call with dw_api_fetch(api = ..., cache_key = ..., ...). Give load-bearing fetches a metadata = argument (a reason, a ticket, a vintage) so that context reaches the sidecar.
Run once in producer mode to populate the cache.
Open a pull request. The script passes when a reviewer session can run it end to end from the cache with no network access.

The contract auditor confirms that no raw network calls remain; it and its place in CI are described in Checks and CI.

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
7.1 The core aggregator: aggregate_data_v2
Aggregation is the step where many country-level observations collapse into a few regional or global numbers. It is also where most reproducibility bugs hide: an unweighted mean where a population-weighted one was intended, a “global” figure built from countries that hold a third of the world’s children, a regional rate that silently dropped every country missing the denominator. The aggregation contract exists to make these decisions explicit, auditable and the same in every language a sector team uses.
The contract has two layers. At the bottom sits aggregate_data_v2(), a grouped aggregator that returns each value together with the coverage figures needed to judge whether it can be trusted. On top sit helpers, each pairing one recurring problem with one function: apply_time_window() picks the latest observation in a window, dw_nestweight() redistributes weights over missing rows, dw_pop() fetches population denominators and dw_regions() produces UNICEF regional aggregates. generate_agg_footnote() turns the coverage figures into the caption that travels with the result.
Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
aggregate_data_v2() takes a long data frame, one observation per row, and returns one row per group, a group being defined by the by columns. Each output row carries the aggregated value and a configurable set of coverage columns. Rows with a missing value in any by column are dropped before grouping.
The arguments match across the two languages apart from spelling. Python makes everything after by keyword-only, renames global to global_, and turns R’s dotted flags (pop.coverage) into underscored ones (pop_coverage).

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
RPython


agg <- aggregate_data_v2(
  data,
  value  = "OBS_VALUE",
  weight = "population",
  by     = c("INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"),
  method = "weighted_mean",
  coverage_threshold = 0.5
)


agg = aggregate_data_v2(
    data,
    value="OBS_VALUE",
    weight="population",
    by=["INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"],
    method="weighted_mean",
    coverage_threshold=0.5,
)




7.1.1 Arguments
