R also takes verbose and debug, which follow getOption("dw.verbose") and getOption("dw.debug") when left NULL (see dw_verbosity()). The Python aggregator has neither.


7.1.2 Methods
Pick the method to match the kind of indicator, because each method encodes a different assumption about what the numbers mean:








Method
Formula within group
Use for




weighted_mean
weighted.mean(value, weight)
rates and percentages weighted by population


mean
mean(value)
a simple unweighted average


sum
sum(value) / sum(weight) * 100 (not an additive total; see below)
a population-weighted rate expressed as a percent


proportion
sum((value/100) * weight) / sum(weight_non_na) * 100
indicators given as percentages, reweighted to a population proportion


total
sum(value)
additive person counts (refugees, displaced persons, births), where the regional value is the sum of the country values



Two method names mislead. sum does not return a plain total; it divides the summed values by the summed weights. If you want a genuine count, the literal sum of the country figures, use total. Missing values are dropped, so a group with no reported values totals 0; set coverage_threshold if such a group should come back missing instead.
proportion reads the value column as a percentage (it divides by 100), rebuilds the number affected, and expresses that as a share of the covered population. Use it when each country reports, say, “12.4 % of children stunted” and you want a population-correct regional percentage rather than an average of country percentages.


7.1.3 Coverage and the threshold
The coverage accounting is the reason to prefer this aggregator over a hand-written group_by() |> summarise() or pandas groupby().agg(). For every group the function computes:

Pop_Covered: the share of the group’s total weight that sits on rows with a value. A region whose reporting countries hold 90 % of its population has Pop_Covered = 0.9; the other 10 % shows up here rather than vanishing into a falsely confident average.
Country_Coverage and Total_Countries: the number of distinct countries with a value, and the number of distinct countries in the group, both counted on country_id. If that column is absent, validation warns and both fall back to a row count, which overstates coverage when a country has several rows.
Total_Population and Data_Population: the summed weight over all rows and over rows with a value (returned only when total.population / total_population is on).
Number_Affected: the rebuilt count, returned only when number.affected is on and method == "proportion".

coverage_threshold turns Pop_Covered into a gate. Give it a fraction in [0, 1] and the aggregator sets Aggregate to missing for any group below it, while still returning the coverage columns so the reader can see why. The common UNICEF convention, and the value the error message suggests, is 0.5: report a regional figure only when the reporting countries hold at least half the population. With validation on, a value outside [0, 1] is an error.
The output always starts with the by columns and Aggregate, then adds the metadata columns you asked for:
# Output column order, with the default flags:
#   <by...>, Aggregate, Pop_Covered, Country_Coverage, Total_Countries


7.1.4 The global row
With global = TRUE (the default), the same calculation runs once more over the whole input, ignoring the groups, and comes back as one extra row whose by columns all hold global_label (default "WORLD"). The threshold applies to it too. Turning the global row on converts the by columns to character, so that the label fits. Set global = FALSE when you stack aggregates yourself, as dw_regions() does.


7.1.5 Validation and the error envelope
With validate on (the default), the function checks that value, weight and every by column exist. If one is missing it stops with the toolkit’s standard envelope, [cso_toolkit.aggregate_data_v2] Missing required column(s): ..., followed by the first ten data columns and a one-line fix (Appendix C). R raises it with stop(), Python with KeyError. An unknown method is refused whether or not validation is on. Set validate = FALSE on hot paths where you have already checked the schema; dw_regions() does so and runs its own checks first.

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
7.2 Building the standard footnote: generate_agg_footnote

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
Coverage numbers only help if they reach the reader. generate_agg_footnote() turns them into the one-line caption that sits under aggregated tables and charts: "N/M countries (P % population coverage)", with an optional "Based on latest estimates from YYYY to YYYY." prefix and optional Exemptions: and Exclusions: suffixes.

RPython


note <- generate_agg_footnote(
  country_coverage = 41,
  total_countries  = 48,
  pop_coverage     = 0.87,
  start_year = 2015, end_year = 2023
)
# "Based on latest estimates from 2015 to 2023. 41/48 countries (87 % population coverage)"


note = generate_agg_footnote(
    country_coverage=41,
    total_countries=48,
    pop_coverage=0.87,
    start_year=2015, end_year=2023,
)



pop_coverage is a fraction in [0, 1], printed as a whole percent. The prefix appears only when both years are given. exemptions and exclusions take country codes and append them as notes: the same codes you pass to apply_time_window(), so a windowed aggregate and its footnote agree.

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
7.3 Picking the latest observation: apply_time_window

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
Most regional aggregates use the latest available estimate per country within a window. apply_time_window() makes that selection. Within each country it keeps the single row with the most recent time_col, but only if that year falls inside the inclusive window [start_year, end_year].

RPython


latest <- apply_time_window(
  data,
  country_col = "REF_AREA",
  time_col    = "TIME_PERIOD",
  start_year  = 2015,
  end_year    = 2023,
  exemptions  = c("SOM", "YEM")   # fragile states: keep latest regardless
)


latest = apply_time_window(
    data,
    country_col="REF_AREA",
    time_col="TIME_PERIOD",
    start_year=2015,
    end_year=2023,
    exemptions=["SOM", "YEM"],
)



Two lists tune the selection. Countries in exemptions keep their latest observation even when it predates the window, the usual treatment for fragile states whose most recent survey is old but still the best available. Countries in exclusions are dropped before ranking and never reach the aggregate. The result has one row per surviving country; a country that meets neither the window nor an exemption disappears. The helper’s working columns are removed from the output, and so is any column of yours whose name starts with . (R) or _ (Python), so rename such columns first.
start_year and end_year have no defaults in either language, and in Python every argument after data is keyword-only, so pass them by name. country_col and time_col default to "REF_AREA" and "TIME_PERIOD".

title: 7  Aggregation
section: 7.4 Redistributing weights over missing rows: dw_nestweight
text:
7.4 Redistributing weights over missing rows: dw_nestweight

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
When a survey value is missing on some rows, and the missingness is not completely at random within a stratum, a weighted mean over the observed rows undercounts. dw_nestweight() corrects this by reweighting. Within each stratum (the single column named in by) it scales up the weights on the observed rows so that they sum to the stratum’s total weight. The total is preserved; the mass moves onto the rows that contribute to the estimate. A stratum with no observed rows gets weight 0 throughout.
\[ \text{scale}_l = \frac{\sum_{i \in l} w_i}{\sum_{i \in l,\ v_i \text{ observed}} w_i}, \qquad w'_i = w_i \cdot \text{scale}_l \ \text{ if } v_i \text{ observed, else } 0. \]
(This ports the World Bank EduAnalyticsToolkit’s edukit_nestweight, by Diana Goldemberg.)

RPython


adj <- dw_nestweight(
  data,
  value      = "stunting",
  by         = "stratum_id",
  weight     = "hh_weight",
  new_weight = "hh_weight_adj"
)
# adj now has hh_weight_adj; sum(hh_weight_adj) == sum(hh_weight) per stratum


adj = dw_nestweight(
    data,
    value="stunting",
    by="stratum_id",
    weight="hh_weight",
    new_weight="hh_weight_adj",
)



The function returns the input with one new column, new_weight (default "weight_adj"); it does not aggregate. Pass that column to aggregate_data_v2(weight = "hh_weight_adj", method = "weighted_mean") for the estimate itself. The details:

weight = NULL (R) / weight=None (Python) uses a unit weight, so the helper reduces to per-stratum counts of observed rows.
only takes a logical mask with one entry per row (a boolean Series in Python) that restricts which rows count as observed, for example only respondents who were asked the question.
Rows with a missing stratum get weight 0, with a warning.
A non-numeric weight column stops in R. Python coerces it to numbers, so values that cannot be converted are treated as missing and get weight 0.
Verbose output reports the pooled mean of value under the original and the redistributed weights, but only for a numeric value; otherwise it prints a note and skips the comparison. In R, verbose and debug follow the global options; Python has verbose only, defaulting to True.

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
7.5 Demographics helpers: dw_pop and dw_regions
The last two helpers wrap the population-and-regions workflow. Both fetch through dw_api_fetch, so they inherit the external-API contract exactly: a producer session may fetch and cache, a reviewer session reads the cache and never goes to the network.

7.5.1 dw_pop: population denominators

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
dw_pop() wraps dw_api_fetch(api = "wb") for the World Bank total-population indicator SP.POP.TOTL. Every population-weighted regional mean needs a denominator; dw_pop() hides the indicator code, the cache key and the column clean-up, and returns three columns, REF_AREA, TIME_PERIOD and OBS_VALUE, sorted by country and year.

RPython


# All countries, latest year per country
pop <- dw_pop()

# All countries, a specific year
pop_2023 <- dw_pop(year = 2023)

# A specific country list
pop_sahel <- dw_pop(countries = c("BFA", "MLI", "NER", "TCD"))


from cso_toolkit import dw_pop

pop = dw_pop()
pop_2023 = dw_pop(year=2023)
pop_sahel = dw_pop(countries=["BFA", "MLI", "NER", "TCD"])



The arguments are year (a year or several; NULL/None returns the latest year per country), indicator (default "SP.POP.TOTL"), countries (a filter on ISO3 or M49 codes; NULL/None keeps all), refresh (force a live fetch and replace the cache, producer only) and cache_key (default "wb_population_sp_pop_totl"). Both languages use the same names, defaults and cache key. The function looks for the country, year and value columns under several names (iso3c or iso2c; date or TIME_PERIOD; value, OBS_VALUE or the indicator code), because World Bank client packages have changed their columns over time, and stops with a fix if any of the three cannot be found. It drops rows missing any of the three, so sparse World Bank aggregate rows do not leak through.


7.5.2 dw_regions: UNICEF regional aggregates

Languages: R. Python: No (redesign tracked in #40); Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
dw_regions() is the highest-level helper here. Give it a country-level table and it returns that table with UNICEF regional rows appended: one row per region in the taxonomy (and per by tuple), each carrying the aggregate and its coverage columns.
# Country-level tibble with INDICATOR + TIME_PERIOD + OBS_VALUE
national <- dw_use(name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk")

# Add population-weighted UNICEF region rows
enriched <- dw_regions(national, value = "OBS_VALUE")

# Or weight by a sector-specific column already in the data
alt <- dw_regions(national, value = "OBS_VALUE", weight = "births_under5")
It runs five steps:

Resolve the country-to-region map. It fetches "<taxonomy>.csv" from the public unicef-drp/Country-and-Region-Metadata repository with dw_api_fetch(api = "github_raw"), cached as regions_<taxonomy in lower case>. The default taxonomy is UNICEF_REP_REG_GLOBAL; refresh_metadata = TRUE forces a re-fetch. The country column may be called REF_AREA, ISO3, iso3c or country_code, the region column REGION, region, REGION_CODE or UNICEF_REGION. Rows with a blank region are dropped.
Attach the weight. With weight = "population" (the default), dw_pop() supplies World Bank denominators, merged on REF_AREA and TIME_PERIOD when the data has TIME_PERIOD, and on REF_AREA alone otherwise. Where the World Bank has not yet published a year, the country’s latest population fills in. Any other string names a weight column that must already be in data.
Join the data to the region map. Country codes missing from the taxonomy are excluded with a warning that names them, not dropped silently.
Aggregate per region with aggregate_data_v2(by = c("REGION", by), global = FALSE, validate = FALSE, method = method). There is no global row and no coverage_threshold: every regional value is returned, so check Pop_Covered before you publish one.
Stack. The regional rows are made to match the input (REGION becomes REF_AREA, Aggregate becomes your value column) and appended to the original rows. Regional rows also carry the coverage columns (Pop_Covered, Country_Coverage, …), left missing on the country rows.

The arguments are data, value, weight (default "population"), method (passed to the aggregator, default "weighted_mean"), taxonomy (default "UNICEF_REP_REG_GLOBAL"), by (the grouping columns kept within each region, default c("INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD")) and refresh_metadata.
dw_regions adds two guards. It checks up front that REF_AREA, value and every by column are present, raising the toolkit envelope itself because it turns off the aggregator’s validation. And it refuses a value that clashes with one of the aggregator’s output names (Aggregate, Pop_Covered, Country_Coverage, Total_Countries, Total_Population, Data_Population, Number_Affected), which would otherwise fail obscurely inside the aggregator. If you hit it, rename the value column before the call.

title: 7  Aggregation
text:
7.6 Putting it together
The helpers chain. dw_nestweight() belongs at the survey stage, where it adjusts the weights behind each country’s estimate. Once you have one row per country and year, a regional pipeline in R reads:
latest <- apply_time_window(national, start_year = 2015, end_year = 2023,
                            exemptions = c("SOM", "YEM"))
out    <- dw_regions(latest, value = "OBS_VALUE", by = "INDICATOR")

regional <- out[!is.na(out$Pop_Covered), ]   # the appended region rows
note <- generate_agg_footnote(
  country_coverage = regional$Country_Coverage[1],
  total_countries  = regional$Total_Countries[1],
  pop_coverage     = regional$Pop_Covered[1],
  start_year = 2015, end_year = 2023,
  exemptions = c("SOM", "YEM")
)
Pass by = "INDICATOR" here. After apply_time_window() each country’s row can come from a different year, so grouping on TIME_PERIOD as well (the default) would split each region by year; the regional rows come back with TIME_PERIOD missing. The population merge still uses each country’s own year.
In Python, run apply_time_window, dw_pop and generate_agg_footnote the same way, join your own country-to-region map, and call aggregate_data_v2(..., by=["REGION", "INDICATOR"], global_=False) for the regional step.

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
8.1 Two kinds of repository
Every repository that uses the toolkit needs the same floor before its first line of analysis: a .gitignore that keeps data out and provenance in, the local checks and the hook that requires a record of them, a test suite, the project’s collaboration setting, a home for the vendored helpers, a profile that every script sources first, and a README and contributing guide that tell a co-author what to do on their first clone.
This chapter covers both ways to get there. A new repository gets all of it in one call, from the toolkit’s own templates. An existing repository adopts it step by step, and the second half of the chapter walks through those steps. The detail of each piece lives in the next three chapters: Profiles and the mode switch, Vendoring and updates and Checks and CI.
There are two scaffolders, because there are two kinds of repository:
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
create_research_project()
create_official_stats_project()




For
a paper, an analysis, a replication package
a DW sector pipeline, an SDMX or data.unicef.org publication pipeline, a survey-processing repository


Canonical store for results

the deposit (Teams and Z:), then SDMX and data.unicef.org


Results in the repository
committed

What is committed after a release

a release record, releases/<vintage>/


Code lives in
R/ (numbered scripts)
01_dw_prep/012_codes/<sector>/


Inputs
data/
the deposit’s 011_rawdata; local copies in 01_dw_prep/011_rawdata/<sector>/ and inputs/ (filled by dw_fetch_inputs())


.gitignore
research-project.gitignore
official-stats.gitignore




8.1.1 Which one?
Ask where the results live and who may see them before publication. If the answer is “in git, and anyone with access to the repository may read them”, it is a research project. If the results are deposited and published by the office, and nobody may see a figure before its release date, it is an official-statistics repository, however small.
The difference is not cosmetic. The official-statistics template ignores output folders outright, sidecars included, and its checks fail on anything tracked in them, because a pre-release table committed by accident stays in git history (Checks and CI).
A paper written from official figures after their release is a research project. A research team that also runs a production pipeline keeps the two in separate repositories.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
8.2 Creating a repository
Both functions take the folder of the new repository and the collaboration model. The model is required and has no default, just as dw_mode has none: how many people may produce results is a decision for the project, not something the toolkit guesses. Leave it out and the call stops before writing anything.

RPython


create_research_project(
  "C:/GitHub/learning-mobility",
  collaboration   = "multi-producer",           # or "single-producer"
  members         = c("jpazvd", "kavanesian"),  # optional, informational
  title           = "Schooling Mobility Is Not Learning Mobility",
  vendor          = TRUE,                       # copy helpers from a clone ...
  toolkit_source  = "C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit",
  toolkit_version = "v0.9.1",                   # ... at this tag (default: latest)
  git             = TRUE)                       # git init, develop, hook path

create_official_stats_project(
  "C:/GitHub/DW-Nutrition",
  collaboration = "single-producer",
  vendor = TRUE, toolkit_source = "C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")


from cso_toolkit import create_research_project, create_official_stats_project

create_research_project(
    "C:/GitHub/learning-mobility", "multi-producer",
    members=["jpazvd", "kavanesian"],
    title="Schooling Mobility Is Not Learning Mobility",
    vendor=True, toolkit_source="C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit",
    toolkit_version="v0.9.1", git=True)

create_official_stats_project(
    "C:/GitHub/DW-Nutrition", "single-producer",
    vendor=True, toolkit_source="C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")



The files are the same, byte for byte, whichever language writes them. The .gitignore covers Stata’s files too, and the checks in tools/check.R only read files, so a Stata project is created once from R or Python and then works like any other.

8.2.1 The arguments

collaboration. "single-producer" (one person produces, the others review) or "multi-producer" (several co-authors produce). It is written to cso_project.yml; see The collaboration setting below.
members. Optional user names or GitHub handles, listed under members: in cso_project.yml. They are informational. Each must be letters, digits, ., _ or -, so it stays plain YAML.
title. The README’s title. By default, the folder name.
vendor, toolkit_source, toolkit_version. vendor is FALSE by default. TRUE copies the default helper set into 00_functions/ from a release tag of a git clone of cso-toolkit and writes 00_functions/.toolkit_manifest.yml, with that tag as pulled_version and the commit it points to as pulled_commit. The clone is toolkit_source, else the CSO_TOOLKIT_ROOT environment variable, else the source checkout the package was loaded from. The tag is toolkit_version ("0.9.1" is read as "v0.9.1"); by default it is the clone’s latest release tag, never a pre-release such as v1.0.0-rc1. The files are read from the tag’s commit in the clone’s history, never from its working tree, so a clone on another branch or with local edits still vendors exactly the released bytes. A tag the clone does not have stops the call before anything is written (git fetch --tags first).
What vendor = TRUE copies. The R helpers from r/R/, whichever language runs the scaffolder: dw_io.R, dw_api.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R, dw_provenance.R, dw_deposit.R, dw_project.R, test_scripts.R and zzz.R, plus profile_helpers.R and create_sector_script.R for official statistics. A helper of that set which the tag does not have yet is skipped and named in a message. A character vector instead of TRUE picks the files, all of which must exist at the tag; dw_io.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R and test_scripts.R are always added, because tools/check.R needs them. Without vendoring, tools/check.R leaves out the contract-audit and vintage checks, with a comment saying to add them back once 00_functions/ is filled. What the manifest’s fields mean, and how to update later, is in Vendoring and updates.
workflows. FALSE by default: checks run locally. check-record.yml, which only verifies the local check record on pull requests (no R, about 10 seconds), is always written. TRUE adds the opt-in GitHub Actions workflows: ci-hygiene.yml, ci-contract-audit.yml and ci-r-tests.yml, plus ci-manuscript.yml for a research project (Checks and CI).
git. FALSE by default. TRUE runs git init (when the folder is not a repository yet) with develop as the first branch, because main is created at the first release. It sets core.hooksPath to .githooks and stages .githooks/pre-push and tools/check with their executable bit, so they also run on macOS and Linux clones. It never commits, creates a remote or pushes.
overwrite. FALSE by default; see below.

In R, verbose and debug control the messages, as for every helper; the Python functions log through the standard logging module instead. In Python every argument after collaboration is keyword-only.


8.2.2 Nothing is replaced silently
Before writing anything, the functions compare every target with what they would write. A file with the same bytes is left alone and reported as unchanged. A file with different content stops the whole call, with nothing written, unless overwrite = TRUE. A target path that is a folder also stops it. Both functions return a table with one row per file, path and status (written, overwritten or unchanged); in R it is returned invisibly. A second identical call therefore changes nothing and says so. The last message points to the README’s quick start.

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
8.3 What each function writes

8.3.1 A research project
create_research_project() writes:

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (run once from R or Python). See the coverage matrix.
learning-mobility/
├── .gitignore                   research-project.gitignore, unchanged
├── .gitattributes               LF for the hook, tools/check, vendored helpers
│                                and sidecars; output/ kept byte for byte

├── .checks/README.md            check records: .checks/<content-hash>.json
├── .githooks/pre-push           requires a check record before every push

├── README.md                    quick start for a new co-author, layout
├── CONTRIBUTING.md              ground rules, first clone, workflow, checks

│                                and .toolkit_manifest.yml
├── R/README.md                  numbered scripts; R/functions/ for tested code
├── data/
│   ├── README.md                the provenance policy and the inputs table
│   ├── input_manifest.csv       file, sha256, bytes, origin, sidecar
│   └── provenance/README.md     sidecars of microdata kept outside the repo
├── output/README.md             tables and figures, each with its sidecar
├── paper/README.md              the manuscript, paper/main.tex
├── references/README.md
├── docs/README.md
├── tests/
│   ├── testthat.R               the runner (reviewer mode; sources R/functions/)
│   └── testthat/
│       ├── helper-project.R     fixtures, local state, expect_envelope()
│       └── test-project.R       cso_project.yml, manifest vs sidecars, mode
├── tools/check.R                every local check
├── tools/check                  sh tools/check --record: run, then record
├── .github/workflows/           check-record.yml (always); four more with
│                                workflows = TRUE
├── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md         rules for AI coding agents (CLAUDE.md: @AGENTS.md)
├── decisions.md                 decisions, who made them and why; AI use
└── .claude/settings.json        Claude Code: the cso-toolkit plugin; no edits
                                 to 00_functions/
The agent files are explained in Working with AI coding agents.


8.3.2 An official-statistics repository
create_official_stats_project() follows DW-Production and the deposit’s stage numbering:

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (run once from R or Python). See the coverage matrix.
DW-Nutrition/
├── .gitignore                       official-stats.gitignore, unchanged
├── .gitattributes                   LF for the hook, vendored helpers and sidecars
├── profile_DW-Nutrition.R           sourced first: mode, deposit paths, Z:, helpers
├── .checks/README.md                check records
├── .githooks/pre-push               requires a check record
├── cso_project.yml                  collaboration: single-producer
├── README.md, CONTRIBUTING.md       embargo, release record, first clone
├── _config_template/user_config.yml placeholder per-person configuration
├── 00_documentation/README.md       SOPs, data flows, release checklist
├── 00_functions/                    README.md (+ helpers and manifest)
├── 01_dw_prep/
│   ├── README.md                    the stages: what each holds, what reaches git
│   ├── 010_metadata/README.md       reference metadata (codelists, maps), committed
│   ├── 011_rawdata/README.md        local raw inputs: ignored, sidecars committed
│   ├── 012_codes/README.md          pipeline code, one folder per sector
│   └── (013_wrkdata/)               local work data and outputs: ignored, embargoed
├── inputs/
│   ├── README.md                    filled from the deposit, verified
│   └── input_manifest.csv
├── releases/README.md               releases/<vintage>/, after publication
├── tests/testthat.R, tests/testthat/helper-project.R, test-project.R
├── tools/check.R                    OUTPUT_DIRS, DATA_DIRS, AUDIT_PATHS set
├── tools/check                      sh tools/check --record
├── .github/workflows/               check-record.yml (always); three more
│                                    with workflows = TRUE
├── AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md             agent rules, the embargo section included
├── decisions.md                     decisions and the record of AI use
└── .claude/settings.json            the plugin; no edits to 00_functions/
The canonical raw data, API caches and promoted work data live in the deposit (Teams 060.DW-MASTER/01_dw_prep/011_rawdata and 013_wrkdata). The profile’s teamsRawData and teamsWrkData point there in producer mode and to the sandbox in reviewer mode (Profiles and the mode switch).
The repository keeps folders of the same names for local work, as DW-Production does, because a sector script made by create_sector_script() reads 01_dw_prep/011_rawdata/<sector>/ and writes 01_dw_prep/013_wrkdata/<sector>/ relative to the repository. 01_dw_prep/012_codes/README.md shows the call that scaffolds a sector’s driver against the project’s own profile. The contents of these folders never reach git: .gitignore ignores 013_wrkdata/ outright, like every output folder, and keeps only the READMEs, sidecars and manifests of 011_rawdata/. 013_wrkdata/ has no tracked file at all, so it appears with the first run.
After publication, the release pull request commits releases/<vintage>/: an output_manifest.csv (file, sha256, bytes, deposited_at, deposit_path) and copies of the deposited files’ sidecars. Never before the publication date: those hashes describe embargoed figures.


8.3.3 Set for the kind
The .gitignore, the hook, the test helper and the workflows are the toolkit’s templates byte for byte, so the rules a repository starts with are the ones the toolkit tests. Three files are set for the kind of project:

tools/check.R. An official-statistics repository gets OUTPUT_DIRS = "output outputs results wrk 013_wrkdata" (the embargo: nothing tracked there), 011_rawdata added to DATA_DIRS, and AUDIT_PATHS = "01_dw_prep/012_codes". The contract audit is AUDIT_MODE = "advisory" in a research project, where it reports raw reads such as haven::read_dta() without failing the checks, and "blocking" in official statistics, where any of them fails. What each setting does is in Checks and CI.
tests/testthat.R. Which folder of function files the tests source: R/functions/ in a research project, none in official statistics.
cso_project.yml. The model, today’s date as collaboration_since, and the members.



8.3.4 The profile
Every repository gets profile_<project>.R, named after its folder: the script every analysis script and interactive session sources first, as profile_DW-Production.R is in DW-Production. Both kinds are written from one template, templates/profile/profile.R; the official-statistics one adds a deposit block from templates/profile/deposit.R. The generated profile:

reads ~/.config/user_config.yml, the user’s block first and top-level keys as a fallback, and resolves dw_mode with no default; when it is not set, it stops and shows the lines to add, with the user name filled in;
sources the vendored helpers from 00_functions/, zzz.R first, and reads the vintage from .toolkit_manifest.yml;
never installs a package: a missing one stops the session with the list to install;
resolves the collaboration model from cso_project.yml and ends with a sentinel, profile_<project> <- TRUE, where each run of characters other than letters, digits and _ in the folder name becomes _ (profile_DW_Nutrition). Sector scripts test the sentinel before they run.

The official-statistics profile also derives the deposit paths from dw_mode (teamsRoot for a producer, sandboxRoot for a reviewer) and checks the Z: mirror without ever stopping on it. Its user_config.yml keys are in _config_template/user_config.yml.
Both pass review_profile() with no failure; the research profile shows one warning, for the Z: advisory it does not need. How the profile reads the configuration, the precedence of dw_mode_by_project over dw_mode, the globals it derives and the ten checks of review_profile() are all in Profiles and the mode switch. The profile is yours once written: extend it.

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
8.4 The collaboration setting
cso_project.yml records how many people may produce results. You choose it when you create the repository, and it is committed, so it is the same for everyone. A person’s dw_mode stays in their own configuration.
Pick single-producer when one person produces and the others review, as in a production pipeline with one Database Manager. Pick multi-producer when every co-author may produce, always through a pull request; dw_save() then guards each output against being replaced by someone else’s concurrent or unrecorded change. Change it later with dw_set_collaboration(), in one reviewed pull request, never by editing the file alone. What each model changes, and why switching midway is safe, is in Roles and the mode contract, “Collaboration model”.

title: 8  Starting a repository
section: 8.5 First steps for the person who created it
text:
8.5 First steps for the person who created it

Fill in the paragraphs the README leaves as comments: the question or the indicators, the authors, the outlet or the publication channel (and, for official statistics, the Database Manager).
Vendor the helpers if you did not (00_functions/README.md says how), and put contract-audit and vintage back in CHECKS at the top of tools/check.R.
Run sh tools/check. Every line should pass.
Stage by path and make the first commit on develop. Create main from it when you first release or circulate a version.
Create the remote (private unless the project says otherwise), push both branches, make develop the default branch and protect both trunks, so changes reach them only through pull requests (docs/git_workflow.md). On GitHub, require the check-record status and up-to-date branches for both.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 8  Starting a repository
text:
8.6 First clone, for a co-author
The generated README.md (“Quick start”) and CONTRIBUTING.md (“Joining the project”) carry these steps, so a co-author can follow them without this chapter:

Clone, then git config core.hooksPath .githooks, once, so every push needs a passing check record.
In ~/.config/user_config.yml, under their user name, set dw_mode: reviewer. They switch to producer only for a session in which they deliberately produce or refresh results, or for this repository alone with dw_mode_by_project: and the repository’s name. In an official-statistics repository they copy _config_template/user_config.yml, or add its keys to the file they already have, and also set teamsRoot and a sandboxRoot outside the repository and outside OneDrive. Their filled-in copy is never committed. source("profile_<project>.R") then tells them what is still missing.
Get the inputs. In a research project they obtain each input under their own licence (data/README.md) and verify that the bytes match the manifest before running anything; a mismatch means a different release or vintage. In official statistics they fill inputs/ with dw_fetch_inputs(), which checks every copy’s sha256 against the deposit and stops on a mismatch. Then their results are built from the same inputs.
In official statistics, reproduce the latest vintage in reviewer mode and compare it with the deposit (dw_compare(), dw_provenance_diff()). A clean comparison means their setup reproduces the published figures.
Run sh tools/check, and sh tools/check --record before the first push.
In a multi-producer project, add their handle under members: in cso_project.yml in their first pull request.

title: 8  Starting a repository
section: 8.7 Adopting the toolkit in an existing repository
text:
8.7 Adopting the toolkit in an existing repository
An existing repository cannot simply be scaffolded over: the functions refuse to replace a file that differs, and its code already reads and writes data its own way. Adoption is a sequence of steps instead. Each step below says what to do and links to the chapter with the detail.
The running example is a deposit-bearing pipeline, call it unicef-drp/UNPD-Population, one of the DW-Production-style repositories that publish curated data to the shared Teams and Z: warehouse. Every step is repository-neutral: substitute your own owner, repository and sector codes. A research repository follows the same steps, with outputs in output/ instead of the deposit.
By the end, the pipeline writes to the canonical deposit only in producer mode, isolates reviewer runs in a sandbox, and proves on every push that no script bypasses the IO and API contracts.
A quick way to get the files you will copy: run the matching scaffolder into an empty scratch folder with vendor = TRUE, then copy what you need from there into the repository.

8.7.1 1. Decide what to adopt
Before copying anything, settle two questions.
Which helpers does the pipeline need? The toolkit is modular. A repository that only reads and writes deposit files needs the IO contract (dw_save(), dw_use(), dw_compare()) and the sync helper. One that also fetches from upstream APIs needs the external-API contract (dw_api_fetch(), dw_api_cached(), dw_api_inventory()). Vendor only what the code calls; the manifest’s vendored: list says what you took.
Which languages? The three implementations do not cover the same functions. The coverage line under each function in this handbook says where it exists, and the coverage matrix has them all. Check the functions your pipeline would use now, before the migration starts. In particular, if the Stata code needs a remote source and the API wrapper is not available there, keep the fetching in R or Python, let it cache the source in the deposit, and have the Stata code read the cache with dw_use.


8.7.2 2. Vendor and pin
Copy the helpers into 00_functions/, commit them, and pin the vintage in 00_functions/.toolkit_manifest.yml, next to the helpers it tracks. The committed copies freeze the vintage in your git history, so a reviewer with no network access can still re-run the pipeline. Keep vendored: honest: list a file only if it is in 00_functions/.
For a deposit, pulled_version must be a real release tag, never inrepo or an unreleased suffix: the Database Manager’s pre-deposit checklist (templates/dbm_submission_template.md) blocks sign-off otherwise.
The routes for R, Python and Stata, every manifest field and the update functions are in Vendoring and updates.


8.7.3 3. Wire the profile
This is the load-bearing step. Which folder a dw_save() lands in, and whether an API fetch is allowed, both follow from dw_mode and the globals the profile derives from it.
The profile must hard-fail when dw_mode is missing or is anything other than producer or reviewer. Defaulting to either side is unsafe: defaulting to producer corrupts the deposit, and defaulting to reviewer surprises a Database Manager mid-deposit. It must also print a banner that makes the session’s mode unmistakable.
You can take the generated profile_<project>.R from the scratch scaffold, generate one with create_profile(), or keep your own and audit it with review_profile(). In a pipeline with a conductor script, shadow the path globals once at the top of the conductor rather than editing every sector script. All of this is in Profiles and the mode switch.


8.7.4 4. Move raw IO to dw_use() and dw_save()
Now find every raw read, write and HTTP call in the pipeline and route it through the wrappers. The contract audit lists them for you: copy tools/check.R from the scratch scaffold, set AUDIT_PATHS to your code folders and run it with AUDIT_MODE advisory, which reports each violation without failing:
AUDIT_MODE=advisory sh tools/check --only contract-audit
Each reported line becomes a wrapper call. Reads go through dw_use():

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.
Writes go through dw_save():

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.

RPythonStata


# Before: raw paths, no provenance, no mode routing
wpp <- read.csv(file.path(teamsRawData, "pop", "wpp_2024.csv"))
write.csv(df, file.path(teamsWrkData, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

# After: routed by dw_mode, with a provenance sidecar on every write
wpp <- dw_use(name = "wpp_2024.csv", sector = "pop", kind = "raw")
dw_save(df, name = "dw_pop_tot.csv", sector = "pop", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"),
        metadata = list(title = "Total population, by area and year"))


# Before
wpp = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(teamsRawData, "pop", "wpp_2024.csv"))
df.to_csv(os.path.join(teamsWrkData, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"), index=False)

# After
wpp = dw_use(name="wpp_2024.csv", sector="pop", kind="raw")
dw_save(df, name="dw_pop_tot.csv", sector="pop", kind="wrk",
        isid=["REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"],
        metadata={"title": "Total population, by area and year"})


* Before
use "$teamsRawData/pop/wpp_2024.dta", clear
save "$teamsWrkData/pop/dw_pop_tot.dta", replace

* After
dw_use , filename("wpp_2024.dta") path("$teamsRawData/pop")
dw_save , filename("dw_pop_tot.dta") path("$teamsWrkData/pop") ///
          idvars("REF_AREA TIME_PERIOD")                       ///
          title("Total population, by area and year")



Calls to an external API go through dw_api_fetch(), which caches the response in the deposit and records where it came from:

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python. See the coverage matrix.

RPython


wb <- dw_api_fetch(
  api        = "wb",
  cache_key  = "wb_lp_primary_2000_2024",
  indicator  = "SE.LPV.PRIM",
  start_date = 2000,
  end_date   = 2024)


wb = dw_api_fetch(
    "wb", "wb_lp_primary_2000_2024",
    indicator=["SE.LPV.PRIM"], start_date=2000, end_date=2024)



The arguments of each wrapper, the cross-language differences in their options, and the full list of supported APIs are in The IO contract and External APIs. A line that legitimately reads a file raw, such as the profile’s own read of user_config.yml, is marked # cso-allow: <rule> (Checks and CI).
The first producer run. Switch your user_config.yml to dw_mode: "producer", confirm that the banner says PRODUCER, and run the pipeline. Two things happen on this run that never happen again, because the run fills state that later runs reuse. Each API source is fetched live and cached, so later runs hit the cache; caches never expire on their own, and the Database Manager decides when to refresh them (refresh = TRUE). And each output is written to the deposit where no earlier vintage exists, with its sidecar, and mirrored to Z: when the profile finds it.
Then list what you cached, for the deposit checklist:

Languages: R, Python. Stata: Route via R or Python. See the coverage matrix.

RPython


dw_api_inventory()   # every cache, with size, mtime and fetched_at


dw_api_inventory()





8.7.5 5. Re-run as a reviewer and compare
Now prove the deposit is reproducible. Switch a second person, or your own configuration, to dw_mode: "reviewer" with a sandboxRoot, and confirm the banner says REVIEWER. Run the same pipeline. Every artifact lands in the sandbox, and the canonical deposit’s modification times are the same before and after the run. A cache that is missing is not fetched: dw_api_fetch() stops and says the input must be deposited first, which is the contract working as designed.
Then compare the reviewer’s file with the deposited one. The reference side is read through the *Canonical alias, which reviewer-mode code may read but never write:

Languages: R, Python, Stata. See the coverage matrix.

RPythonStata


report <- dw_compare(
  current            = file.path(teamsWrkData, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"),
  reference          = file.path(teamsWrkDataCanonical, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"),
  by                 = c("REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"),
  value_cols         = c("OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"),
  numeric_value_cols = "OBS_VALUE",
  tol                = 1e-5,
  label              = "dw_pop_tot",
  write_report_to    = file.path(tempdir(), "pop_compare"))
report$summary


report = dw_compare(
    current=os.path.join(teamsWrkData, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"),
    reference=os.path.join(teamsWrkDataCanonical, "pop", "dw_pop_tot.csv"),
    by=["REF_AREA", "TIME_PERIOD"],
    value_cols=["OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"],
    numeric_value_cols=["OBS_VALUE"],
    tol=1e-5,
    label="dw_pop_tot",
    write_report_to=os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "pop_compare"))
report["summary"]


dw_compare , current("$teamsWrkData/pop/dw_pop_tot.dta")              ///
             reference("$teamsWrkDataCanonical/pop/dw_pop_tot.dta")   ///
             idvars("REF_AREA TIME_PERIOD")                           ///
             valuevars("OBS_VALUE DATA_SOURCE")                       ///
             tol(1e-5) label("dw_pop_tot")                            ///
             report("`c(tmpdir)'/pop_compare.md")



The summary counts the rows added, removed and changed. On a clean reproduction all three are zero. When they are not, the Database Manager’s submission template classifies each non-zero result:







Class
Meaning




stale-cache
the API cache was not refreshed after the source changed upstream


retired-upstream-indicator
an indicator in the earlier vintage was retired upstream


methodology-change
the sector’s code changed and the new outputs are correct


rounding
floating-point differences below the tolerance


bug
a new finding, which needs an issue


uninvestigated
not classified yet



A deposit cannot be signed off while any row is still uninvestigated.
This reviewer re-run and its compare report are what adoption means in practice: a reviewer-mode run produces every artifact under sandboxRoot, the canonical deposit is unchanged, and the report exists.


8.7.6 6. Run the checks
Finally, make the guarantees hold on every push rather than depend on someone remembering them. Copy from the scratch scaffold tools/check.R, tools/check, .githooks/pre-push, .checks/README.md and .github/workflows/check-record.yml, set the settings at the top of tools/check.R for your folders, and enable the hook once per clone (git config core.hooksPath .githooks). Merge the scaffold’s .gitignore into yours rather than replacing it.
Once step 4 is done and the code reads through the wrappers, set AUDIT_MODE to "blocking", so a new raw read fails the checks. Then sh tools/check --record records a passing run, which the pre-push hook and the check-record status require.
Checks never run the pipeline in producer mode. CI cannot reach the corporate-network-only APIs, and it must never write to a real deposit: it audits the contract with cached fixtures in reviewer mode, and live fetching belongs in a producer session on a machine with network access. Every check, the check records, the hook and the opt-in workflows are in Checks and CI.


8.7.7 Recap: the adoption checklist
A repository has adopted the contract when all of these hold. They match the sign-off section of the Database Manager’s submission template.








#
Check
How to confirm




1
Helpers vendored into 00_functions/
files present and committed


2
Manifest pins a real tag
pulled_version in .toolkit_manifest.yml is vX.Y.Z, not inrepo


3
Profile hard-fails without dw_mode
sourcing it with the key absent stops the session


4
Mode banner is unmistakable
a reviewer session prints the sandbox banner


5
Conductor shadows the path globals
the globals are reassigned before any other script is sourced


6
First producer run caches and deposits
dw_api_inventory() shows the caches; each deposited file has its sidecar


7
Reviewer run is deposit-safe
every artifact under sandboxRoot; the deposit’s modification times unchanged


8
Compare report exists
the dw_compare() summary is written; no row left uninvestigated


9
No script bypasses the contracts
the contract audit, in blocking mode, passes


10
Checks gate every push
sh tools/check --record passes; the pull request’s check-record status is green



Rows 7 and 8, and the reviewer run behind them, are the test that the contract is real and not merely declared. Once they pass and the checks enforce them, the repository is a deposit-bearing consumer of the same contract as DW-Production. To keep it current as the toolkit releases new vintages, see Vendoring and updates.

title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
9.1 The switch: dw_mode in user_config.yml
Every session in a CSO repository starts by sourcing one script, the profile (profile_<repo>.R or .py, or a profile do-file in Stata). It works out who is running, reads their personal configuration, settles whether the session is a producer or a reviewer, and sets the globals every toolkit helper reads. Roles and the mode contract explains the two modes. This chapter is the operational side: how a repository makes its own code honour that contract, and the helpers that write and audit the scripts involved.
The idea that holds it together is single-switch routing. You set dw_mode once, in one file, and everything downstream is derived from it: where writes land, whether live API calls are allowed, where reads fall back to. No script needs editing and no call needs a flag. Get one step wrong, though, and the failure the contract prevents comes back silently: a reviewer overwriting the canonical deposit, or a reviewer run reaching a live API and breaking provenance.
Each person keeps a configuration file at ~/.config/user_config.yml (on Windows, %USERPROFILE%/.config/user_config.yml). It is per machine and per user and is never committed. One file serves every CSO project on the machine. Following DW-Production’s template (_config_template/user_config.yml, which create_official_stats_project() also writes), your settings sit in a block named after your user name: USERNAME on Windows, USER on macOS and Linux.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository
9  Profiles and the mode switch

title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
jpazevedo:
  githubFolder: "C:/GitHub/mytasks"
  teamsRoot: "C:/Users/jpazevedo/UNICEF/Chief Statistician Office - Documents"
  dw_mode: "reviewer"                                # producer | reviewer
  sandboxRoot: "C:/Users/jpazevedo/dw-repro"         # used only when dw_mode = reviewer
  dw_mode_by_project:                                # optional, per repository
    learning-mobility: "producer"

9.1.1 Precedence
The profile reads each setting from your block first and from top-level keys only as a fallback, so an older flat file still works. dw_mode then resolves in this order:

dw_mode_by_project for this repository, keyed by the profile’s repo_name;
dw_mode.

dw_mode_by_project wins over dw_mode the way DW-Production’s dw_mode_by_sector wins for the active sector (that sector map stays a DW-Production extension, ahead of both). It must be a map from project names to modes: a single value such as dw_mode_by_project: producer stops the profile with an error saying so.


9.1.2 No default
dw_mode must be exactly "producer" or "reviewer". If neither key gives a valid value, the profile stops. Defaulting either way is unsafe. A default of producer would let a reviewer corrupt the canonical deposit the first time they forgot the key; a default of reviewer would divert a database manager’s writes into a sandbox in the middle of a legitimate deposit. There is no safe default, so the profile refuses to guess and prints the YAML to add, with your user name and the project filled in:
[X] No valid dw_mode ("producer" or "reviewer") for Proj-X.
    Add it to C:/Users/tester/.config/user_config.yml, in your user block:
      tester:
        dw_mode: "reviewer"
    or, for this project only:
      tester:
        dw_mode_by_project:
          Proj-X: "producer"
The three languages resolve the mode the same way:

RPythonStata


user_block <- if (is.list(user_config[[USERNAME]])) user_config[[USERNAME]] else list()
user_setting <- function(key) {
  if (!is.null(user_block[[key]])) user_block[[key]] else user_config[[key]]
}
dw_mode <- user_setting("dw_mode_by_project")[[repo_name]]
if (is.null(dw_mode)) dw_mode <- user_setting("dw_mode")
if (!(is.character(dw_mode) && length(dw_mode) == 1 &&
      dw_mode %in% c("producer", "reviewer"))) {
  stop(...)  # names the file and shows the YAML to add
}
dw_apis_allowed <- identical(dw_mode, "producer")


user_block = user_config.get(USERNAME) if isinstance(user_config.get(USERNAME), dict) else {}
def user_setting(key):
    value = user_block.get(key)
    return value if value is not None else user_config.get(key)
dw_mode = (user_setting("dw_mode_by_project") or {}).get(repo_name)
if dw_mode is None:
    dw_mode = user_setting("dw_mode")
if dw_mode not in ("producer", "reviewer"):
    raise ValueError(...)  # names the file and shows the YAML to add


* Reads your user block (then top-level keys), resolves dw_mode as
* dw_mode_by_project for the project, then dw_mode, and stops with
* error 459 and the YAML to add if neither is valid.
dw_load_config, project(my-project)
* -> sets the global $dw_mode



The parity certificate’s config_user_block case runs six configurations (the user block, a project override, another project’s override, a flat file, a top-level map, and a file with no mode) through a generated R profile, a generated Python profile and dw_load_config, and checks that all three resolve them alike (How the three languages stay in step).
When a producer session runs inside Claude Code (which sets CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1), the generated profiles print a notice that an agent is working as producer. Nothing is blocked; Working with AI coding agents explains the rule behind it.


9.1.3 Stata: dw_load_config

Languages: Stata. R: inside create_profile output; Python: inside create_profile output. See the coverage matrix.
In R and Python the profile itself reads the YAML. Stata cannot link an external YAML library on AppLocker-locked corporate Windows installs, so dw_load_config.ado ships a small hand-rolled parser and a profile do-file calls it near the top:
dw_load_config, project(learning-mobility)
dw_load_config, filepath("`c(tmpdir)'/dw_test_config.yml") user(tester) project(proj-x)

filepath() overrides the default path, $HOME/.config/user_config.yml, then %USERPROFILE%/.config/user_config.yml. Note the order: Stata looks at HOME first, the R and Python profiles at USERPROFILE first. If both are set and differ, pass filepath().
user() is the block to read. The default is USERNAME, then USER, then c(username), the profiles’ order.
project() is the name looked up in dw_mode_by_project. The default is the name of the folder holding .git, searched upward from the working directory. Always pass it in a profile: in a git worktree the folder name is not the project.

The parser handles the subset the schema needs: key: value lines, nesting by indentation two levels deep (the user block, then dw_mode_by_project), optional single or double quotes, blank lines, # comments and trailing inline comments. It does not handle lists, anchors or multi-line strings. Any other block, such as a datalib: block another tool reads, is skipped whole, so its keys never become toolkit globals. Unknown keys are ignored.
It recognises dw_mode, dw_mode_by_project, teamsWrkData, teamsRawData, teamsWrkDataCanonical, teamsRawDataCanonical, teamsFolderCanonical, dwZDrive, dwZDriveUNC (read by dw_map_drive) and sandboxRoot. Each key found is set as a matching $-global and returned in r(), along with r(filepath), r(user), r(project) and r(dw_mode_source) (which key the mode came from). A missing file stops with error 601; a missing or invalid dw_mode, or a scalar dw_mode_by_project, stops with error 459 and the YAML to add.
dw_load_config sets exactly the keys the YAML provides. It does not derive mode-aware paths (next section); the profile do-file does that itself after the loader returns.






sandboxRoot is mandatory in reviewer mode, because the reviewer’s write globals are built from it. The official-statistics profile (templates/profile/deposit.R, below) stops with the YAML to add when it is missing, and stops the same way when teamsRoot is missing. A profile from create_profile() derives no paths and so never reads it, and dw_load_config does not check it either. If you write the derivation yourself, check sandboxRoot alongside dw_mode, or a reviewer session ends up with empty or malformed write paths instead of a clear error at load time.

section: 9.2 Deriving the producer and reviewer globals
text:
9.2 Deriving the producer and reviewer globals
Once dw_mode is known, the profile derives a small set of path globals from it. In producer mode they point at the canonical deposit; in reviewer mode the working globals point at your private sandbox, while a parallel set of *Canonical aliases keeps a read-only view of the deposit so that reviewer code can still compare its outputs against it.
The reference derivation is the official-statistics profile’s deposit block (templates/profile/deposit.R, patterned on DW-Production’s profile_DW-Production.R). The deposit is Teams 060.DW-MASTER under your teamsRoot:








Global
Producer mode
Reviewer mode




teamsFolderCanonical
<teamsRoot>/060.DW-MASTER
<teamsRoot>/060.DW-MASTER (read only)


teamsRawDataCanonical
teamsFolderCanonical/01_dw_prep/011_rawdata
same


teamsWrkDataCanonical
teamsFolderCanonical/01_dw_prep/013_wrkdata
same


teamsFolder
teamsFolderCanonical
sandboxRoot


teamsRawData
teamsRawDataCanonical
sandboxRoot/01_dw_prep/011_rawdata


teamsWrkData
teamsWrkDataCanonical
sandboxRoot/01_dw_prep/013_wrkdata


dw_apis_allowed
TRUE
FALSE



Two patterns matter. First, the split between diverted write globals and preserved read aliases. In reviewer mode teamsRawData and teamsWrkData lead into the sandbox, but the *Canonical aliases still lead to the deposit. Reviewer code can therefore read canonical inputs and outputs for a compare-against-warehouse step without being able to write over them. In producer mode the aliases and the working globals are the same paths, because the producer reads and writes the same place.
Second, dw_apis_allowed. This one boolean is TRUE only in producer mode. It is what dw_api_fetch consults before going to the network, and it is the single place the “reviewers never touch live APIs” rule is encoded. (In the templates it is set right after dw_mode resolves, not in the deposit block.)
The deposit block also does some housekeeping. It warns, without stopping, when the deposit folder is not there (Teams not synced). In reviewer mode it creates the two sandbox folders. It sets the repository’s own stage folders (dwMetaData, dwCodes, dwWrkData under 01_dw_prep/), which hold local copies only and never reach git. And it probes the Z: mirror of the deposit (zDrive in your block overrides the default "Z:/"), setting dw_z_available and dwZDrive. The probe runs vol in a child process capped at three seconds, because dir.exists() on a mapped but unreachable drive letter (Z: off VPN) can block for the full SMB timeout. A missing mirror prints a warning and never stops the session.

9.2.1 How each language carries the state

RPythonStata


# The R profile sets the derived globals directly in .GlobalEnv.
# The helpers read them from there (through the internal .try_get()).
teamsRawData          <- file.path(teamsFolder, "01_dw_prep", "011_rawdata")
teamsRawDataCanonical <- file.path(teamsFolderCanonical, "01_dw_prep", "011_rawdata")
dw_apis_allowed       <- identical(dw_mode, "producer")


# The Python profile pushes the state into the shared cso_toolkit._state
# module; the helpers read it back through _state._get(...).
from cso_toolkit import _state as _cso_state

_cso_state.configure(
    dw_mode=dw_mode,
    dw_apis_allowed=(dw_mode == "producer"),
    teamsRawData="/path/to/raw",
    teamsRawDataCanonical="/path/to/raw-canonical",
)


* dw_load_config sets $dw_mode and whichever team* / canonical /
* sandboxRoot keys the YAML holds, but derives nothing. The profile
* do-file makes the producer/reviewer swap itself after it returns,
* e.g. $teamsWrkData at the canonical root for a producer and under
* $sandboxRoot for a reviewer.



The Python _state module is the explicit counterpart of R’s global environment. Its configure() accepts only the session globals the helpers know (the error lists them) and raises AttributeError on any other key, so a typo such as a lowercase teamswrkdata fails at once instead of creating a dead attribute. The accessor _state._get() returns its default only when a name is unset or None; falsy values such as False or "" come back as they are, so dw_apis_allowed = False is seen as False.


9.2.2 The mode banner
A profile should announce its mode at load time, so you can never be unsure which side of the contract you are on. The official-statistics profile prints one of:
[!] PRODUCER mode: writes go to the canonical deposit, <teamsFolder>
[OK] REVIEWER mode: writes go to <sandboxRoot>; the deposit is read only.
and ends with a summary line: [OK] profile_<project>.R loaded: user <name>, dw_mode <mode>, <collaboration model>, cso-toolkit <version>. The banner is cheap and catches most accidental cross-mode runs: you notice the wrong banner scroll past. DW-Production’s own profile prints the same message with emoji markers; if your terminal renders emoji poorly, use the plain [OK] / [!] / [X] markers the toolkit uses everywhere else. A profile from create_profile() prints no mode banner, only the collaboration model and a loaded line, so add one when you add the path derivation.

title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
9.4 The conductor shadow pattern
The shadow pattern re-binds the path globals once, at the top of the run driver, so that no sector script needs editing. It is the most error-prone step of the wiring, and where adoption most often succeeds or fails.
The problem is scale. A sector typically has ten to forty scripts, each referring to teamsRawData, teamsWrkData and the other working roots directly. Editing every one to make it mode-aware is exactly wrong: it multiplies the change, it buries the analysis diff under unrelated churn that reviewers then have to read, and sooner or later someone edits thirty-nine scripts and forgets the fortieth.
Instead, at the top of each sector’s run driver (0_execute_conductor.R in DW-Production), after sourcing the profile, the conductor re-binds the working globals. R, Python and Stata all look those names up when each later script runs, so every script keeps its code and still gets the right paths:

RPythonStata


# After computing outputdir for this run (with branch-slug isolation):
finaldir <- file.path(outputdir, "final")

# Conductor-level shadow: redirect downstream reads and writes
# without editing any sector script.
teamsRawData <- teamsRawDataCanonical   # read canonical inputs
teamsWrkData <- finaldir                # writes go to this run's final/
dwWrkData    <- finaldir


# After computing outputdir for this run (with branch-slug isolation):
finaldir = os.path.join(outputdir, "final")

# Conductor-level shadow: re-point the shared state so every helper
# call downstream resolves the mode-correct paths.
from cso_toolkit import _state
_state.configure(
    teamsRawData=_state.teamsRawDataCanonical,  # read canonical inputs
    teamsWrkData=finaldir,                      # writes go to this run's final/
)


* After computing $outputdir for this run:
global finaldir "$outputdir/final"

* Conductor-level shadow: every later save or dw_save against
* $teamsWrkData lands in final/ without per-call edits.
global teamsRawData "$teamsRawDataCanonical"
global teamsWrkData "$finaldir"



The shadow reads from the canonical alias and writes to finaldir, which is derived from the mode-aware teamsRawData. In reviewer mode, inputs come from the read-only deposit and every output stays in the sandbox. In producer mode the canonical alias equals the working global, so the first line is a harmless identity and outputs flow to the deposit as before. One pattern serves both modes, with no branching in the sector scripts.






The shadow must run before any other script is sourced by the conductor. A script sourced before the shadow captures the old values. The order is: source the profile, compute outputdir and finaldir, shadow the globals, then source the pipeline.




9.4.1 Branch-slug isolation
A second, optional but recommended layer keys output folders to the current git branch, so two feature branches, or a feature branch and the canonical line, never write to the same folder, even within one sandbox. The conductor reads the branch, turns it into a filesystem-safe token, and routes non-canonical branches into branches/<slug>/:
branch <- tryCatch(
  system("git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD", intern = TRUE),
  error = function(e) "main"
)
branch_slug <- gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9._-]", "-", branch)

canonical_outputdir <- file.path(teamsRawData, sector, "output")
outputdir <- if (branch %in% c("main", "dev", "master")) {
  canonical_outputdir
} else {
  file.path(canonical_outputdir, "branches", branch_slug)
}
This is a conductor convention, not a toolkit function; each conductor writes it inline, in its own language. It layers cleanly on the mode contract. In reviewer mode teamsRawData is already under sandboxRoot, so a feature-branch run lands at <sandboxRoot>/.../<sector>/output/branches/<slug>/. Only main, dev and master write to the un-suffixed folder, and in reviewer mode even those stay inside the sandbox.

text:
9.5 Scaffolding a profile: create_profile()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
create_profile() is a code generator, not a runtime helper: it writes a profile template to disk and returns its path. The template is patterned on DW-Production’s profile_DW-Production.R.

RPython


# Generic project:
create_profile("My-Sector-Project", project_title = "My Sector Project")

# DW-Production, with the Z: drive advisory, replacing an existing file:
create_profile("DW-Production",
               project_title         = "UNICEF DW Production",
               include_z_drive_check = TRUE,
               overwrite             = TRUE)


create_profile("My-Sector-Project", project_title="My Sector Project")

create_profile("DW-Production",
               project_title="UNICEF DW Production",
               include_z_drive_check=True,
               overwrite=True)



Stata has no scaffolder: write the profile do-file by hand, call dw_load_config in it, and derive the paths after it returns.








Argument
Default
Purpose




repo_name
(required)
Repository name. Sets the filename (profile_<repo_name>.R / .py), the literal repo_name that dw_mode_by_project is looked up by, and the sentinel profile_<repo_name> with runs of - and . turned into _.


project_title
repo_name
Title for the header block.


output_path
"."
Folder the file is written to; created if missing.


include_dw_mode
TRUE
Emit the dw_mode block and the dw_require_no_api() guard.


include_z_drive_check
FALSE
Emit the Z: advisory. The Z: drive is the legacy Azure file-share mirror of the deposit, so this is DW-Production-specific.


author
the system user
Author in the header.


overwrite
FALSE
Stop if the file exists, unless TRUE.



In Python every argument after repo_name is keyword-only, and the function raises FileExistsError when the file exists. The R version also takes verbose and debug (see dw_verbosity()) and returns the path invisibly.
The generated profile opens with a header (title, filename, author, timestamp, a pointer to the toolkit repository) and a reproducibility seed (set.seed(12345) / random.seed(12345)), then nine numbered blocks:

User identification. Reads USERNAME, falling back to USER, and USERPROFILE, falling back to the home folder, so the same file works on Windows, macOS and Linux.
Flags and controls, such as create_missing_folders <- FALSE.
Repository name and root: the literal repo_name <- "DW-Production", then rootFolder (the working directory, unless you set rootFolder before sourcing the profile) and projectFolder <- rootFolder, the folder that sector scripts build their paths from.
Z: drive advisory (only with include_z_drive_check). Non-blocking, with the three-second vol probe described above.
Config load. Reads ~/.config/user_config.yml with yaml::read_yaml() / yaml.safe_load() and stops if the file is missing (the R profile first checks that the yaml package is installed). Defines user_block and user_setting(): your block first, then top-level keys.
Producer/reviewer mode (only with include_dw_mode). Resolves dw_mode as above, rejects a scalar dw_mode_by_project, sets dw_apis_allowed, prints the agent notice, and defines dw_require_no_api().
Collaboration model. Calls dw_collaboration(refresh = TRUE) when the toolkit is loaded and prints the model read from cso_project.yml; otherwise it says the model is resolved on the first dw_save().
Packages / imports. The R block lists dplyr, tidyr, readr and yaml for you to edit, and never installs anything: a missing package stops the session with the list and the install.packages() call to run once. The Python block imports pandas.
Profile sentinel. Sets profile_<repo> <- TRUE (R) or profile_<repo> = True (Python) and prints a confirmation. Sector scripts can refuse to run without it.

Block 6 hides a real difference between the languages. The Python profile imports cso_toolkit._state and calls _cso_state.configure(dw_mode=..., dw_apis_allowed=(dw_mode == "producer")), so dw_save, dw_use and dw_api_fetch route by mode. The R profile needs no such call: sourced into the global environment, its dw_mode and dw_apis_allowed are the globals the R helpers read. Block 9 differs too: the Python profile also defines a log_message() there, for sector scripts to import.
create_profile() stops at the mode. It does not derive the deposit paths of the table above or print a mode banner; add those yourself when the project has a deposit.






The YAML load in block 5 is the one place a profile must read a file directly: it bootstraps the configuration before any toolkit helper is available. The generated line carries an exemption for the contract auditor, yaml::read_yaml(config_path)  # cso-allow: io-yaml (yaml.safe_load(_f) or {}  # cso-allow: io-yaml in Python). The auditor and its # cso-allow: directive are in Checks and CI.




9.5.1 The project profile template
create_research_project() and create_official_stats_project() do not call create_profile(). They write profile_<project>.R from templates/profile/profile.R, and the official-statistics kind splices in templates/profile/deposit.R, the deposit block described above. Starting a repository covers what each kind writes. Compared with create_profile() output, this template finds the repository root (the folder holding cso_project.yml) and sets rootFolder and projectFolder from it. It sources the vendored helpers from 00_functions/ (zzz.R first) and reports the vendored version from .toolkit_manifest.yml. And it checks packages through a require_packages() function that scripts can also call. Its sentinel replaces each run of characters outside A-Za-z0-9_ with _. Both templates follow the same conventions: no default for dw_mode, no package installs, sentinel last.

text:
9.6 Scaffolding sector drivers: create_sector_script()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
Where create_profile() scaffolds the once-per-repository profile, create_sector_script() scaffolds a once-per-sector run script, <base_dir>/<sector_code>/00_run_<sector_code>.R (or .py). The template runs out of the box: it verifies the profile, sets up logging and timing, builds input and output paths, and wraps the placeholder work in error handling.

RPython


# Generic: writes ./ws/00_run_ws.R
create_sector_script("WASH", "ws")

# Into a chosen subtree:
create_sector_script("Nutrition", "nt", base_dir = "pipelines/sectors")


create_sector_script("WASH", "ws")
create_sector_script("Nutrition", "nt", base_dir="pipelines/sectors")



In Stata, write 00_run_<sector>.do by hand and have it check that $dw_mode is set (that is, that dw_load_config ran) before doing the sector’s work.









Argument
R default
Python default
Purpose




sector_name
(required)
(required)
Full name, e.g. "Nutrition"; used in headers and log lines.


sector_code
(required)
(required)
Short code, e.g. "nt"; names the folder and file.


base_dir
"."
"."
Parent of <sector_code>/00_run_<sector_code>.*.


profile_name
"projectFolder"
"profile_DW_Production"
The variable the script requires before it runs.


profile_file
"profile_DW-Production.R"
"profile_DW-Production.py"
The profile the script names (R) or loads (Python).


input_subpath
c("01_dw_prep", "011_rawdata")
("01_dw_prep", "011_input")
Input folder, relative to projectFolder; the sector code is appended.


output_subpath
c("01_dw_prep", "013_wrkdata")
("01_dw_prep", "013_output")
Output folder, likewise.


overwrite
FALSE
False
Stop if the file exists, unless TRUE.



In Python the arguments after base_dir are keyword-only; the R version also takes verbose and debug.
The generated R script has these parts:

0. Profile verification: if (!exists(profile_name) || is.null(profile_name)) stop(...), telling you to source profile_file. Any non-null value satisfies it. The R default checks projectFolder rather than the sentinel because the script also builds its paths from projectFolder, so the guard and the paths share one source of truth.
A log_message() fallback: a minimal timestamped logger, installed only if the profile did not define one.
An errorOccurred flag, initialised to FALSE so the error handler can set it with <<- for the top-level runner to read.
1. Logging: a “Starting  module” line and start_time.
2. Sector execution block: a tryCatch() that defines input_folder and output_folder from projectFolder, creates the output folder, leaves commented placeholders for load, process and export, and logs the duration. On error it sets errorOccurred <<- TRUE and logs the message.

The Python script covers the same ground with try/except and pathlib.Path. Loading the profile takes more work there. A filename like profile_DW-Production.py contains a hyphen, so it cannot be imported as a module. The script walks up from its own folder (then the working directory) to find profile_file, loads it with importlib.util.spec_from_file_location, and reads the sentinel, log_message and projectFolder from the loaded module. It raises RuntimeError if the profile is not found, the sentinel is false, or log_message or projectFolder is missing; there is no logger fallback. Because it reads the sentinel from the module, the Python default profile_name is the sentinel, "profile_DW_Production" (underscores), not "projectFolder".






Paths and projectFolder. The default subpaths differ between the languages (R: 011_rawdata / 013_wrkdata; Python: 011_input / 013_output). If you scaffold the same sector in both, set input_subpath and output_subpath explicitly so the two drivers agree.
Both templates also need projectFolder. A profile from create_profile() sets it to the folder you source the profile from, so run the sector script from the repository root, or set rootFolder before sourcing the profile; a hand-written profile must define it (the R script otherwise stops with Project profile not loaded ("projectFolder" is not set), the Python one with Project profile missing required exports (log_message, projectFolder)). In Python, also pass the right profile_name ("profile_<repo>") and profile_file for your repository.




9.6.1 create_dw_sector_script()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
A thin wrapper that fills in the DW-Production layout: the script lands at <project_root>/01_dw_prep/012_codes/<sector>/00_run_<sector>.* and checks for the DW-Production profile. Its only other arguments are project_root (default ".", the DW-Production root) and overwrite. R reads from 011_rawdata and writes to 013_wrkdata; Python, as with the generic defaults, uses 011_input / 013_output.
create_dw_sector_script("WASH", "ws")   # from the DW-Production root
Use the wrapper inside DW-Production and the generic create_sector_script() everywhere else.

text:
9.7 Auditing a profile: review_profile()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
review_profile() is for a profile that someone wrote by hand, edited, or inherited from before the scaffolder existed. It reads the file and runs ten presence checks, reporting pass, warn or fail for each. The audit is pattern-based, not parse-based: it searches for the load-bearing lines rather than parsing the script, so it tolerates the stylistic variety of older profiles. It never runs the profile.

RPython


review_profile("profile_DW-Production.R")

# A profile that never touches the IO or API helpers:
review_profile("profile_my-project.R", require_dw_mode = FALSE)


review_profile("profile_DW-Production.py")
review_profile("profile_my-project.py", require_dw_mode=False)












#
Check
Fails at
What it looks for




1
Profile sentinel object
fail
A line profile_<name> <- TRUE (R) or = True (Python). Without it, sector scripts cannot tell the profile ran.


2
Cross-platform user identification
fail
Sys.getenv("USERNAME" or "USER" (R); os.environ.get( the same (Python).


3
Reproducibility seed
warn
set.seed( (R); random.seed(, np.random.seed( or numpy.random.seed( (Python).


4
user_config.yml load
fail
A mention of user_config.yml and a read_yaml( / yaml::yaml.load call (R) or yaml.safe_load / yaml.load (Python).


5
User block in user_config.yml
warn
user_config[[USERNAME]], user_config$USERNAME or user_block (R); user_config[USERNAME], user_config.get(USERNAME or user_block (Python). A profile that reads only top-level keys finds no dw_mode in a file nested by user name.


6
dw_mode (producer/reviewer) resolution
fail*
The strings dw_mode, producer and reviewer all present.


7
dw_require_no_api guard
fail*
dw_require_no_api defined or called.


8
Z: drive availability advisory
warn†
dw_z_available, or network_root assigned a "Z: string.


9
Collaboration model block
warn
dw_collaboration(. Missing it is a warning only when the cso_project.yml found above the profile sets multi-producer (or cannot be read); otherwise the check passes.


10
Packages block (R) / Imports block (Python)
warn
requireNamespace(, install.packages( or library( (R); an import or from statement (Python).



* Checks 6 and 7 drop to warn with require_dw_mode = FALSE, for a profile that never touches the IO or API helpers. † Check 8 is a warn unless require_z_drive_check = TRUE, when it becomes a fail.
Both versions return a data frame with columns check, status and detail: invisibly in R, directly in Python. With verbose (the default) they also print a summary with [OK] / [!] / [X] markers and a tally. In CI, gate on status == "fail".
A profile from create_profile() with its defaults scores nine passes and one warning, for the Z: advisory it does not include; with include_z_drive_check = TRUE it passes all ten. The project profile template likewise passes with no failure.
