title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
9.8 Verification checklist
A sector is not wired until it passes this short checklist. Steps 4 to 6 are the real test of adoption: they prove the contract holds, rather than that it appears in the code.

The profile loads green. With dw_mode: "reviewer", sourcing the profile prints the reviewer banner naming the sandbox.
The conductor shadows the globals. The run driver computes finaldir and shadows the working globals before sourcing any other script.
No back-door network calls. No script in the sector calls a remote except through dw_api_fetch. Search for the obvious culprits: httr::GET, httr::POST, httr::request, RETRY and read.csv("http in R, and the equivalents in Python and Stata.
A reviewer run stays in the sandbox. An end-to-end reviewer run writes every artefact under sandboxRoot, and the modification times in the canonical deposit are the same before and after.
A producer run reaches the deposit. An end-to-end producer run writes every artefact to the deposit, exactly as before adoption.
The compare step works in reviewer mode. The sector’s compare-against-warehouse script runs in reviewer mode and writes a per-segment report under the sandbox’s output/temp/.

review_profile() checks that the profile has the blocks step 1 relies on, and the contract auditor, test_scripts(), finds the raw HTTP calls of step 3 (Checks and CI). The rest needs a person and a real run.






Step 4’s modification-time check is not ceremony. It is the only test that catches a script which reads a canonical global correctly but writes through a stale handle captured before the conductor shadow ran. No static check can see that; only an end-to-end run with a before-and-after comparison can.

title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
9.9 A note on naming
Both packages export dw_-prefixed aliases of the scaffolders: dw_create_profile, dw_review_profile and dw_create_sector_script (an alias of the generic helper, not of create_dw_sector_script), alongside dw_test_scripts for the auditor. They are the same functions under a second name. The dw_ spelling avoids the cosmetic clash between test_scripts and unit-test naming such as testthat::test_*, and keeps the toolkit’s names uniform. Prefer the dw_ names in new code. The full alias map is in the function reference.

title: 9  Profiles and the mode switch
text:
9.10 Where this fits
Roles and the mode contract sets the obligations; The IO contract, The external-API contract and Aggregation describe the helpers this wiring routes. Starting a repository writes a profile that already follows this chapter, Vendoring and updates puts the helpers it loads into 00_functions/, and Checks and CI keeps raw IO and HTTP out once the repository is wired. With one switch in user_config.yml, the derived globals, the conductor shadow, optional branch isolation and a passing checklist, every helper call a repository makes is mode-correct. Wire it once and every script inherits it.

9  Profiles and the mode switch

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.1 What vendoring means
The toolkit is vendored, not installed. A repository that uses it copies the helper files into its own 00_functions/ folder, commits them to its own git history, and records the release it copied in a small manifest, .toolkit_manifest.yml. Nothing is source()d from the network, pip installed at session start or net installed from a share. This chapter explains why, shows how to vendor the helpers in each language, documents the manifest field by field, and then covers the other half of the bargain: how you find out that your copy is behind a release, see what changed, and update it on your own terms.
Vendoring is copying a dependency’s source code into your project instead of declaring it for an installer to resolve later. When a pipeline repository such as DW-Production adopts the toolkit, the helper files it needs (dw_io.R, dw_api.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R and the siblings it actually calls) are copied from the toolkit’s r/R/ folder into the repository’s 00_functions/ and tracked there. The copies freeze the vintage: every commit of the consuming repository records exactly which helper code was in effect.
The manifest next to the copies says what was copied and from where: the upstream repository (source), the release tag (pulled_version) and the list of files (vendored). It is committed with the helpers and updated every time they are refreshed. Its fields are described below.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.2 Why vendor instead of install
Four reasons drive the choice, and they reinforce one another. The toolkit’s strategy document and README make the same case.
Reproducibility. A publication that cites a dw_<sector>.csv deposit in 2026 must, two years later, give identical numbers when someone re-runs the pipeline. That fails the moment the helper code can drift out from under the analysis. With vendoring there is no situation where “the repository’s pinned version was X but the running session installed Y”: a 2026-05 release is re-run with the helper code as it stood in 2026-05, because that code is physically in the repository at that commit. Network sourcing resolves to whatever is current at run time, which is precisely the drift the toolkit exists to prevent.
Producer-controlled refresh. Updates are never pulled automatically. The producer reads the release notes, decides whether the new release suits the current work, and refreshes explicitly. This reverses the usual package-manager default, where dependencies creep forward on their own: a vendored copy does not change until someone chooses to change it and commits the result.
Offline reviewers. A reviewer with no network access, on a plane or behind a corporate proxy, can still re-run the whole pipeline, because the helpers are in the repository. Reviewer mode forbids external network calls (Roles and the mode contract), so a reviewer could not fetch helpers even if the design allowed it. The frozen deposit, the frozen API cache and the frozen helper code all travel with the repository.
One model for three languages. A package model fits two of the languages tolerably and Stata poorly. Copying files in and pinning the release works the same way everywhere: R helpers go into 00_functions/, the Python package into 00_functions/cso_toolkit/, the Stata .ado and .sthlp files into ado/.
A practical fifth reason: UNICEF laptops block many script-installable paths outright (AppLocker). Copying files into a project folder always works where a network installer may be silently denied. Vendoring trades a small, explicit refresh step for vintage permanence across three languages and any number of repositories.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.3 Development install and production vendoring
Each language also has a native install path. It is a convenience for working on the toolkit itself or for experimenting, not the model a consuming repository ships with: the reproducibility, offline and producer-control guarantees above all depend on the production path being vendored.

RPythonStata


# Development: install the package from a clone
devtools::install_local("r/")

# Production: the vendored copies, sourced from 00_functions/
source("00_functions/dw_io.R")
source("00_functions/dw_api.R")


# Development: editable install from a clone
#   pip install -e python/
#   pip install -e "python/[all]"   # with the optional libraries
# Extras: excel, parquet, yaml, http, sdmx, worldbank, test, all

# Production: import the vendored package (see below)
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "00_functions")
from cso_toolkit import _state, dw_save, dw_use


* Development: put the clone's source folder on the adopath
adopath ++ "C:/Github/myados/cso-toolkit/stata/src"
which dw_save

* Production: copy the files into the project's ado/ (or the PERSONAL
* adopath); Stata finds them once they are on the path.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
section: 10.4 What lives in cso-toolkit and what lives in your repository
text:
10.4 What lives in cso-toolkit and what lives in your repository
The boundary is sharp, and keeping it sharp is what lets many repositories share one contract without leaking sector detail upstream. The rule: if a helper would need to mention a specific sector to do its job, it does not belong in the toolkit. The toolkit supplies the reproducibility floor (uniform IO, mode-aware API caching, provenance sidecars, the aggregation and scaffolding families); your repository supplies the domain logic on top of it.
In cso-toolkit, anything repository-neutral and reusable:







Subtree
Content




r/R/
The R helpers (dw_io.R, dw_api.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R, aggregation, scaffolding, demographics)


python/src/
The Python package with the same helpers, plus _state.py for session configuration


stata/src/
The Stata .ado and .sthlp files, with dw_stata_helpers.py and _dw_py.ado


templates/
.toolkit_manifest.yml, cso_project.yml, the project scaffolds (project/, profile/, testthat/, agents/), tools/check.R and the pre-push hook, the .gitignore and .gitattributes files, the opt-in workflows, dbm_submission_template.md


docs/
Operational docs: roles and workflow, mode-contract integration, per-function references


r/tests/, python/tests/, stata/tests/, conformance/
Tests of the helpers


NEWS.md and git tags
Release notes and the release tags



In your repository, never in the toolkit, anything sector- or repository-specific: your profile script and sector code; your user_config.yml (the mode, the paths); sector data, indicator lists and pipeline conductors; anything that refers to a particular sector’s domain.
This division is why new repositories (UNPD-Population, datalib, future deposit-bearing ones) inherit the floor instead of reinventing it. It is also why a drift problem the project hit early, four regional-metadata CSVs read independently by five sectors with no shared vintage record, does not recur once everyone vendors the same helpers and pins them in one manifest.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.5 Vendoring the helpers
The scaffolders do this for you: create_research_project() and create_official_stats_project() with vendor = TRUE copy a default set of helpers from a release tag of a local clone and write the manifest with pulled_version and pulled_commit filled in (Starting a repository). They always vendor the R helpers, from r/R/, whichever language you call them from; a Python package copy is vendored by hand, as below. To vendor by hand, into a repository that already exists, copy the files from a clone of cso-toolkit checked out at a release tag, never from a branch, so the bytes you commit are the bytes the manifest will name. Copy only the helpers your pipeline calls, and list exactly those in the manifest.

RPythonStata


# From the root of your repository; TK is a clone of cso-toolkit
git -C "$TK" switch --detach v0.12.0
mkdir -p 00_functions
cp "$TK"/r/R/dw_io.R "$TK"/r/R/dw_api.R "$TK"/r/R/cso_toolkit_sync.R \
   "$TK"/r/R/test_scripts.R "$TK"/r/R/zzz.R  00_functions/
cso_toolkit_sync.R uses small internals defined in dw_io.R, so vendor the two together. tools/check.R needs three files in 00_functions/ for its contract-audit and vintage checks: dw_io.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R and test_scripts.R (Checks and CI). The generated profile sources every .R file in 00_functions/, zzz.R first because it defines internals the other helpers call:
fs <- sort(list.files(dwFunct, pattern = "\\.R$", full.names = TRUE))
for (f in c(fs[basename(fs) == "zzz.R"], fs[basename(fs) != "zzz.R"])) {
  sys.source(f, envir = globalenv())
}


The Python helpers are one package (its modules import each other), so copy the whole folder into 00_functions/cso_toolkit/:
git -C "$TK" switch --detach v0.12.0
mkdir -p 00_functions/cso_toolkit
cp -r "$TK"/python/src/* 00_functions/cso_toolkit/
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "00_functions")           # makes `cso_toolkit` importable
from cso_toolkit import dw_save, dw_use, dw_compare, dw_api_fetch
from cso_toolkit import _state as cso_state
The sync helpers below expect vendored files flat, next to the manifest, so syncing a package copy is not supported yet (issue #230). Until it is, update a package copy as you would a Stata one: copy python/src/ again from the new tag and edit the manifest by hand (Updating a copy by hand).


Copy the .ado and .sthlp files into the project’s ado/ folder (or the PERSONAL adopath), together with dw_stata_helpers.py and _dw_py.ado: they are the Python side of dw_save and dw_collaboration (hashes, UTC time, the sidecar JSON, git), and _dw_py finds the .py file on the adopath.
git -C "$TK" switch --detach v0.12.0
mkdir -p ado
cp "$TK"/stata/src/*.ado "$TK"/stata/src/*.sthlp "$TK"/stata/src/dw_stata_helpers.py ado/



Then copy the manifest template, templates/.toolkit_manifest.yml, to 00_functions/.toolkit_manifest.yml, set pulled_version to the tag you copied, and commit the helpers and the manifest together.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.6 The manifest: .toolkit_manifest.yml
The manifest is the single record of which vintage a repository carries. It lives in 00_functions/, next to the helpers it tracks, because that is where the sync helpers look: in R the folder named by the dwFunct global (read from the global environment only, so a local variable of that name in a sector script cannot redirect it), in Python the dwFunct value in _state; without it, <working directory>/00_functions. The profile sets dwFunct (Profiles and the mode switch).
The template, as shipped:
source: "unicef-drp/cso-toolkit"
pulled_version: "v0.4.0"
pulled_date: "2026-05-26"
pulled_by: "<your-name>"
# target_version: "v0.4.0"   # optional: warn when pulled_version is behind

# Files vendored from cso-toolkit/r/R/ into consumer's 00_functions/
vendored:
  - dw_io.R
  - dw_api.R
  - cso_toolkit_sync.R
  # Optional — copy only the ones your pipeline uses:
  # - dw_project.R
  # - aggregate_data.R
  # - test_scripts.R
  # ...

# Local edits applied on top of vendored files. List paths here so that
# `cso_toolkit_pull()` skips them on update. (Empty by default.)
local_edits: []







Field
Meaning




source
GitHub owner/repo of the upstream toolkit. The check asks this repository for its latest release; diff, pull and sync read the release from it.


pulled_version
The tag the copies came from, e.g. "v0.12.0": the pin.


pulled_commit
Optional. The 40-hex commit pulled_version pointed to, so a moved or re-created tag can be noticed. The scaffolders and cso_toolkit_pull() write it.


pulled_date
ISO-8601 date of the pull. Some repositories call it pulled_at; an update keeps whichever the file has. No helper parses it.


pulled_by
Who ran the pull. A breadcrumb; an update writes the USERNAME (or USER) environment variable.


vendored
The files copied in: *.R from r/R/, *.py from python/src/. README.md, if listed, follows the other files (r/R/README.md when they are all R, python/src/README.md when they are all Python); leave it out when the repository keeps its own README, as scaffolded ones do. Diff, pull and sync iterate this list; tools/check.R confirms each listed file is present.


local_edits
Files in vendored with deliberate local changes. An update skips them, and it also skips a file that differs from what pulled_version shipped, listed or not.


target_version
Optional. The version this repository has decided it must run on, e.g. "v0.9.1". cso_toolkit_check() compares pulled_version with it offline, in both modes, and warns loudly when the copy is behind.


files
Optional, not in the template. A block of per-file sha256 values (DW-Production keeps one, dw_io.R: "<64-hex>"). An update refreshes the hashes it finds there; it does not add the block.



Keep vendored: honest: list a file only if it is in 00_functions/.

10.6.1 The inrepo pin
A pulled_version that is not a version number cannot be compared with anything. The convention is plain inrepo: helpers that were edited in the repository and should not trigger update warnings. cso_toolkit_check() never reports an inrepo copy as behind a target, and reports no newer upstream release for it (in producer mode it still asks GitHub, but updates_available comes back FALSE). This was the escape hatch for repositories whose scaffolding lived in-house before the toolkit’s own repository existed.
Only a plain inrepo is exempt. A value that starts with a version, such as "0.0.0-inrepo-2026-05-24", is read as that version (0.0.0) and is reported as behind.
Because a stray inrepo silences every drift warning, keep it out of production. The DBM pre-deposit checklist (templates/dbm_submission_template.md) requires 00_functions/.toolkit_manifest.yml to be on a tagged cso-toolkit version, with no inrepo or unreleased suffix. To leave an inrepo pin, run cso_toolkit_sync(): it treats the copy as behind any release and prints only the target release’s notes.


10.6.2 inrepo versus local_edits
The two are different tools. inrepo is a manifest-wide switch on pulled_version that silences the whole comparison. local_edits is a per-file list: the check still runs, and an update leaves those files alone.
Neither should be routine. A change to a helper belongs in cso-toolkit as a pull request; once it is released, a producer re-vendors the new release. If a local edit cannot wait, list the file under local_edits: and say why in the pull request that makes it. Every entry is a small breach of the vendoring model, a sign that the published toolkit was not sufficient on its own; a second repository adopting the toolkit with an empty local_edits: [] is part of the gate for v1.0.0 (Versioning and releases).






The update helpers compare file bytes, so line endings matter. The toolkit pins LF (.gitattributes), so a vendored file has the same bytes on Windows, Linux and macOS as the blob at its tag, and a scaffolded repository’s .gitattributes keeps 00_functions/** LF too. The comparison also ignores CRLF-only differences when it decides a file is unchanged, so a clone that checks files out with CRLF does not see every file as changed; the sha256_local it reports is still of the bytes on disk.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.7 Am I behind? cso_toolkit_check()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (update by hand; see Vendoring and updates). See the coverage matrix.
cso_toolkit_check() is meant for session start. By default (quiet = TRUE) it prints nothing and returns its result invisibly, so a profile can call it on every load without filling the console; pass quiet = FALSE for a readable verdict.
It compares pulled_version with two references:

A target version, from the target_version argument or else the manifest’s target_version: key. This is a requirement. The comparison needs no network, so it runs in producer and reviewer mode alike, and being behind is never silent.
The latest upstream release. This is information. Only producer mode asks GitHub for it; with quiet = FALSE a newer release produces a boxed notice.


RPython


res <- cso_toolkit_check()                    # silent; returns a list
res <- cso_toolkit_check(quiet = FALSE)       # logs the verdict

# Require a version (overrides the manifest's target_version: key)
cso_toolkit_check(quiet = FALSE, target_version = "v0.9.1")

if (!is.null(res) && isTRUE(res$updates_available)) cso_toolkit_sync()


from cso_toolkit import cso_toolkit_check, cso_toolkit_sync

res = cso_toolkit_check()                     # silent; returns a dict
res = cso_toolkit_check(quiet=False)          # logs the verdict
cso_toolkit_check(quiet=False, target_version="v0.9.1")

if res is not None and res["updates_available"]:
    cso_toolkit_sync()



The R function also takes verbose and debug; the Python one takes only quiet and target_version. In Python the boxed notices are WARNING-level log records and the other messages INFO-level ones. Both return the same keys:







Key
Meaning




source
The upstream slug from the manifest.


pinned_version
The manifest’s pulled_version ("0.0.0" when the key is missing).


upstream_version
The latest release found upstream; NA/None when not asked (reviewer mode) or not reachable.


updates_available
TRUE/True when the pin is older than the upstream release; FALSE for an inrepo pin; NA/None when upstream was not asked.


target_version
The target in effect; NA/None when there is none.


target_source
"argument", "manifest", or NA/None.


behind_target
TRUE/True when the pin is older than the target; NA/None with no target or an inrepo pin.


updated_files
Always NULL/None; the per-file view is cso_toolkit_diff().




10.7.1 When it returns nothing
The check returns NULL/None when there is nothing it can check:

No manifest. Without a .toolkit_manifest.yml in the helpers’ folder there is nothing to compare. R says so only with quiet = FALSE; Python logs it at INFO level. If the YAML package itself (yaml in R, PyYAML in Python) is missing, the check warns, even when quiet, and returns nothing.
Reviewer mode without a target. The upstream lookup is a network call, which reviewer mode forbids, so it is skipped; with no target to compare offline, nothing is left to check. With a target, a reviewer does get the comparison.
Producer mode, no target, and no upstream answer. If GitHub cannot be reached, the repository has no releases, or the manifest has no source:, the lookup resolves to “no result” rather than an error.

Versions compare numerically: a leading v and any pre-release or build suffix (-rc1, +meta) are dropped and the dotted numbers compared, so 0.10.0 is newer than 0.9.1, and a copy that is ahead of the latest release is not reported as behind.


10.7.2 A newer release: the boxed notice
When upstream has a newer release and quiet is off, a producer sees a notice with the next commands. It is information only; no warning is raised:
+-----------------------------------------------+
| A newer cso-toolkit release is available      |
|   vendored : v0.9.0                           |
|   latest   : v0.9.1  (unicef-drp/cso-toolkit) |
|                                               |
| To see the changes and update:                |
|   cso_toolkit_diff(target_version = "v0.9.1") |
|   cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "v0.9.1") |
+-----------------------------------------------+


10.7.3 A target version: loud when behind
A project that has decided to run on a given release, for example one that fixes a bug it depends on, records it as target_version: in the manifest (or passes target_version from the profile). When the copy is behind it, the check is deliberately loud:

it raises a warning in the error-envelope shape, carrying the exact cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = ...) command, even with quiet on, so a required re-vendor is never silent;
with quiet = FALSE it also prints a boxed alert with the vendored, target and (in producer mode) latest versions;
in reviewer mode it only warns: no network call is made and no file changes.

In a reviewer session with target_version: "v0.9.1" in the manifest and v0.9.0 vendored, cso_toolkit_check(quiet = FALSE) prints
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
| cso-toolkit is BEHIND its target version                      |
|   vendored : v0.9.0                                           |
|   target   : v0.9.1  (manifest target_version)                |
|                                                               |
| Producer mode is needed to update (reviewer mode only warns): |
|   cso_toolkit_diff(target_version = "v0.9.1")                 |
|   cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "v0.9.1")                 |
+---------------------------------------------------------------+
and raises
[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_check] The vendored cso-toolkit (v0.9.0) is behind its target version v0.9.1 (from the manifest's target_version key).
 Reviewer mode: no network call was made and nothing was changed; ask the producer to re-vendor.
 Fix: in producer mode, run cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "v0.9.1"): it prints the release notes, then updates the vendored copy and re-pins the manifest. (Re-vendoring v0.9.1 by hand also means updating pulled_version in .toolkit_manifest.yml.)
In producer mode the middle line reads “Pipelines run on the older helpers until the re-vendor.” A pin at or above the target passes silently, and an inrepo pin is never behind. The vintage check of tools/check.R runs this comparison and fails when the copy is behind its target; a newer upstream release is not a failure there (Checks and CI).


10.7.4 How the latest release is found
The lookup tries three routes in order:

The gh CLI, when it is on the PATH: gh api repos/<source>/releases/latest --jq .tag_name. Using gh avoids an authentication flicker when gh auth status is already good.
The GitHub API, https://api.github.com/repos/<source>/releases/latest (with httr in R, requests in Python), reading tag_name from a 200 response.
Git over HTTPS: git ls-remote --tags --refs https://github.com/<source>.git, taking the highest vX.Y.Z tag (no pre-releases, compared numerically). This works on networks that block api.github.com but let git through, as UNICEF proxies often do.

Git is run without a credential prompt and with a timeout. If no route gives a tag, the check stays silent about upstream.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
section: 10.8 Where an update reads the release from
text:
10.8 Where an update reads the release from
cso_toolkit_diff(), cso_toolkit_pull() and cso_toolkit_sync() read the helpers of a release tag, never a working tree or a branch, so the bytes you receive are exactly those of the release the manifest will name. There are two sources:

A local clone. With toolkit_source = "<clone>", or the CSO_TOOLKIT_ROOT environment variable, the tag is read from the clone’s git history with git cat-file blob <commit>:<path>. The clone is never fetched, checked out or otherwise changed; its branch and any local edits do not matter. A tag the clone lacks stops the call with a fix of git -C <clone> fetch --tags. No network is needed, so this works offline, and (for the diff) in reviewer mode.
GitHub. Otherwise the tag is cloned shallowly and without a checkout into a temporary folder, deleted afterwards: git clone --depth 1 --branch <tag> --no-checkout https://github.com/<source>.git. Git over HTTPS works where proxies block api.github.com.

With no tag given, the latest release is used: the clone’s highest vX.Y.Z tag, or GitHub’s latest release found as above. Pre-release tags such as v1.0.0-rc1 are passed over. A tag written without its v ("0.10.0") gets one.
A vendored file’s place in the toolkit follows from its extension: *.R from r/R/, *.py from python/src/, and README.md from the folder of the others (a README.md listed with both .R and .py files, or with neither, stops the call). Any other file under vendored:, an .ado for example, stops the call with an error naming it; vendor such files by hand.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.9 What changed? cso_toolkit_diff()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
cso_toolkit_diff() compares every file under vendored: with the same file at a release tag, prints a one-paragraph summary and returns a table. It writes nothing.

RPython


d <- cso_toolkit_diff()                              # the latest release
d <- cso_toolkit_diff(target_version = "v0.12.0")
d[d$status != "unchanged", ]
attr(d, "target_commit")

cso_toolkit_diff(toolkit_source = "C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")   # offline


from cso_toolkit import cso_toolkit_diff

d = cso_toolkit_diff()                               # a pandas DataFrame
d = cso_toolkit_diff("v0.12.0")
d[d.status != "unchanged"]
d.attrs["target_commit"]

cso_toolkit_diff(toolkit_source="C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")    # offline



The arguments are target_version (default: the latest release), toolkit_source, verbose and debug. In Python, toolkit_source, verbose and debug are keyword-only, and verbose defaults to True; in R, verbose = NULL and debug = NULL follow the session’s verbosity options.
Each row has file, status, sha256_local and sha256_target (missing where the file is absent). The table also carries the source, pulled_version, the target tag and its 40-hex commit (R attributes, Python df.attrs). Without a manifest the diff returns NULL/None. The status is one of:








Status
Meaning
What an update does




unchanged
The vendored bytes are the tag’s (line endings aside).
nothing


changed
The tag has a different version, and the vendored copy is what pulled_version shipped.
writes the tag’s file


local_edit
Listed under local_edits:, or different from what pulled_version shipped: someone edited it here.
skips it and lists it


missing_upstream
The tag has no such file (removed or renamed upstream).
keeps the vendored copy and warns


missing_local
Listed under vendored: but not in the folder.
adds it



Telling a local edit from an upstream change needs the pulled_version tag as well (fetched alongside the target when reading from GitHub); the manifest’s pulled_commit is the fallback. When neither can be read, a file that differs from the target is reported as changed, and the per-file prompt of the update is the safeguard.
Reading from GitHub is a network call, so in reviewer mode the diff stops with an error unless toolkit_source (or CSO_TOOLKIT_ROOT) names a local clone.
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.10 Updating: cso_toolkit_sync() and cso_toolkit_pull()

10.10.1 cso_toolkit_sync(): the one call

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
cso_toolkit_sync() is the call to remember. It resolves the target (target_version, or else the latest release), says “up to date” and stops when pulled_version is already there (or, with no target given, past it), and otherwise:

prints the upstream NEWS.md, read from the target tag, for every version after pulled_version up to the target, marking with !! the lines under a Breaking or Changed heading and any line that says BREAKING: these may need changes in your own code;
compares and updates exactly as cso_toolkit_pull() does, with the same guards, confirm, dry_run and manifest update.


RPython


cso_toolkit_sync(dry_run = TRUE)    # release notes and the diff; writes nothing
cso_toolkit_sync()                  # then update, asking per file
cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "v0.12.0", toolkit_source = "C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")


from cso_toolkit import cso_toolkit_sync

cso_toolkit_sync(dry_run=True)
cso_toolkit_sync()
cso_toolkit_sync("v0.12.0", toolkit_source="C:/GitHub/cso-toolkit")



[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_sync] release notes v0.11.1 -> v0.12.0 (NEWS.md at v0.12.0; !! = Breaking or Changed: read before updating)

   ## v0.12.0 (2026-11-24)
   ### Added
   - ...
!! ### Changed
!! - ...
flagged:
   v0.12.0: ### Changed
It takes the same arguments as cso_toolkit_pull() except allow_downgrade: to go back to an older release, use cso_toolkit_pull(..., allow_downgrade = TRUE). It returns NULL/None when up to date, and otherwise the pull table with the printed release-note lines attached (attr(x, "news"), df.attrs["news"]). From an inrepo pin it prints the target release’s notes only.


10.10.2 cso_toolkit_pull(): move to a named tag

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a. See the coverage matrix.
cso_toolkit_pull() updates the vendored files to a release tag you name and re-pins the manifest. It skips the release notes, so most people reach it through cso_toolkit_sync(); call it directly to move to a specific tag or to go back.

RPython


cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0", dry_run = TRUE)      # what would change; writes nothing
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0")                      # asks per file
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0", confirm = FALSE)     # in scripts and Rscript
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.11.1", allow_downgrade = TRUE)


from cso_toolkit import cso_toolkit_pull

cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0", dry_run=True)
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0")
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.12.0", confirm=False)
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.11.1", allow_downgrade=True)











Argument
Default
Meaning




target_version
required
The release tag, e.g. "v0.12.0" ("0.12.0" gets a v).


confirm
TRUE / True
Ask per file: overwrite, skip, or show the diff. Needs an interactive session.


dry_run
FALSE / False
Report what would change; write nothing.


toolkit_source
NULL / None
A local clone to read the tag from; otherwise CSO_TOOLKIT_ROOT, otherwise GitHub. Keyword-only in Python.


allow_downgrade
FALSE / False
Allow a tag older than pulled_version. Keyword-only in Python.


verbose, debug
R NULL; Python True, False
Progress messages and troubleshooting detail. In R, NULL follows getOption("dw.verbose", TRUE) and getOption("dw.debug", FALSE) (see dw_verbosity()).



In order, a pull (and a sync):

Refuses in reviewer mode, even with a local clone: an update changes the vendored helpers and the pin, which is a producer’s decision (and reading GitHub is a network call reviewer mode forbids). The error’s fix is to switch the profile to producer mode: dw_mode: producer in user_config.yml for R; _state.configure(dw_mode="producer", dw_apis_allowed=True) in Python (Profiles and the mode switch). A missing manifest, or one without source:, stops too.
Resolves the tag. A pull without target_version stops and points to cso_toolkit_sync().
Refuses a downgrade, a tag older than pulled_version, unless allow_downgrade = TRUE.
Starts from a clean folder. When 00_functions/ is inside a git repository, any uncommitted change under it (git status --porcelain) stops the call: an update must be one reviewable commit. dry_run skips this check.
Compares every file as cso_toolkit_diff() does. If the tag is the one already pinned, it reports “already at” and writes nothing; if the manifest’s pulled_commit differs from the commit the tag points to now, it warns that the tag was moved or re-created upstream.
Writes. local_edit files are skipped and listed; missing_upstream files are kept, with a warning; changed and missing_local files are written atomically (a temporary file in the same folder, then a rename). With confirm = TRUE each file is offered as overwrite, skip or show diff; in a non-interactive session confirm = TRUE stops before anything is written, and the fix is confirm = FALSE after a dry run. A file you decline now differs from the tag: list it under local_edits: or pull again.
Re-pins the manifest by editing its lines in place, so comments, line endings and keys the toolkit does not know survive: pulled_version; pulled_commit (added after pulled_version if absent); the date key the file already has, pulled_date or pulled_at (pulled_date if neither); pulled_by; and the hashes of an existing files: block. vendored, local_edits and target_version are never touched. The edits are byte-identical across languages (a test pulls one repository with each and compares).

It returns the diff table with an action column: updated, added, skipped (declined at the prompt), skipped_local_edit, kept (missing upstream), none, or with dry_run would_update and would_add. It ends with the next steps:
[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_pull] v0.11.1 -> v0.12.0 (5f0ee3c): updated 2 (dw_io.R, cso_toolkit_sync.R), added 0; skipped 0 local edit(s); kept 0 missing upstream; manifest re-pinned.
[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_pull] next: read NEWS, run tools/check.R and the tests, commit 00_functions/ in one commit naming old and new tags ("Update cso-toolkit v0.11.1 -> v0.12.0").
Every error follows the toolkit’s envelope: a [cso_toolkit.<function>] prefix, why, and a Fix: (Error taxonomy). Python raises PermissionError in reviewer mode, FileNotFoundError without a manifest, ValueError for a malformed tag, a pull without one, a missing source: or a refused downgrade, RuntimeError for uncommitted changes or a prompt in a non-interactive session, LookupError for a tag a local clone lacks, and ConnectionError when the latest release cannot be found or the tag cannot be read from GitHub.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.11 The refresh decision flow
The helpers compose into one producer-driven loop:
cso_toolkit_check()    at session start (producer mode)
     |                 newer release?  -> boxed notice, "vendored v0.11.1, latest v0.12.0"
     |                 behind target?  -> warning in both modes
     |                 otherwise       -> silent (also in reviewer mode, or for inrepo)
     v
the producer decides:  update now, or keep the pin (a valid, deliberate state)
     |
     v
cso_toolkit_sync()     NEWS.md since the pin, Breaking/Changed marked
     |                 per-file diff (cso_toolkit_diff)
     |                 write changed files, asking per file; re-pin (cso_toolkit_pull)
     v
checks + tests  ->  one commit: "Update cso-toolkit v0.11.1 -> v0.12.0"
Three properties make the loop safe by design:

It is producer-only. The upstream lookup and every write are gated on dw_apis_allowed. Reviewers never ask GitHub and never change the pin; they run the pinned vintage. A reviewer can still inspect a diff offline against a local clone. To validate against a different vintage, a reviewer cannot do it from a reviewer session: someone refreshes the pin in a producer session and commits it.
Updates are never automatic. Nothing changes without an explicit call, and the default asks before each file. A repository can sit two releases behind indefinitely.
The pin is the audit trail. The manifest is committed with the helpers, and an update starts from a clean folder and ends in one commit, so the repository’s history shows which toolkit release was in effect at every commit.


10.11.1 Moving to a new release, step by step

See where you stand. cso_toolkit_check(quiet = FALSE) names the pinned version and the latest release.
Work on a branch off develop, with 00_functions/ committed and clean.
Read what changes, writing nothing: cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "<tag>", dry_run = TRUE). Read every !! entry and its Migration: note; while the toolkit is in its 0.x line, a breaking change can ride in a minor release, so the release notes, not the version number, tell you whether your code must change. Note every local_edit.
Update: cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "<tag>"), or with confirm = FALSE in a script.
Re-run the checks and the tests (Checks and CI). A test that pins published numbers and now fails means the update moves numbers: find out which and why before going on, and never re-pin a test just to make it pass.
Commit the vendored files and the manifest together, in one commit naming the old and new tags, record the checks (sh tools/check --record), and open the pull request listing the release-note entries that matter to your repository.

One tag covers all three languages: there is one v0.12.0, not one per language. A release can add a function in one language before the others, so look up your language in the coverage matrix, not the tag. A published tag is never moved, which is what makes a pin mean the same bytes forever; how releases are cut is in Versioning and releases.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.12 Asserting a minimum version: dw_toolkit_version()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (each .ado carries its own version header). See the coverage matrix.
dw_toolkit_version() returns the release the vendored dw_io was taken from, as a version string without the v ("0.12.0"). A sector script can assert a floor before relying on a feature of a recent release. It touches no network and works in every mode. The same value is recorded in the sidecar dw_stage() writes and in dw_publish() payloads.

RPython


if (utils::compareVersion(dw_toolkit_version(), "0.4.0") < 0) {
  stop("This script requires cso-toolkit >= 0.4.0; ",
       "found ", dw_toolkit_version(), ". Update with cso_toolkit_sync().")
}


from cso_toolkit import dw_toolkit_version

if tuple(map(int, dw_toolkit_version().split("."))) < (0, 4, 0):
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"This script requires cso-toolkit >= 0.4.0; found {dw_toolkit_version()}."
    )



The R function takes an optional debug; the Python one takes no arguments. Python has no compareVersion, so compare tuples as above.






The stamp is a constant written into each language’s source (_TOOLKIT_VERSION in Python’s dw_io.py), not read from the manifest. The two are meant to move together at each release but can drift (in an earlier release R returned "0.5.0" while Python returned "0.4.0"). Treat the value as a floor for the language you call it from, not as a cross-language equality check, and treat the manifest’s pulled_version as the record of what the repository vendored.



Stata .ado files carry their own *! version header instead (for example dw_save.ado: *! version 1.3 21NOV2026): a per-file version and date, not the toolkit release.

title: 10  Vendoring and updates
text:
10.13 Updating a copy by hand
A Stata copy, and a Python package copy until #230 is closed, is updated by hand. Nothing detects drift for you, so make it a documented step of the repository’s routine:

Read NEWS.md from your pulled_version up to the new tag, as cso_toolkit_sync() would print it.
Check out the new tag in a clone (git -C "$TK" switch --detach <tag>) and copy the files again: for Stata, the .ado and .sthlp files, dw_stata_helpers.py and _dw_py.ado into ado/; for Python, python/src/ into 00_functions/cso_toolkit/.
Edit .toolkit_manifest.yml: pulled_version (the tag), pulled_commit (git -C "$TK" rev-list -n 1 <tag>), pulled_date and pulled_by.
Run the checks and the tests, and commit the files and the manifest in one commit naming the old and new tags.

Two cautions. The vendored: list is read by the update helpers, which map files by extension to r/R/ and python/src/; an .ado listed there makes cso_toolkit_diff(), cso_toolkit_pull() and cso_toolkit_sync() stop with an error naming it. And the vintage check of tools/check.R looks for every listed file in 00_functions/. So in a repository that also vendors R helpers, record the Stata copy’s tag in pulled_version and keep the .ado files off the vendored: list. A target_version: in the manifest still works for a Stata copy: run cso_toolkit_check() in the same repository, in a language that has it (see its languages line above), and it warns when the pin is behind.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.1 Data stay out; their provenance goes in
A repository that follows the contract still needs something that tells it when it stops following it. This chapter covers the checks a consumer repository runs before its changes merge: that no data slipped into git, that no secret did either, that the provenance sidecars it commits are well-formed, that the analysis code goes through the dw_* wrappers, that the vendored toolkit is the vintage the repository claims, and that the project’s own functions still do what their tests say.
Those checks run locally first, with one command. A committed check record proves they passed on the exact content being merged, and GitHub verifies that record in seconds without running R. The full checks run on GitHub Actions only when a repository opts in. The chapter ends with the contract auditor, test_scripts(), the check that turns the IO and API contract into a build gate.
Everything here ships as copyable material in the toolkit repository:
create_research_project() and create_official_stats_project() write all of this, set for the repository’s kind (Starting a repository). They write the wrapper, the hook, check-record.yml and .checks/README.md every time, and the other workflows only with workflows = TRUE. They print the branch-protection steps but do not change repository settings.
The rule the rest of the chapter enforces fits in one line: data never enter git, and the provenance sidecars that say exactly which bytes each result came from always do. Data live in the deposit (the Teams folder and its Z: mirror, the microdata archive, Gitea LFS), and dw_fetch_inputs() fills a local, gitignored inputs folder from it (The IO contract). What git holds is the record: every dw_save() output carries a <file>.provenance.json sidecar with the file’s hash and, through metadata.inputs, the hashes of the inputs it was built from (Provenance and errors; fields in Appendix B). Committing the sidecars puts that record under version control while the data stay out, so a reviewer can tell from git alone which bytes produced a result, and dw_provenance_diff() can tell whether a re-run reproduced it.
A sidecar sits next to its file when the file is inside the repository but ignored: data/derived/panel.csv.provenance.json is tracked and panel.csv is not. Microdata kept outside the repository get their sidecars under data/provenance/<path>/, mirroring where the file lives, so the sidecar for S:\datalib-edu\KEN\2022\hh.dta is committed as data/provenance/S/datalib-edu/KEN/2022/hh.dta.provenance.json.
The .gitignore pattern that does this has four kinds of line, and the second is the one people drop:
Git cannot re-include a file whose parent directory is excluded: it never looks inside an excluded directory, so a ! rule for a file in one is never consulted. Because data/** also matches the sub-directories, !data/**/ (the trailing slash means “directories only”) lets git look inside them again; the files there stay ignored unless a later ! line names them. For the same reason the folder rule is data/**, never data/: the latter excludes the directory itself, and nothing below it can come back.
The templates repeat the block for inputs/, _apis/ (the API cache) and _frozen/ (frozen URL downloads). They then ignore data formats wherever they appear (*.dta, *.rds, *.parquet, …), secrets and personal configuration (.env, *.pem, *.key, user_config.yml, .Renviron), and the build noise of R, Python, Stata, Quarto and LaTeX. Both re-include .checks/*.json after every rule that could ignore it, so check records are always tracked.

title: 11  Checks and CI

data/**                       # ignore everything below data/
!data/**/                     # re-include the directories
!data/**/README.md            # then only these files
!data/**/.gitkeep
!data/**/*.provenance.json
!data/**/input_manifest.*



11.1.1 Research projects and official statistics
The two templates differ in where results live. In a research project git is the canonical store for results: the small tables and figures a reader checks the paper against are tracked, each with its sidecar.
In an official-statistics repository (a DW sector pipeline, an SDMX or data.unicef.org publication pipeline, a survey-processing repository) the canonical store is the deposit, then SDMX and data.unicef.org, and pre-release figures are embargoed. Access to the repository is not authorization to release what is in it, and git history keeps whatever was committed. So official-stats.gitignore ignores output folders outright (**/output/**, **/outputs/**, **/results/**, **/wrk/**, and **/013_wrkdata/**, the work-data stage of the deposit layout), sidecars included, and a small pre-release CSV cannot be committed by accident. The raw-data stage, **/011_rawdata/**, keeps only its READMEs, sidecars and manifests, like inputs/.
What such a repository commits instead is a release record. After publication, as part of the release pull request, it adds releases/<vintage>/output_manifest.csv (one row per deposited file with file, sha256, bytes, deposited_at and the path relative to the deposit root) and copies of the deposited files’ .provenance.json sidecars. The template re-includes exactly those files under releases/. A release record is never committed before the publication date: its hashes describe embargoed figures.

_config_template/user_config.yml



Both templates ignore a reviewer’s local artefacts, sandbox/ and the *.staged.json sidecars dw_stage() writes. The blocks they share (data formats, secrets, language noise, OS and editors) are kept identical by a test in the toolkit’s own suite, so edit both copies together.






TipCheck the rules, not your memory of them



git check-ignore -v <path> prints the line that decides a path. git ls-files -i -c --exclude-standard lists tracked files the rules now say should be ignored; after adopting a template it must print nothing. git rm --cached -- <path> untracks a file without deleting it. History still holds anything committed before. Removing it from history is a separate decision, taken with the repository owner (and the data owner, for confidential microdata), and a leaked secret is rotated first, whatever happens to history.


The ignore file is the safety net, not the first line of defence. That is the staging habit: never git add -A or git add .; stage by path (git add -- R/clean.R results/t1.csv results/t1.csv.provenance.json) and read git diff --cached --stat before committing. The checks below catch what both miss.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.2 Design principles
Ten principles shape the checks. Each earns its place by a failure it prevents.

Checks run locally first. Every check runs on your machine with one command from the repository root and prints a PASS / WARN / FAIL / SKIP line per check, exiting non-zero on any failure. GitHub Actions are opt-in and call the same script, so they add an independent run, never a different check. Actions minutes run out, and a failure reproduced on your machine gets fixed before the push.
CI never needs real data. Tests use tiny synthetic fixtures. Reproduction against real data runs locally in reviewer mode, and its evidence (the dw_provenance_diff() status, dw_check_deposit() output, a dw_compare() summary) goes in the pull request. Data must not be on a hosted runner, and a check that needs data cannot run on every push. For the same reason CI never runs in producer mode: the checks put their own session in reviewer mode (tools/check.R before it loads the vendored helpers, tests/testthat.R before it sources anything), no workflow template sets dw_mode, and a job must never set dw_mode: producer, which would allow network calls and canonical writes from a runner.
Default checks are fast, under ten minutes. A check people wait for gets skipped, and a pre-push hook that takes too long gets bypassed.
Merges are gated by the check record. The gate is a committed record that check.R passed on the pull request’s exact content, verified on GitHub without running R (Check records) and required by branch protection. A check that can be merged around is advice, not a gate.
Every bug fix ships a regression test that fails on the old code and names the issue. The bug cannot return silently, and the test records what went wrong.
Least privilege, pinned actions. Workflows start from permissions: contents: read, and actions are pinned to a version. A compromised dependency should not be able to write to the repository or alter results unnoticed.
No secrets in logs. Prefer checks that need no secret; scanners redact. Logs, and check output pasted into a pull request, are readable by everyone with access to the repository.
Fail with an actionable message, in the toolkit’s WHAT / Why / Fix envelope (Provenance and errors). A red check that says how to turn it green costs minutes.
Spend minutes where they buy something. When Actions run, default to ubuntu-latest and few jobs, since each is billed by the started minute; run Windows and macOS on a schedule or on release. Private repositories pay for minutes, and Windows minutes count double and macOS minutes ten times.
CI is documentation. The README has a short section listing the checks, the local command, and which workflows are switched on.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.3 Running the checks: tools/check
From the repository root:
sh tools/check                   # every default check
sh tools/check --record          # ... and, if none fails, commit a check record
sh tools/check --only tests      # one check (comma-separate several)
sh tools/check --skip tests      # all but one
sh tools/check --list            # the default and available names
tools/check is a small shell wrapper around Rscript --no-init-file tools/check.R, which takes the same arguments. Use --no-init-file, never --vanilla: --vanilla also drops .Renviron and the library path it sets. If Rscript is not on the PATH, as is common on Windows, set RSCRIPT to its path, or the wrapper looks in the default Windows install folder.
Windows. Started from Git Bash, R takes Git Bash’s HOME (C:\Users\<user>) as its home folder. It then misses a .Renviron that lives in Documents (often redirected to OneDrive), and with it the user library, and the checks fail with “there is no package called testthat”. tools/check therefore starts R with env -u HOME, so R falls back to Documents, and passes the original HOME as CHECK_GIT_HOME, which the git calls inside check.R get back, so git still finds user.name and user.email.
check.R needs R, git on the PATH, and the packages testthat (for tests), jsonlite (for sidecars; testthat installs it) and yaml (for vintage). When the repository has renv/activate.R, the script activates renv itself, since --no-init-file skips the project’s .Rprofile; CHECK_NO_RENV=true turns that off, as the workflows do. It prints a header line with the repository, commit (marked when there are uncommitted changes), R version and time, then one line per check, each failure with a Why: and a Fix: line, then a tally.
tools/check.R is an R script. A Python-only or Stata repository can still run the hygiene and sidecar checks with it, because they read files only and need just R and jsonlite: drop contract-audit, vintage and tests from CHECKS, and run pytest alongside.

11.3.1 Settings
The settings sit in one CONFIG block at the top of tools/check.R. An environment variable of the same name overrides any of them for one run, for example AUDIT_MODE=blocking sh tools/check.

tracked-data lists every tracked file outside ALLOW_PATHS that sits in a DATA_DIRS folder without matching DATA_ALLOW, has a DATA_EXTS extension, is a secret or personal configuration file (.env, .env.* but not .env.example, *.pem, *.key, *.p12, *.pfx, .netrc, .Renviron, user_config.yml), or sits in an OUTPUT_DIRS folder outside releases/. The fix it prints is git rm --cached -- <path>, which keeps the file on disk, plus the matching .gitignore rule.
large-files fails on any tracked file over MAX_FILE_MB. Git keeps every version forever, and GitHub rejects files over 100 MB. Move the file to the deposit and commit its sidecar instead.
secret-scan runs gitleaks git --redact over the full history. Locally it is skipped when gitleaks is not installed; in CI (CI=true) a missing gitleaks is a failure. A finding means the secret is compromised: rotate it first, then remove it from the code. A known false positive goes in .gitleaksignore, by the fingerprint from the report, with a comment saying why.
sidecars parses every tracked *.provenance.json and checks the shape Appendix B documents: path, format, written_at, dw_mode and a 64-character hex sha256 for an R or Python sidecar; datasignature in place of the hash for a Stata one (format dw_save.provenance/1); url, fetched_at, dw_mode and sha256 for an API-fetch or frozen-URL sidecar. It does not re-compute hashes: the data are not in the repository, so the bytes are checked locally or in reviewer mode, where dw_read_provenance(), dw_check_deposit() and dw_provenance_diff() have the files to hash. An R sidecar with no sha256 usually means the digest package was missing when it was written.
contract-audit loads dw_io.R and test_scripts.R from TOOLKIT_DIR, in reviewer mode, and runs test_scripts() over each folder in AUDIT_PATHS, skipping the vendored folder itself. It audits with the exact code and vintage the repository runs, not a fresh install. It fails when the vendored files or every AUDIT_PATHS folder are missing, or when AUDIT_MODE is neither blocking nor advisory. The auditor itself is described below.
vintage reads 00_functions/.toolkit_manifest.yml, requires source, pulled_version and vendored, confirms every vendored: file is present, and runs the vendored cso_toolkit_check() in reviewer mode, which compares against target_version offline. It fails when pulled_version is behind target_version. A newer upstream tag is not a failure: refreshing remains the producer’s decision (Vendoring and updates).
tests runs tests/testthat.R in a fresh R process (through renv when the repository has it), so the runner’s reviewer-mode globals do not leak into the check run. In an R package (a DESCRIPTION at the root) it is skipped with a pointer to R CMD check.
lint runs lintr::lint_dir(), excluding the vendored folder, renv and the test fixtures. It only ever warns, and is skipped when lintr is not installed.
manuscript builds PAPER_DIR/ROOT_FILE with latexmk from the committed tables and figures and fails when the PDF is over MAX_PAGES (0 turns the limit off). Without latexmk it is skipped locally and fails in CI; without pdfinfo the page count is not checked.



11.3.3 Contract audit: blocking or advisory
AUDIT_MODE decides what a contract violation does. blocking, the template’s default, fails the run. advisory lists the violations under a [WARN] line and does not fail it. Official statistics keep it blocking, because a raw read there is an input without provenance in a published figure. A research project created by create_research_project() starts advisory, because its first scripts read their data directly (haven::read_dta(), read.csv()) long before they move to dw_use(). The audit reports each such line from the first day, and the project switches to "blocking" once its code reads through the wrappers.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.4 testthat in every R repository
A sector pipeline or a paper is not an R package, so it has no R CMD check to run its tests. The templates/testthat/ skeleton fills that gap with a runner, tests/testthat.R, that works without a DESCRIPTION. It puts the session in reviewer mode, so a test that reaches for the network or a canonical deposit fails instead of fetching; sources the vendored helpers from TOOLKIT_DIR (dw_io.R first); sources the project’s function files from SOURCE_DIRS (files that define functions, never scripts that run an analysis); and calls testthat::test_dir(), exiting non-zero on any failure. The scaffolders set SOURCE_DIRS to R/functions for a research project and leave it empty for official statistics.

RPython


# Locally, from the repository root:
#   sh tools/check --only tests
# (or the runner on its own: Rscript --no-init-file tests/testthat.R)

# A regression test names the issue and fails on the pre-fix code.
test_that("regression #12: codes with stray whitespace or lower case are kept", {
  ind <- read_fixture("indicators_synthetic.csv")   # tiny, synthetic
  out <- merge_country_names(ind, countries)
  expect_setequal(out$TIME_PERIOD[out$country == "Kenya"], c(2021, 2022))
})

test_that("an unknown code fails loudly with a WHAT / Why / Fix error", {
  err <- expect_error(merge_country_names(bad, countries))
  expect_envelope(err, "merge_country_names")
})


# No Python skeleton ships. Use pytest with the same rules: synthetic
# fixtures under tests/fixtures/, a regression test per fixed bug named
# after the issue, errors asserted on the "[<scope>.<function>] ... Fix:"
# envelope, and the session configured with dw_mode="reviewer",
# dw_apis_allowed=False.



The example in the skeleton is the pattern to copy rather than the function to keep: a small project function, a fixture that carries the very codes that once broke it, and a test whose title names the issue. Run against the old implementation, an inner join on raw codes, the test fails; against the fix it passes. The skeleton follows the toolkit’s own suite: helpers in helper-*.R (read_fixture(), local_tempdir(), local_dw_state(), expect_envelope()), session state set through a local setter that restores on exit, and errors asserted with expect_envelope(). No Stata test runner ships; the hygiene and sidecar checks still cover a Stata repository, since they read only files.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.5 Check records
Local-first checks leave one gap: nothing proves they were run on what gets merged. A forgotten hook, git push --no-verify, or a co-author who never enabled the hook all go unnoticed. Required status checks close that gap only by running the full checks on GitHub, which is what local-first avoids. A check record closes it at almost no Actions cost.

The record. sh tools/check --record runs the checks and, when none fails, writes .checks/<content-hash>.json and commits it, alone, with the message Check record <hash>. It needs a clean working tree on a commit (untracked files do not count), because a record certifies committed content: commit your changes first, and do not stash them, since worktrees share one stash list. --record refuses --only and --skip: a record never certifies a partial run. If a passing record for the content already exists, it says so and writes nothing.
What it holds. schema (check_record/1), content_hash, the commit and branch checked, result (pass), each check’s result in checks (pass; advisory for a WARN, such as an advisory contract audit or lint; skipped), toolkit (the manifest’s pulled_version), r_version, platform, user (git’s user.name), checked_at in UTC, and check_script_sha, the git hash of tools/check.R itself.
The content hash is git’s tree ID of the repository with .checks/ left out: git ls-tree HEAD | grep -v '\t.checks$' | git mktree. A record certifies content, not a commit ID, so the commit that adds the record keeps the same content hash, which avoids the chicken-and-egg problem. Computed from git objects, the hash is the same on Windows and Linux.
One file per checked state, about 1 KB each: records never conflict between branches, and history keeps every checked state.
Merging develop into a branch changes its content, so record again before pushing. A pull request whose content is identical to an already recorded state, such as the release pull request develop → main right after a feature merge, reuses that record.
Limits. A record can be written by hand. It prevents forgotten checks, not forgery, like any honour-based gate. Shared or mirrored repositories with different content need their own records.


11.5.1 The pre-push hook
templates/hooks/pre-push is tracked in the repository as .githooks/pre-push. Enable it once per clone:
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
The scaffolders do this for you when called with git = TRUE, and stage the hook and tools/check with their executable bit, so they run on macOS and Linux clones too.
The setting MODE at the top of the hook decides what it does, and CHECK_HOOK_MODE overrides it for one push:

MODE=verify (the default) requires, for each pushed branch, a passing record for the commit’s content, committed in that commit (the record must say "result": "pass"). It runs no R, so pushes stay fast. Branch deletions and tags are not checked. A refused push prints the command to run: sh tools/check --record, then push again.
MODE=run runs the checks instead (sh tools/check, or tools/check.R directly when the wrapper is missing), for repositories that do not use records. CHECK_ARGS="--skip tests" git push runs a subset, and RSCRIPT points at R when it is not on the PATH.

To skip the hook once, when you must, use git push --no-verify or CHECK_SKIP=1 git push, and say so in the pull request. The pull request’s check-record status still fails without a record.


11.5.2 The check-record workflow
check-record.yml is the one workflow on by default. It runs on pull requests into develop and main (and by hand), never on push. It checks out the pull request’s head commit, not GitHub’s merge commit, recomputes the content hash, and requires .checks/<hash>.json to exist and say pass; it then prints the record’s summary. It needs no R and no data, takes about 10 seconds, and has contents: read and pull-requests: read permissions. GitHub bills it as one minute on a private repository.
Automated pull requests (a bot rebuilding the handbook, a sync job) carry no record. List the generated paths they touch in the workflow’s EXEMPT_PATHS (space-separated shell patterns, where * also matches /, for example docs/handbook/*). A pull request whose every changed file matches one passes without a record. Anything that changes other files still needs one, whoever opened it.
Branch protection (Settings > Branches, for develop and main): require the status check check-record, and tick Require branches to be up to date before merging. Then what merges is exactly the checked content. The toolkit repository itself uses its parity certificate (How the three languages stay in step) and its package CI instead.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.6 The opt-in workflows
With workflows = TRUE, the scaffolders also write the workflows that run the full checks on GitHub: ci-hygiene.yml, ci-contract-audit.yml and ci-r-tests.yml for both kinds, and ci-manuscript.yml for a research project only. Each calls tools/check.R with --only, so they run exactly the local checks, and each is configured at the top of tools/check.R, not in the YAML.








Workflow
Runs
Notes




ci-hygiene.yml
tracked-data,large-files,secret-scan,sidecars
One job, not four. Full history (fetch-depth: 0) for the secret scan. Installs a pinned gitleaks binary (8.21.2): the gitleaks GitHub Action needs a licence key for organisation repositories, the binary does not.


ci-contract-audit.yml
contract-audit,vintage
Installs only yaml: test_scripts() needs base R.


ci-r-tests.yml
tests
Restores renv.lock when there is one, otherwise installs testthat, withr, yaml and jsonlite (add your project’s packages). An advisory lintr job runs on manual runs only, with continue-on-error. A commented r-package job runs R CMD check instead, for a repository that is an R package.


ci-manuscript.yml
LaTeX build and page count
Builds with xu-cheng/latex-action, checks pages with pdfinfo against MAX_PAGES, and uploads the PDF as an artifact for 14 days. A commented job does the same for Quarto.



By default they run only when started by hand and on pull requests into main (the release pull request), so routine pushes cost no Actions minutes, and every release gets an independent run on a clean runner for a few minutes. The manuscript workflow also has a paths: filter on paper/**. Each workflow carries a commented on: block that switches it to every push and pull request.
They are not required checks by default: with the default triggers they do not run on pull requests into develop, and a required check that never runs blocks the merge forever. A repository that has the minutes switches each workflow’s on: block, lets the workflows run green once, and then marks the Tier 0 and Tier 1 jobs as required on develop and main. Two details matter then. GitHub matches a required check by its job name, so the templates give each job a stable name:. And a required workflow must not carry a paths: filter: when a pull request touches no matching path the workflow never runs, and its required check waits forever. Path filters belong on advisory workflows only, which is why the manuscript workflow is advisory. Windows and macOS runs belong on a schedule or on release (the commented block at the end of ci-r-tests.yml), never on every push. The gitflow itself is in docs/git_workflow.md.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.7 The contract auditor: test_scripts()

Languages: R, Python. Stata: n/a (no Stata auditor). See the coverage matrix.
The contract says that file and network access go through a small set of wrappers: file IO through dw_save() / dw_use() / dw_compare() / dw_merge() (The IO contract), external APIs through dw_api_fetch() / dw_api_cached() (External APIs). A contract that is only documented decays. New scripts reach for read_csv() out of habit, a quick httr::GET() slips into a one-off fetch, and a reviewer approves the pull request without noticing either.
test_scripts() closes that gap. It walks a directory of analysis scripts and flags every line that calls a raw IO or HTTP function the toolkit wraps, together with the wrapper to use instead. Run interactively it is a code-review aid; with error_on_violation = TRUE it is a build gate.
The auditor and the wrappers are two layers of the same defence. The wrappers enforce the contract at the call site: once you call dw_save(), mode routing and provenance happen. The auditor enforces it at review time, catching the calls that never reached a wrapper at all.

11.7.1 What it does
For each file whose name matches pattern, the auditor reads the file line by line. Before matching, it replaces string literals with empty strings (so a URL or file name inside quotes does not trigger a rule) and strips trailing comments (so commented-out code is not flagged), while keeping any # cso-allow: directive, which it reads from the raw line. It then tests the line against every rule. A match is a violation.
It is a lexical check, not a parser: fast, with no dependencies beyond base R or pandas, but it sees text, not an abstract syntax tree. The false positives section says what that costs.

RPython


test_scripts(
  path,
  pattern            = "\\.R$",
  recursive          = TRUE,
  ignore_files       = c("dw_io.R", "dw_api.R", "cso_toolkit_sync.R",
                         "profile_helpers.R", "test_scripts.R"),
  ignore_dirs        = c(".git", "renv", "packrat",
                         "node_modules", ".Rproj.user"),
  custom_rules       = NULL,
  error_on_violation = FALSE,
  verbose            = TRUE,
  debug              = NULL
)


test_scripts(
    path,
    pattern=r"\.py$",
    *,
    recursive=True,
    ignore_files=("dw_io.py", "dw_api.py", "cso_toolkit_sync.py",
                  "profile_helpers.py", "test_scripts.py", "_state.py",
                  "__init__.py"),
    ignore_dirs=(".git", ".venv", "venv", "env", "__pycache__",
                 ".tox", ".pytest_cache", "node_modules"),
    custom_rules=None,
    error_on_violation=False,
    verbose=True,
)



path is a directory (searched recursively unless recursive = FALSE) or a single file. The file-name pattern is matched case-insensitively. ignore_files skips the toolkit’s own implementation files, which must call the raw commands; ignore_dirs skips machinery folders (version control, dependency caches, virtual environments). Both are overridable. A path that does not exist is an error with the [cso_toolkit.test_scripts] envelope: a stop() in R, a FileNotFoundError in Python. Python reads files as UTF-8 and silently skips a file it cannot decode.
R has one extra argument, debug (default NULL, which inherits options(dw.debug)). When TRUE it prints the file count, the rule count and per-family tallies, and implies verbose; it does not change what the auditor flags.
Both return a data frame (an R data.frame, a pandas DataFrame) with seven columns: file, line, rule, family, message, suggest and snippet. An empty frame means a clean scan. The columns are stable, so a CI step can read them to post annotations or build a report. R returns the frame invisibly: assign it (v <- test_scripts(...)) to inspect it, since a bare call at the console prints the summary but not the frame. Python returns it normally.


11.7.2 The rules
Every rule has five fields: id, family, pattern, message and suggest. The family is "io" or "api", and only those two families can fail a build. The pattern is a regular expression (PCRE in R) matched against the scrubbed line. The message names the bypass and suggest names the wrapper that replaces it, so a caught read_csv does not just say that a rule matched: it says Direct CSV read and points to dw_use(name = ..., sector = ..., kind = ...).

The two registries differ because the raw calls differ by ecosystem.
