A few rules reach further than their names suggest: io-xlsx also flags sheet enumeration (getSheetNames, excel_sheets, loadWorkbook), because dw_use(sheet = NULL) reads all sheets; io-load-save flags any save( or load(; api-httr flags GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE and httr2’s request; and api-download flags download.file and curl’s curl_download, curl_fetch_memory and curl_fetch_disk.
The Python rules target pandas (read_* and the .to_* methods), pickle, json, yaml, requests, httpx (including Client and AsyncClient), urllib, sdmx, wbgapi and wbdata. io-json flags json.dump and json.load on file handles, not json.dumps or json.loads on strings. io-open-write is a heuristic: it flags open() called with an explicit mode, read or write, as open(<path>, "<mode>") or open(..., mode="<mode>"), and leaves open(path) with no mode alone; its suggestion notes that a raw open() is fine for scratch files but should not touch warehouse paths.


11.7.3 Extending the rule set
Both implementations accept custom_rules, merged with the built-in registry. A consumer repository that wraps another data source adds a rule for it without editing the toolkit. Each custom rule supplies the same five fields.

RPython


my_rules <- list(
  list(id      = "api-mysource",
       family  = "api",
       pattern = "(?<![a-zA-Z0-9_.])mysource_fetch\\s*\\(",
       message = "Direct mysource_fetch call bypasses the cache.",
       suggest = "dw_api_fetch(api = 'mysource', cache_key = ...)")
)
test_scripts("01_dw_prep", custom_rules = my_rules)


from cso_toolkit.test_scripts import _Rule, test_scripts

my_rules = [
    _Rule(
        id="api-mysource", family="api",
        pattern=r"\bmysource_fetch\s*\(",
        message="Direct mysource_fetch call bypasses the cache.",
        suggest="dw_api_fetch(api='mysource', cache_key=...)",
    )
]
test_scripts("01_dw_prep", custom_rules=my_rules)



A custom rule under some other family is reported but never fails a build, which makes it a way to add advisory checks.


11.7.4 Reporting and the build gate
With the default verbose = TRUE, the auditor prints a fixed-format block: a header, the file count, the violation count, then one stanza per violation with the rule id, file and line, message, offending line and suggested replacement. (It shows every column except family, which only governs the gate.) A clean run prints [OK] Clean.. The format is the same in both languages.
cso-toolkit contract audit
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Files scanned : 14
Violations    : 1

[io-read-csv] 01_dw_prep/012_codes/nt/build.R:42
  Direct CSV read.
  > df <- read_csv("raw/nt.csv")
  -> dw_use(name = ..., sector = ..., kind = ...)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
By default the function only reports. The gate is error_on_violation. When it is TRUE and at least one violation belongs to the io or api family, the function raises after printing, with the toolkit’s error envelope: the [cso_toolkit.test_scripts] prefix, the number of violations and files, up to five offending files (with “and N more”), and a Fix: line that says to replace the raw call with its wrapper or annotate a legitimate exception with # cso-allow:. In R this is a stop(), in Python a RuntimeError; either way the process exits non-zero, which is what a CI runner needs to mark the step failed.

RPython


# Interactive: report only, inspect the frame.
v <- test_scripts("01_dw_prep/012_codes")

# CI gate: stop (non-zero exit) on any io/api violation.
test_scripts("01_dw_prep/012_codes", error_on_violation = TRUE)


# Interactive: report only, inspect the frame.
v = test_scripts("01_dw_prep/012_codes")

# CI gate: raise RuntimeError (non-zero exit) on any io/api violation.
test_scripts("01_dw_prep/012_codes", error_on_violation=True)





11.7.5 Exceptions: # cso-allow:
The contract has principled exceptions. The canonical one is the profile’s own configuration read: a profile reads user_config.yml with a raw yaml::read_yaml() / yaml.safe_load() because it bootstraps the configuration before any toolkit path resolution exists, and forcing it through dw_use() would be circular (Profiles and the mode switch).
For those, append # cso-allow: <rule-id> to the line. The auditor skips exactly the named rules on that one line; every other rule still applies to it, and every other line is still scanned. Several ids can be listed, comma-separated.

RPython


# Profile bootstrap: the one routine legitimate raw YAML read.
config <- yaml::read_yaml(config_path)  # cso-allow: io-yaml

# Silence two rules on one line:
x <- read_csv(p)  # cso-allow: io-read-csv, io-write-csv


# Profile bootstrap: the one routine legitimate raw YAML read.
with open(config_path, encoding="utf-8") as _f:
    user_config = yaml.safe_load(_f)  # cso-allow: io-yaml

# Silence two rules on one line:
x = pd.read_csv(p)  # cso-allow: io-read-csv, io-to-csv



The generated profiles already carry these annotations, and so do a few toolkit files (the CSV read in generate_markdown_report, the fixture reader in the testthat skeleton). Two rules of discipline follow. An allow is line-scoped and rule-scoped: it never silences a whole file or a whole rule, so a stray comment cannot quietly disable the contract for a folder. And an allow is a documented exception, not a convenience: it marks a call that genuinely cannot go through a wrapper, and it asks for the reviewer’s attention rather than dodging it.


11.7.6 False positives and limits
Because the auditor matches text, it misfires in predictable ways.

Same name, different function. In R, any function called request(, save( or load( matches, whatever package it comes from. The Python patterns have no lookbehind, so pl.read_csv( (polars) and a project function named my_read_csv( both match io-read-csv. Rename the project function, or mark a genuine exception with # cso-allow:.
Aliases hide calls. import wbgapi as wb followed by wb.data.DataFrame(...) is not caught; api-wbgapi sees only the full module name. The same holds for any call reached through an alias or a variable.
api-fromjson-url does not fire. The rule looks for fromJSON("https://…"), but the URL is a string literal and is scrubbed before matching, so the call passes the audit. Use dw_api_fetch(api = 'json_get', ...) regardless.
It cannot judge a correct call. A lexical scan cannot tell whether a dw_save() uses the right sector or isid. It removes the most common, most mechanical failure, a raw call written by hand; it does not replace review.



11.7.7 Using it in CI
In a repository created by the scaffolders, the auditor is already wired: the contract-audit check runs the vendored test_scripts() over AUDIT_PATHS on every sh tools/check, and so before every push through the check record. To run it on GitHub too, copy templates/workflows/ci-contract-audit.yml to .github/workflows/ (or create the repository with workflows = TRUE). It runs the same command you can run locally:
Rscript --no-init-file tools/check.R --only contract-audit,vintage
A repository without tools/check.R can call the auditor directly. The job below uses the helpers vendored in 00_functions/, the exact code the repository runs, rather than installing the toolkit from GitHub, and lets the non-zero exit fail the build. Like the templates, it runs on manual runs and pull requests into main.

RPython


name: contract-audit
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  audit:
    name: contract audit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          use-public-rspm: true
      # test_scripts() needs base R only; the vendored copy is the one the repo runs.
      - name: Run contract auditor (vendored helpers)
        run: |
          Rscript --no-init-file -e 'for (f in c("dw_io.R", "test_scripts.R")) sys.source(file.path("00_functions", f), envir = globalenv()); test_scripts("01_dw_prep", error_on_violation = TRUE)'


name: contract-audit
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  audit:
    name: contract audit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.11"
      - name: Install the vendored package's dependencies
        run: pip install pandas numpy
      - name: Run contract auditor (vendored helpers)
        run: |
          python -c "import sys; sys.path.insert(0, '00_functions'); from cso_toolkit import test_scripts; test_scripts('01_dw_prep', error_on_violation=True)"



The R job sources dw_io.R before test_scripts.R, as tools/check.R does, because the auditor uses internals defined there. The Python job installs only the package’s own dependencies, pandas and numpy; the vendored package (in 00_functions/cso_toolkit/; see Vendoring and updates) imports as cso_toolkit once 00_functions/ is on the path. Installed rather than vendored, the R package is named csotoolkit and the Python distribution cso-toolkit.
A few practical notes:

Keep the audit job separate from the test or build job, so a contract violation shows as a clearly labelled red check rather than hiding inside a larger failure.
No credentials needed. The auditor only reads source text: no network, no database, no data. It is fast and safe on every pull request.
Scope the path tightly. Point it at the folder that holds analysis scripts (the sector or prep folder), not the repository root, so vendored code and generated files stay out of scope on top of ignore_dirs.
The gate fires narrowly. Only io and api violations fail it, so the build fails on exactly the bypasses the contract forbids.
Report, then gate. For more than pass or fail, run the auditor once with error_on_violation = FALSE and write the frame to an artifact (a CSV, or a Markdown table), then run the gate. The first run gives a reviewer the full list with file, line, message and fix; the second turns the build red.

The toolkit’s own repository tests the auditor rather than running it: r-check.yml runs R CMD check on Ubuntu (release and devel), macOS and Windows, and the suite’s test-test_scripts.R asserts a clean frame on conforming code, catching a direct read_csv and a direct httr::GET, honouring # cso-allow:, and raising the envelope under error_on_violation = TRUE and on a missing path.






WarningSame version, not necessarily the same rules



python/pyproject.toml and r/DESCRIPTION declare the same version in each release. That is not a promise that the two registries catch the same calls: R has 16 rules and Python 19, as the table shows. If a rule matters to your contract, check that the vintage you vendored carries it in the language you use. Adding a rule can newly fail a build that was green, so rule-set changes follow the same semantic-versioning discipline as the rest of the API (Versioning and releases).




11.7.8 A note on the name
test_scripts() audits call sites; it is not a unit-test runner, despite a prefix that collides with testthat’s test_* naming. Both packages export dw_test_scripts() as an identical dw_-prefixed alias, and a future release may rename the function to something like dw_audit_scripts(). The aliases of the scaffolders are covered in Profiles and the mode switch.

title: 11  Checks and CI
text:
11.8 How the pieces fit
The .gitignore keeps data out and the committed sidecars keep their provenance in. A handful of fast checks, none of which needs data, credentials or network, and all of which run on the author’s own machine, turn both, and the contract, into gates a pull request has to pass, and the check record proves they ran on what merges. test_scripts() checks that the analysis code honours the contract; review_profile() checks that the repository is wired to it (Profiles and the mode switch). A repository worked on with AI coding agents adds AGENTS.md, which tells every agent to run these checks before it pushes (Working with AI coding agents).
crumbs: Part III — Setting Up and Running a Repository

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.1 The instructions file
Toolkit repositories are increasingly worked on with AI coding agents: Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex and their peers read the repository, run its scripts and propose commits. An agent follows the instructions it is given and fills every gap with a plausible guess. The contract of this handbook is full of rules that a plausible guess breaks. Left to itself, an agent edits the vendored helpers in 00_functions/ to make a call work. It reads a file with read.csv() instead of dw_use(), and the output loses its provenance. It runs as a producer because that is what the person’s user_config.yml says. It passes takeover = TRUE to get past a collaboration guard. And the reasons behind the project’s choices end up in one person’s private agent memory, where co-authors cannot see them.
None of this needs new machinery. It needs the repository to say, in a file every agent reads, which rules apply, and the people working with agents to keep a few habits. This chapter sets out both: the instructions file every toolkit repository carries, what an agent may and may not do, what it may see, where project knowledge lives, how agent output is checked, and how its use is disclosed.
Every toolkit repository has an AGENTS.md at its root. AGENTS.md is the tool-neutral convention: Codex, Copilot’s coding agent and most other agents read it on their own. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md instead, so the repository also carries a one-line CLAUDE.md that imports the first:
One file, read by every agent, means one set of rules, edited in one place and reviewed like code. Tool-specific files beyond that import (.github/copilot-instructions.md, .cursor/rules/) are better avoided: two copies of the rules drift apart.
The toolkit ships the file as a template, templates/agents/AGENTS.md, and create_research_project() and create_official_stats_project() write it into every new repository with {project_name} replaced by the repository’s name, together with CLAUDE.md, decisions.md and the shared .claude/settings.json described below (Starting a new repository). An existing repository copies the files by hand. The template, as it stands:
An official-statistics repository appends one more section, templates/agents/AGENTS-official-stats.md, for the embargo:
The file is a starting point, not a ceiling. A repository adds what is specific to it: its layout, the scripts to run from which folder, the tests that pin published numbers. It keeps the rules short and imperative, because an agent weighs every line it reads and a long file dilutes the rules that matter. Five rules carry most of the weight:

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
@AGENTS.md


# Instructions for coding agents

This repository follows the cso-toolkit conventions: <https://unicef-drp.github.io/cso-toolkit/>. Read `README.md` and `decisions.md` before changing anything.

## Layout

- `profile_{{project_name}}.R`: the session profile. Every script sources it first. It reads the person's `user_config.yml`, sets `dw_mode`, and loads the toolkit copy in `00_functions/`.
- `00_functions/`: a copy of a cso-toolkit release, pinned in `.toolkit_manifest.yml`. **Never edit it.** Changes go to `unicef-drp/cso-toolkit`, and the copy is replaced by a newer release.
- `tools/check.R`: the local checks; `sh tools/check` runs them, and
  `sh tools/check --record` also commits a check record (`.checks/`).
- `decisions.md`: the project's decisions and its record of AI use.
- `.claude/settings.json`: shared Claude Code settings: the cso-toolkit plugin (skills such as `/cso-toolkit:check`), and edits to `00_functions/` denied. Personal settings go in `.claude/settings.local.json`, which git ignores.

## Rules

- **R:** run scripts with `Rscript --no-init-file`, never `--vanilla` (it also drops `.Renviron` and the user library it sets).
- **The toolkit is already here.** Never clone, install or `library()` cso-toolkit to run anything in this repository; the profile loads the pinned copy. If a toolkit function seems wrong, describe what happened and propose an issue for `unicef-drp/cso-toolkit` to the person running the session. Never work around it by editing the copy.
- **Read and write through the toolkit:** `dw_use()` and `dw_save()`, so every output gets a provenance sidecar. No direct `read.csv()`, `haven::read_*()` or `write.csv()` on project data.
- **Session setup:** if the profile stops (missing `user_config.yml`, `dw_mode` or a package), report its exact message to the person. Never create or edit their `user_config.yml`, and never install packages without asking.
- **Session mode:** work as `dw_mode: reviewer` unless the person running the session sets `producer`. Never pass `takeover = TRUE` to `dw_save()` without their explicit approval, and never write to the canonical deposit (Teams, Z:) yourself.
- **No data in git.** Never commit microdata, extracts or caches. A new input gets a provenance sidecar and an `input_manifest.csv` row, committed with the code that uses it.
- **What you read leaves the machine.** Whatever you open is sent to the AI service. Never print rows of microdata or personal records (`head()`, `View()`, `cat` of a data file). Variable names, labels, counts and code are fine.
- **Before every push:** run `sh tools/check --record` from the repository root (after committing) and fix what fails. The pre-push hook refuses a push without a passing record, and the pull request's `check-record` status checks it again. Never skip it with `--no-verify`, and never write a record by hand.
- **Git:** branch off `develop`; one logical change per commit, staged by path (never `git add -A`); pull requests into `develop`. Never force-push, and never push to `main`.
- **Tests:** a failing test means something changed. Find out why. Never change an expected value to make a test pass unless the person running the session agrees the change is intended, and list what moved in the pull request.
- **Numbers:** every number in a text traces to a file in `output/`. After a rerun, check comparative claims ("flat", "the same", "robust") against the new tables, not only the levels.
- **Decisions** go in `decisions.md` (dated, who decided, why), not in personal agent memory. Write an entry only after the person who decided confirms its wording.
- **Parallel sessions:** one git worktree per session. Never two sessions in the same folder, and never a second clone.
- **Ask before** adding collaborators, changing repository settings, sharing any file outside the team, or deleting anything you did not create.


## Official statistics: the embargo

- **Pre-release figures are embargoed** until their publication date. Do not open, print or summarize files in the output folders before then, unless the organization's AI-use policy allows the AI service in use to see pre-release figures. Never paste them into issues, pull requests or messages.
- **Output folders are never committed.** The `.gitignore` and `tools/check.R` refuse them. A release record (`releases/<vintage>/`) is committed only after publication, in the release pull request.
- **Deposits and releases are made by a person.** Never write to Teams, Z:, SDMX or data.unicef.org, and never prepare a release record unless asked.




Rule
What it prevents




Rscript --no-init-file, never --vanilla
A run that misses the user library and fails, or silently uses another package version


Never edit 00_functions/
A vendored copy that no longer matches its manifest, so results no longer trace to a toolkit release (Vendoring and updates)


Read and write through dw_use() / dw_save()
Outputs without provenance sidecars (Appendix B)


Run sh tools/check --record before every push
Data, secrets or contract violations reaching the remote; the pre-push hook and the pull request’s check-record status refuse a push without a passing record (Checks and CI)


Atomic commits, pull requests into develop
Changes no reviewer can follow, and unreviewed changes on main




12.1.1 Shared Claude Code settings
The scaffolders also write .claude/settings.json, the settings every member’s Claude Code reads in that repository:
{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/claude-code-settings.json",
  "permissions": {
    "deny": [
      "Edit(**/00_functions/**)"
    ]
  },
  "extraKnownMarketplaces": {
    "unicef-cso": {
      "source": {
        "source": "github",
        "repo": "unicef-drp/cso-toolkit"
      }
    }
  },
  "enabledPlugins": {
    "cso-toolkit@unicef-cso": true
  }
}

The deny rule makes “never edit 00_functions/” a rule Claude Code enforces, not only one it is told. Edit rules cover every file-editing tool, and **/ matches wherever the session was started. The vendored copy still changes through cso_toolkit_sync(), which runs in R. A person who must edit it locally overrides the rule in their own .claude/settings.local.json.
The plugin. The cso-toolkit marketplace and plugin (the skills /cso-toolkit:check, /cso-toolkit:update-toolkit and three more) are offered to everyone who trusts the folder. Enabling a plugin in a committed file does not install it: each member runs claude plugin install cso-toolkit@unicef-cso --scope project once in their clone.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.2 What an agent may do
The toolkit’s two modes (roles and modes) apply to agents with one change of default.

An agent session runs as reviewer unless a person deliberately sets producer for it. A reviewer re-runs, compares and writes to its sandbox. It cannot write canonical outputs or call live APIs: the reviewer-mode guard refuses both. Most agent work is of that kind: reproducing an output, finding why a number moved, writing tests, refactoring code whose outputs must not change.
Producer work is a person’s decision, made per session. When an agent is to write outputs, the person running the session sets producer and stays responsible for what is written.
An agent never writes to the canonical deposit (Teams, Z:, SDMX, data.unicef.org) and never prepares a release on its own.
An agent never passes takeover = TRUE to dw_save() without a person’s explicit approval. The collaboration guards of a multi-producer project (the collaboration model) exist to stop one writer from overwriting another’s output. An agent that overrides them to finish its task defeats them.
An agent never edits a person’s user_config.yml, and never installs packages without asking. When the profile stops, the agent reports the exact message and the person fixes their own configuration.

dw_mode is read from the person’s user_config.yml, which cannot tell whether a person or an agent is running the session. The reviewer default is therefore a rule in AGENTS.md, not something the toolkit enforces. It does make the case visible. Claude Code sets CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1 in the commands it runs, and a profile generated by the toolkit (the scaffolders’ and create_profile()’s, in R and Python) prints a notice when that variable is set and dw_mode is producer: “a Claude Code session is running as producer”. Nothing is blocked; the notice puts the choice on the record of the session. (CLAUDECODE=1 is not used for this: IDE extensions also set it in their integrated terminals, where a person works.) Other agents set no such variable.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.3 What an agent may see
Whatever an agent reads is sent to the AI service that runs it. A file the agent opens, a table it prints, the output of a command it runs: all of it leaves the machine. The rules on what may leave follow from that.

No microdata and no personal records. An agent never prints rows of a microdata file or of any file with records on individuals: no head(), no View(), no cat of a data file. Variable names and labels, counts, summary statistics that could be published, and code are fine.
Code and provenance sidecars are fine to share. They hold paths, hashes, schemas and settings, not data.
Pre-release figures stay unseen in official statistics. Official figures are embargoed until their publication date (Checks and CI sets out the release record). Before that date no external AI service sees them, unless the organization’s AI-use policy allows that service to. In practice the agent does not open the output folders of an official-statistics repository before publication.
Use the services your organization has approved, under its terms for confidential material. A personal account on a public service is not the same contract.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.4 Where project knowledge lives
An agent working for weeks on a project accumulates context: why a variable is recoded, which countries are dropped and on whose say-so, which robustness check was tried and abandoned. If that context lives in one person’s agent memory or in session transcripts, co-authors cannot see it and the next agent starts from nothing. The rule is that project knowledge goes in the repository, and personal working state does not.








What
Where
In git?




Decisions: what, when, who decided, why
decisions.md, at the root or per product (a paper, a sector)
Yes


Working notes, analysis plans, open questions
the documentation folder (docs/ or 00_documentation/)
Yes


Instructions for agents
AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md
Yes


Shared agent settings (permissions every member uses)
.claude/settings.json
Yes


Personal agent settings
.claude/settings.local.json, CLAUDE.local.md
No (the gitignore templates ignore them)


Personal agent memory, session transcripts
the agent’s own folders, outside the repository
No



The toolkit’s decisions.md template (templates/agents/decisions.md) has one dated entry per decision, with who decided, why and what was set aside. An agent may draft an entry when asked, but the person who made the decision confirms its wording. A decision recorded in the wrong words is worse than none.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.5 Checking what an agent produces
An agent’s output is checked like a junior colleague’s, with one difference: it is fluent and confident whether or not it is right. Four checks catch most of what goes wrong.

Every number traces to a file. A number in a paper, a brief or a release note traces to a file in output/ (or, for official statistics, to the release record). A number that traces to nothing is removed or recomputed.
Tests are not re-pinned to make them pass. When a test that pins published numbers fails, numbers moved. The agent finds out why. A pinned value changes only when a person agrees the change is intended, and the pull request lists what moved.
Comparative claims are checked after every rerun. Levels can barely move while a comparison flips: “flat”, “the same”, “robust”, “larger than”. After a rerun, each comparative claim in the text is checked against the new tables, not only the numbers it quotes.
An independent claim check before submission or release. Someone who did not write the text recomputes every number in it from output/: a co-author, or a fresh agent session given only the text and the repository. The agent that wrote the text is the wrong one to check it: it tends to confirm what it wrote.

The local checks and the check record (Checks and CI) apply to agents as they do to people. An agent that cannot make the checks pass reports the failure. It does not push with --no-verify, and it never writes a check record by hand: a record says the checks passed on that exact content.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.6 Parallel sessions
When two sessions work on one repository at the same time, people or agents, each gets its own git worktree of the one local clone. Two sessions in one folder switch branches under each other. A second clone drifts from the first and gets edited by mistake.
MAIN="$(dirname "$(git rev-parse --path-format=absolute --git-common-dir)")"
git -C "$MAIN" fetch origin
git -C "$MAIN" worktree add --no-track "$MAIN/../<repo>-wt-<topic>" -b feature/<topic> origin/develop
Branches, stashes and configuration are shared between worktrees, so each session works only on its own branch. It never switches, resets or deletes another session’s branch, and it commits instead of stashing, because all worktrees share one stash list. Git-ignored files, inputs among them, are not shared. A new worktree fills its inputs folder with dw_fetch_inputs(), which copies each input from the deposit and checks its SHA-256 against the deposited copy. When the pull request has merged, git worktree remove deletes the worktree. Deleting the folder by hand leaves a stale entry, which git worktree prune clears.

title: 12  Working with AI coding agents
text:
12.7 Recording and disclosing AI use
Journals and statistical offices increasingly ask how AI was used in producing a paper or a release. The answer is easy to give at the end only if it was recorded along the way. The decisions.md template ends with an AI use table: from when, to when, which tool and version, used for what, and who checked the result. Add a row when a tool starts being used for a new purpose, not at submission time.
The declaration then follows from the table. A template line, to adapt to the venue’s own wording:

During the preparation of this work the authors used tool and version to purpose, for example: write and test analysis code; edit the text for clarity. The authors reviewed, tested and verified all code, numbers and text, and take full responsibility for the content of the publication.

Where a venue asks for more (which sections, which prompts), the AI-use table and the pull requests it points to hold the evidence.

Agents do not change the contract; they make it more important that the contract is written down. A repository whose rules live in AGENTS.md, whose decisions live in decisions.md and whose checks run on every push can take an agent’s help without losing track of where its numbers came from.

title: 13  Versioning and releases
text:
13.1 Semantic versioning
The toolkit makes a promise: a 2026 analytics product that cites dw_<sector>.csv must, two years on, re-run to identical numbers from the canonical deposit (the immutable data file the product cites, deposited to the Teams folder and its Z: mirror) and the vendored helper code (the helper files copied into the consumer’s own project) as it stood at release time. That promise holds only if every consumer can point at one exact, immutable version of the toolkit. Versions must therefore be meaningful, immutable, and documented.
Two roles run through this chapter, and the whole reproducibility argument rests on the distinction between them. A producer (the Database Manager) runs a sector pipeline, pulls live APIs, and deposits canonical artefacts; a reviewer re-runs the pipeline from those frozen artefacts to reproduce the numbers and is physically prevented from touching the network. Mode is a session property, not a per-call argument (see the roles and mode-contract chapter). The producer chooses when to refresh the toolkit; the reviewer always runs against whatever vintage the producer has pinned. A consumer is a downstream analytics project that vendors the toolkit; the three siblings are the R, Python, and Stata implementations of the same contract.
A handful of public verbs recur below. dw_use() reads a deposit, dw_save() writes one, and dw_publish() is the call that will submit an artefact to the Helix registry, a dry-run stub today (the dw_save / dw_publish split — filesystem versus API — is the subject of the IO and external-API contract chapters). The cso_toolkit_* family is different in kind: it manages versions of the toolkit itself — checking, diffing, and pulling the vendored copy.
The toolkit follows Semantic Versioning — MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. The three components carry their conventional meanings, interpreted against the toolkit’s public surface: the exported function names, their signatures, the .provenance.json sidecar schema (see the provenance sidecars chapter), and the error-envelope shape — the structure of the object a failing call returns (see the error taxonomy appendix).
The toolkit has also used a four-segment patch (v0.4.3.1) to fix a freshly cut release the same day. v0.4.3 had bumped r/DESCRIPTION’s Version and NEWS.md but missed three hard-coded version stamps inside r/R/dw_io.R: the header banner, the dw_toolkit_version() docstring, and its return value. Because dw_toolkit_version() is stamped into provenance sidecars, the stale "0.4.2" return would have polluted dw_publish() provenance with the wrong toolkit version. The .1 segment corrected the stamps without claiming a new behavioural release.

title: 13  Versioning and releases
text:
Component
Bump when
Example from history




MAJOR
A change breaks source compatibility for an existing consumer — a removed function, a renamed or reordered required argument, a default that flips in a way that changes results, a sidecar-schema change a reviewer would notice. While the toolkit is pre-1.0, breaking changes are still permitted within the 0.x line (see “The road to v1.0.0”).
The 0.x line has shipped breaking changes inside MINOR bumps. v0.4.0 flipped dw_save(overwrite = ...) from TRUE to FALSE, explicitly tagged BREAKING — a change a stable 1.x line would have made a MAJOR.


MINOR
New capability, backward-compatible: a new exported function, a new optional (trailing) argument, a new api = value, or behaviour that broadens what the function accepts without breaking existing calls.
v0.4.10 added the "total" aggregation method and the toolkit-wide verbose / debug convention — all new, trailing, optional arguments. v0.5.0 added dw_use(sheet = NULL) to read every sheet of a workbook while leaving the sheet = 1 default untouched.


PATCH
A bug fix or correctness change with no public-API change. The signature is unchanged; the fix makes the function do what it already promised.
v0.4.2 fixed dw_save(dialect = "base") silently writing comma-separated content to a .tsv file. The signature did not move; callers passing .tsv / .txt with dialect = "base" got correct tab output instead of the silent comma output that was the bug.










The pre-1.0 0.x line is deliberately permissive about breaking changes: under SemVer, anything goes below 1.0.0, and the toolkit has used that latitude to tighten the mode contract (v0.4.0) while the consumer set was small and well-known. The compatibility promise hardens at v1.0.0. Until then, migration notes in NEWS.md — not the version number alone — are how a consumer learns a release will require code changes.




13.1.1 What “public API” means across the three languages
A change is breaking only if it breaks a documented, exported entry point. The cross-language coverage matrix appendix is the authoritative list, but the rule of thumb is symmetric across siblings: the exported dw_* functions, their required arguments, the sidecar schema, and the envelope shape. Internal helpers (the .dw_* family in R) are not part of the contract and can change in a PATCH.
The siblings are versioned in lock-step under a single tag — there is one v0.5.0, not an r-v0.5.0 and a py-v0.5.0. A release may, however, advance one sibling’s coverage while leaving another untouched. v0.4.0 shipped dw_pop() and dw_regions() R-only, with Python and Stata parity tracked at the same GitHub issues for a future minor. That is a MINOR bump — new capability, nothing broken — even though parity is incomplete. The honest reading of the version number is “the contract gained a function in at least one language,” not “every language gained it.” Consumers must consult the coverage matrix, not the tag, to learn whether their language has a given helper.

title: 13  Versioning and releases
text:
13.2 The NEWS.md discipline
The toolkit keeps a single changelog, NEWS.md, following the R-ecosystem convention. Per-release notes — including breaking-change migration notes and per-PR provenance — live there; there is no separate CHANGELOG.md. There is exactly one changelog, and a second must not be added.

13.2.1 The Unreleased → released lifecycle
NEWS.md opens with an ## Unreleased section whose own header documents the discipline:
## Unreleased

_Entries land here as PRs merge into `develop`. When the next release
is cut, this header is renamed `## vX.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)` and a fresh
`## Unreleased` section is added back._
The flow follows three steps:

A PR merges into develop and adds its entry under ## Unreleased.
Entries accumulate as more PRs land in the cycle.
At release time, ## Unreleased is renamed to ## vX.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD) and a fresh empty ## Unreleased is opened above it.

This makes the changelog per-PR rather than reconstructed per-release as an afterthought. Each entry is written at the moment the change is understood, by the person who made it, not pieced together from git log weeks later.


13.2.2 What a good entry contains
The historical entries set a high bar. A strong NEWS.md entry carries, in order:

A bold headline naming the user-visible change — for example, “dw_save() confirms before overwriting a producer deposit.”
Per-PR / per-issue provenance — the issue and PR numbers, linked, so a reader can trace the change to its discussion. Most entries cite both (for example, issue #25 and PR #75).
The empirical origin, where there is one. Many fixes were surfaced by a specific audit run, and the entry says so: the v0.4.3 parquet fix records that it was “surfaced empirically by DW-Production Run #6 (NT pipeline): 13+ stages downstream … failed with ‘object COLUMN not found’.” This is provenance for why the bug mattered, not merely that it existed.
A Migration: note whenever a consumer must change code. These are explicit and actionable.

The migration notes are the load-bearing part of the discipline. The v0.5.0 overwrite-confirmation change states the action a consumer must take:

Migration: non-interactive producer pipelines that re-deposit must add force = TRUE (or run interactively).

The v0.4.3 cols_lenient change spelled out the before/after for each affected call form:
Migration:
- dw_use(cols = dplyr::any_of(c(...)))  ->  dw_use(cols = c(...), cols_lenient = TRUE)
- dw_use(cols = dplyr::all_of(c(...)))  ->  dw_use(cols = c(...))  (strict)
And the headline v0.4.0 breaking change carried a full Migration guide offering two routes — pass overwrite = TRUE for daily re-runs of the same vintage, or sequence writes under a fresh vintage subfolder for archival work — plus an explicit “Reviewer-mode callers do not need changes” reassurance, so a consumer can tell at a glance whether the change touches them.






A breaking change with no migration note is a contract violation, not a tidiness lapse. The version number tells a consumer that something broke; the migration note is the only thing that tells them how to fix it. Every entry flagged BREAKING in the history is paired with a migration note — keep it that way.





13.2.3 Entries are language-agnostic but coverage-honest
Because the siblings share one tag, one NEWS.md covers all three. Entries name which languages a change touches when coverage is uneven — “(R only)”, “R + Python siblings ship in lock-step”, “Stata-side dw_api_fetch and Parquet / RDS read support remain out of scope by design.” This keeps the changelog from implying parity the code does not have — the same honesty the coverage matrix appendix enforces.

title: 13  Versioning and releases
text:
13.3 Tags and the release cut
Releases are Git tags of the form vX.Y.Z (and vX.Y.Z-rcN for release candidates), cut on main with git tag -a vX.Y.Z after the develop → main release pull request merges (see docs/git_workflow.md). The first cut, v0.1.0-rc1, followed the workspace convention of tagging a release candidate before the real release so the untested release flow could be exercised reversibly; v0.1.0 was tagged only once the candidate’s cso_toolkit_pull() flow smoke-tested cleanly. The README’s version table is the human-readable index of tags, each row dated and summarised.

13.3.1 The version is stamped in more than one place
A version stamp that disagrees with the tag silently mislabels the provenance of every artefact written under that release, because dw_toolkit_version() is recorded in dw_stage()’s .staged.json sidecars and in dw_publish() payloads. A release cut must therefore keep several stamps in agreement; they are read by different consumers:
r/DESCRIPTION                    Version: X.Y.Z
r/R/dw_io.R                      header banner, dw_toolkit_version() @return, debug line, return value
r/man/dw_toolkit_version.Rd      regenerated by roxygen2
python/pyproject.toml            version
python/src/__init__.py           __version__
python/src/dw_io.py              header banner, docstrings, _TOOLKIT_VERSION
NEWS.md                          ## vX.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD)
README.md                        version table row
CITATION.cff                     version and date-released (twice)
.zenodo.json                     version and publication_date
r/tests/testthat/test-dw_io-mode-contract.R, test-dw_publish.R   pinned stamp
The v0.4.3.1 incident — three dw_io.R stamps left at "0.4.2" while DESCRIPTION said v0.4.3 — produced a concrete release-cut checklist item that should run before every tag:

The release-cut checklist for the next minor (v0.5.0) should include a grep -rn '0\.[0-9]\.[0-9]' r/R/ step to catch any future stamp drift before tagging.

With two-digit minors that pattern misses versions such as 0.10.0; grep for the outgoing version string instead, across the repository: grep -rnF 'X.Y.Z' --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.parity --exclude-dir=docs .


13.3.2 The three languages must agree before the tag
From v0.11.0 on, the commit being tagged also needs a parity certificate. Run sh tools/certify --record on a machine with R, Python and Stata. It runs the shared cases in all three languages and commits .parity/<content-hash>.json when they agree, known gaps and divergences aside. sh tools/certify --verify, which the Parity certificate workflow runs on pull requests into main, must pass on the release commit. Bump the version stamps first: they live in r/R/ and python/src/, which the certificate hashes, so a certificate recorded before the bump does not cover the release commit. The GitHub release notes link the certificate. The cases, the register of gaps and divergences, and the content hash are described in How the three languages stay in step.
The handbook’s reference tables (the coverage matrix, the API keys, the auditor rules and the parity cases) are generated from the code. Run sh tools/docs-tables after adding, removing or porting a function, and commit book/_generated/; sh tools/docs-tables --check, which the Conformance workflow also runs, fails when a public function has no row in book/_data/coverage.json, when a note there contradicts the code, or when the committed tables are stale.


13.3.3 The tag is immutable
A published tag is never moved. Consumers vendor the helper files into their own repository and record the tag, and the commit it pointed to, in .toolkit_manifest.yml; refreshing to a newer tag is an explicit act by a producer, with the release notes shown first, and a reviewer can never pull at all. The whole reproducibility argument rests on a pinned tag meaning the same bytes for ever: moving one would silently change what every consumer pinned to it runs. How consumers pin, check and update is in Vendoring and updates; if a tag ever had to be withdrawn, cut a new patch release instead.


13.3.4 The release, step by step
This is the sequence the v0.11 and v0.12 releases followed. Each step is a pull request or a command whose result can be checked before the next.

Everything for the release is merged into develop, each change with its tests, handbook update and NEWS.md entry, and develop’s CI is green.
Prepare the release on a branch (release/X.Y.Z-prep) from develop:

stamp the version in every place listed above, including the tests that pin it;
rename ## Unreleased to ## vX.Y.Z (YYYY-MM-DD), add a short summary paragraph, and open a fresh ## Unreleased;
add the README version-table row and update the handbook’s “as of” lines;
run sh tools/docs-tables and the test suites;
commit, then run sh tools/certify --record with R, Python and Stata available, which commits the certificate.

Merge the preparation pull request into develop when CI is green. The handbook build then opens and merges its own pull request to refresh docs/handbook/; let it merge before the next step, so the release pull request’s checks are not held back by a later push.
Open the release pull request from develop into main. Its body is the release notes: what changed, what consumers get, and the checks behind it. The Parity certificate check must pass along with the others. Merge with a merge commit.
Tag the merge commit on main with an annotated tag naming the certificate, after confirming sh tools/certify --verify passes there:
git tag -a vX.Y.Z <merge-commit> -m "cso-toolkit vX.Y.Z: <headline> (parity certificate <hash>)"
git push origin vX.Y.Z
Publish the GitHub release from the tag, marked latest, with the release notes and a link to the certificate file at the tag.
Check that CI passes on main after the merge.
Update the consumers with cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "vX.Y.Z"), one pull request per consumer repository, and record which files changed.

title: 13  Versioning and releases
text:
13.4 The road to v1.0.0
The toolkit is deliberately still in its 0.x line. The README’s version table records the gate for v1.0.0 precisely:

v1.0.0 — committed API — After the ed sector pilot lands and a second sector vendors the helpers without modification.

Two conditions must both hold.

The education (ed) sector pilot lands. The education sector is the first-party proving ground for the full contract.
A second sector vendors the helpers without modification. This is the real test. A second, independent consumer must be able to adopt the toolkit as published — with an empty local_edits: [] in its manifest — rather than carrying local patches.

The second condition is exacting on purpose. Much of the 0.4.x history is fixes that were first applied as local edits inside DW-Production and only later upstreamed: the v0.4.3 dw_use() fixes “landed first on the DW-Production vendored copy as local_edits; this release lets the next cso_toolkit_pull(target_version = "v0.4.3") drop those local edits.” The manifest’s local_edits: field exists precisely to record such divergence so that a later pull skips those files — but every entry in it is a small breach of the vendoring model, because it means the published toolkit was not, on its own, sufficient. A clean second adoption — no local_edits — is the empirical signal that the contract has stabilised enough to commit to. The candidate downstream consumers named in the strategy docs are other repositories in the same programme: unicef-drp/UNPD-Population and unicef-drp/datalib-dev.
One marquee prerequisite is still outstanding. v0.4.0 shipped dw_publish() as a deliberate dry-run-only STUB so sector scripts could wire the canonical call site early and have the live branch “light up automatically when v0.5.0 lands.” That live branch has not landed yet: in the current release, r/R/dw_publish.R still raises [cso_toolkit.dw_publish] Live submission not yet implemented on any dry_run = FALSE call, and its own banner still describes the live Helix submission as “planned v0.5.0.” The v0.5.0 release instead shipped read- and write-side refinements — dw_use(sheet = NULL), dw_is_canonical() Z: recognition, a dw_compare() degenerate-sides fix, and the dw_save() overwrite-confirmation change above. So what remains before 1.0.0 is both the two-part adoption gate — pilot in, second consumer clean — and the live dw_publish() submission branch that the dry-run STUB is still standing in for.
Once v1.0.0 is cut, the SemVer contract hardens: breaking changes can no longer ride inside MINOR bumps as they have through the 0.4.x line; they require a MAJOR bump and a migration note. Until then, read the migration notes, not just the digits.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.1 Two layers of checking
The toolkit is written three times: in R (r/R/, the reference implementation), in Python (python/src/) and in Stata (stata/src/). It promises that the three give the same results. The coverage matrix (Appendix A) records which functions exist in which language; it cannot show that they agree. This chapter explains how agreement is checked, and how a release proves it.
The CI round trip is a fast guard on the input/output contract. The certificate is the full check, and the one a release depends on. Stata is only in the certificate: GitHub’s runners have no Stata licence (#133), so Stata runs where it is installed.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.2 How a run works
sh tools/certify finds a Python (CSO_PYTHON, else python3, python or py -3) and runs conformance/certify.py. That script uses only Python’s standard library, so any Python 3.8 or later can run it.

It reads the cases, every conformance/cases/*.json, or only those named with --cases.
It runs one driver per language, passing it the list of case ids, the fixture folder and an output folder. Each driver loads the implementation from the working tree, never an installed copy:

R: Rscript --no-init-file conformance/drivers/driver_r.R loads r/ with devtools::load_all(). Rscript comes from CSO_RSCRIPT, the PATH, or C:/Program Files/R/R-*/bin on Windows. On Windows the run drops Git Bash’s HOME, so that R finds its own .Renviron.
Python: conformance/drivers/driver_python.py, under CSO_PYTHON or the interpreter running certify.py, copies python/src into a temporary package named cso_toolkit and imports that copy. The interpreter needs the toolkit’s dependencies (pandas, PyYAML and so on).
Stata: certify.py writes a small do-file that sets CERT_CASES, CERT_FIX, CERT_OUT and CERT_ADO, then runs conformance/drivers/driver_stata.do in batch (StataMP-64.exe /e on Windows, -b elsewhere). The driver puts stata/src first on the ado-path. Stata comes from STATA_EXE or the usual install folders.

Each driver gets up to 30 minutes. A case that crashes writes <id>.error.txt; a driver that stops part way is judged on the outputs it did write.
Each driver writes one output per case: <id>.csv for a values case, <id>.json for a json case. It also writes _versions.json, recording its language version and, for R and Python, the toolkit version it loaded; Stata’s ado files carry no version stamp, so Stata records its own version and edition.
certify.py judges every case in every language (next sections) and prints a table of statuses.
With --record, if everything passed, it writes the certificate and commits it.

Outputs and logs (r.log, python.log, stata.log) stay in a temporary folder, or the one given with --out, and the run prints where.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.3 What a case checks
A case is a small JSON file. It gives: - id and title; - the surface: the functions under test; - the kind; - the fixtures it reads; - languages: those expected to run it; - gaps and divergences (see below).
There are two kinds.
values: the data a call returns. The case lists the columns to compare, the keys that identify a row, a numeric tolerance (default 1e-9) and, optionally, the expected number of rows. - The reference is R’s output. A round-trip case sets "reference": "fixture" and compares every language, R included, with the input file itself. - Cells are compared after normalisation: - "", NA, NaN, nan, . and None all count as missing, since CSV cannot tell them apart and each language spells missing its own way; - numbers are equal when |a − b| ≤ tolerance × max(1, |a|, |b|), so 1e+05 and 100000 agree; - anything else is a string and must match exactly; - column names are compared without regard to case. - Rows are sorted by the keys before comparing, so row order never matters. A different row count is a failure.
json: a small record of what happened, compared with the expect block of the case. Examples: did the call stop, did the message carry the [cso_toolkit.<fn>] envelope, was a file written, how many rows were added. - Each key in expect must match. - Numbers compare as numbers, so 1 and 1.0 agree, and nested objects compare without regard to key order. - Extra keys in the output are ignored.
The json kind is how behaviour that has no data output is checked: refusals, guards, sidecars and lifecycle states.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.6 The certificate
sh tools/certify --record writes a certificate only when: - all three languages ran; - every case is PASS, gap or DIVERGES in every language; - the certified paths have no uncommitted change.
It then commits the file on its own, with the message Parity certificate <hash>.
The name is a content hash: SHA-256 over the git trees, at HEAD, of the seven certified paths: - r/R, python/src and stata/src, the three implementations; - conformance/certify.py, conformance/cases, conformance/drivers and conformance/fixtures, the harness.
Any change to an implementation, a case, a driver or a fixture needs a new certificate. Changes elsewhere keep the old one: the handbook, READMEs, NEWS, templates, CI.
The file, .parity/<content-hash>.json with schema cso_toolkit.parity/1, records: - content_hash and trees: the hash and the tree id of each certified path; - commit, created_at (UTC), created_by and platform; - versions: per language, what its driver reported (for example R version 4.6.1, Python 3.11.9, Stata 17 MP); - result (pass) and summary: the count per status; - cases: per case and language, the status, a note, and the SHA-256 of the output file.
The output hashes let anyone check, later, that a re-run produced byte-identical outputs.
sh tools/certify --verify runs no language. It recomputes the content hash and checks that .parity/<hash>.json exists and records a pass for that hash. The Parity certificate workflow (.github/workflows/parity-certificate.yml) runs exactly this on pull requests into main, and on demand. It takes a few seconds and needs only Python and git.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.7 Running it
sh tools/certify                              # all cases, all three languages; exit 1 on any failure
sh tools/certify --languages r,python         # a subset while developing
sh tools/certify --cases stage_lifecycle      # one or more cases (comma separated)
sh tools/certify --out /tmp/parity            # keep outputs in a chosen folder
sh tools/certify --record                     # all three languages; write and commit the certificate
sh tools/certify --verify                     # is there a passing certificate for this tree?
Environment variables: - CSO_PYTHON: a Python with the toolkit’s dependencies, for the Python driver; - CSO_RSCRIPT: Rscript, if it is not on the PATH; - STATA_EXE: the Stata executable, if it is not in a usual folder.
On Windows, a typical call from Git Bash is:
CSO_PYTHON=/path/to/venv/Scripts/python.exe \
STATA_EXE=C:/Users/Public/Software/Stata17/StataMP-64.exe \
sh tools/certify --record
The harness has its own tests in conformance/tests/test_certify.py. They write the outputs a driver would have written and check how certify.py judges them, without running R or Stata: python -m pytest conformance/tests.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.8 Adding a case

Write conformance/cases/<id>.json, copying a case of the same kind. List every language either in languages or in gaps, with the issue (or “coverage matrix”) and a one-line reason.
Add any input file to conformance/fixtures/. Prefer a small, purpose-built file that exercises the edge you care about: missing values, an all-missing group, a duplicate key.
Add a function named after the id to each driver that implements it:

driver_r.R: an entry in the cases list;
driver_python.py: a function plus an entry in CASES;
driver_stata.do: a program named case_<id>.

A driver that does not know an id skips it silently, so a missing driver entry shows up as MISSING.
Reset any session state the case sets. The R and Python drivers’ plain() returns to a plain local session; leaking reviewer mode or a canonical root into the next case makes failures hard to read.
Run sh tools/certify --cases <id>, then the full run, then --record once the code is committed.

For a json case, prefer facts that would differ if the behaviour broke: whether a file exists, whether its hash changed, which error text appeared. “No error” alone is a weak check. For example, stage_lifecycle records whether a second call re-copied the file, and the test suite separately checks that a re-copy would change the file’s modification time.
crumbs: 14  How the three languages stay in step

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.9 In the release checklist
A release is tagged only when sh tools/certify --verify passes on the commit being tagged, and the release notes link the certificate (chapter “Versioning and releases”). The release-prep pull request records a fresh certificate after the version stamps change, since r/R and python/src carry the version.

title: 14  How the three languages stay in step
text:
14.10 What it has found
The first full run, in November 2026, found three defects that had been in the toolkit since May 2026, and fixed them: - Stata’s dw_compare failed on every call: a } else { on one line. - Stata’s dw_save failed on every call that wrote a sidecar, the default: its JSON escaping expanded to invalid syntax, and the sidecar’s file write lines used a _q directive that does not exist. - R’s dw_api_fetch lacked the envelope in reviewer mode: it called a profile-only function with arguments the profile’s version does not take, so the error said “could not find function” or “unused arguments”.
It also registered two divergences, both fixed since: - Stata’s sidecar had no sha256 (#191). Fixed with #168 through Stata’s Python integration. - R read a doubled quote in CSV as two quotes (#192). data.table::fread() keeps them, a long-standing upstream limitation, so dw_use() now unescapes them.
For v0.12.0, the new cases aggregate_total and stage_lifecycle came with the Python ports of method = "total" and dw_stage. The stage_lifecycle case also caught a mistake in its own first draft: it checked the staged file’s hash after the test had already changed the source.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.1 Branches and pull requests
This chapter is for anyone who changes the toolkit itself: a fix, a new function, a port to another language, or a correction to this book. It sets out how a change travels from a branch to a release, and what it must carry on the way. The release itself is in Versioning and releases; how the three languages are kept in agreement is in How the three languages stay in step.
A change is complete when it carries everything a reader of the next release needs:
The repository has two protected trunks and short-lived task branches.
Neither trunk accepts force pushes or deletion. Merge pull requests with a merge commit, not a squash, so the history shows where each branch joined. The full rules, the administrator’s hotfix path and how to recover from a commit on the wrong branch are in docs/git_workflow.md.
Work in a worktree. Keep your main clone on whatever it is checked out to, and give each task its own working folder:
After the pull request merges, remove the worktree (git worktree remove ../cso-toolkit-wt-topic) and the branch. Several worktrees can be open at once, which is how parallel tasks, or parallel coding agents, avoid stepping on each other.
Stacked pull requests. When one change builds on another that is not merged yet, branch the second from the first and open its pull request against the first branch. Merge them in order. After the first merges, retarget the next one to develop and bring develop into it with GitHub’s Update branch, a merge rather than a rebase; retargeting alone does not start CI against develop. Delete a merged branch only after the pull request built on it has been retargeted, or GitHub closes the dependent pull request.
Commits. Make each commit one logical change, and stage it by path, so the history reads as a list of decisions: the code, its tests, its documentation and the regenerated tables can be separate commits in one pull request. Start the subject with the area, in the style feat(python): ..., fix(stata): ..., docs(book): ..., test(conformance): .... To delete files across several commits, remove them with rm and stage each commit with git add -A -- <paths>; a git rm stages the deletion at once, and the next git commit without paths takes it whatever the commit was meant to hold.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.2 A change, start to finish

Open or find an issue describing the problem, with file and line references and, for a bug, the steps that show it.
Branch from an up-to-date develop, in a worktree.
Change R first. R is the reference implementation. Port the change to Python, and to Stata where Stata has the function; where it does not, record why in book/_data/coverage.json.
Test each language you touched (next section), and add a parity case if the change is about behaviour the languages must share.
Update the handbook chapter that owns the behaviour, and only that chapter: other chapters link to it. If a function was added, removed or ported, run sh tools/docs-tables and commit book/_generated/.
Add a NEWS.md entry under ## Unreleased, written for someone deciding whether to update (see Versioning and releases).
Record a parity certificate if the change touches r/R, python/src, stata/src or the conformance harness: commit your change, then run sh tools/certify --record, which commits the certificate itself.
Open the pull request into develop, saying what changed, why, and how it was checked.
Merge when CI is green, with a merge commit. A merge into develop that touches book/ triggers the handbook build, which opens and merges its own pull request to refresh the published site.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.3 Tests
Run the tests of every language your change touches before you push; CI repeats the R and Python ones.

R


# From the repository root. Use --no-init-file, never --vanilla: --vanilla
# also drops the site library settings that find your packages.
#   Rscript --no-init-file -e 'devtools::test("r")'
devtools::test("r")
The suite is in r/tests/testthat/. CI also runs R CMD check on Ubuntu (R release and devel), macOS and Windows (r-check.yml). Help pages are generated by roxygen2; r/DESCRIPTION pins RoxygenNote: 7.3.3, so if your roxygen2 is newer, keep only the .Rd pages your change actually alters. #### Python {.unnumbered .unlisted}
python -m pytest python/tests conformance/tests book/_scripts
python/tests/ is the package’s suite, conformance/tests/ tests the parity harness, and book/_scripts/ tests the handbook table generator. Two scripts under python/tests/manual/ (a smoke test and the error-envelope check) are run by hand. #### Stata {.unnumbered .unlisted}
* In batch from the repository root (Windows: StataMP-64.exe /e do ...):
do stata/tests/test_config_user_block.do
stata/tests/ holds a do-file per area, plus test_dw_stata_helpers.py, run with pytest, for the Python helpers that Stata’s dw_save and dw_collaboration call. GitHub’s runners have no Stata licence (#133), so Stata is tested locally and through the parity certificate.



Behaviour the three languages must share belongs in a parity case as well as in each language’s suite: see “Adding a case” in How the three languages stay in step.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.4 The handbook
Each fact in this book has one home; other chapters link to it by title. When you change behaviour, change the chapter that owns it and nothing else. A few rules keep the book from drifting again:

Never describe language coverage in prose. Which languages have a function comes from the code: the coverage matrix and the one-line notes under each function are generated by sh tools/docs-tables from r/NAMESPACE, Python’s __all__ and stata/src/*.ado, with the notes in book/_data/coverage.json. The Conformance workflow runs sh tools/docs-tables --check, which fails when a function has no row or a note contradicts the code.
Refer to chapters by title, not number. Numbers change whenever the book is reorganised.
Keep old addresses working. When you move, merge or rename a page, list the old file names under aliases: in the new page’s front matter; Quarto writes a redirect page at each old address and keeps any #section part. Code, templates and the Claude plugin cite handbook URLs.
Render before you push: quarto render book --to html should finish without warnings.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.5 What CI runs








Workflow
When
What it checks




R CMD check (r-check.yml)
Push and pull request to main or develop
The R package on four platform and version combinations.


Conformance (conformance.yml)
Push and pull request to main or develop
R and Python round-trip the shared fixture and must agree; the handbook’s generated tables must be current.


Handbook (Quarto book) (publish-book.yml)
Changes under book/
Pull requests: the book renders. Pushes to develop: renders and refreshes docs/handbook/ through a pull request that merges itself.


Parity certificate (parity-certificate.yml)
Pull requests into main, or by hand
A passing certificate exists for the commit (runs no language).


dashboard (dashboard.yml)
Nightly, and after a handbook refresh
Publishes docs/ to GitHub Pages.



Actions minutes are limited, so the checks are designed to run locally first: run the tests, the table check and, for code changes, the certificate before you push, and treat CI as confirmation rather than discovery.

title: 15  Contributing
text:
15.6 Filing issues
An issue is most useful when someone else can act on it without asking. Say what happens and what should happen, point to the code (file:line), give the smallest example that shows it, and propose a fix if you have one. Use the bug, enhancement or documentation label. A finding in one language that is likely to exist in the others is worth checking there before you file, and saying so.

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
16.1 Why a microdata archive
A survey costs millions of dollars and several years to field. Re-analysing the microdata it produces costs an afternoon. That asymmetry is the whole argument for this part of the book. The household- and person-level records that every published indicator ultimately rests on are the most expensive and least reproducible asset the office holds — and, in practice, they are often managed with less rigour than the code that reads them. A pipeline gets a git history, a manifest, and a provenance sidecar; the raw survey it consumes gets a folder on a shared drive whose name means something only to the person who created it. Part V documents datalib, the tool that extends the reproducibility floor — the guarantee, set out in the why-a-toolkit chapter, that a 2026 analysis must re-run identically in 2028 — from the aggregate outputs down to the survey microdata those outputs are built from.
This opening chapter introduces the whole of Part V: the boundary between the microdata archive and the indicator warehouse, the three-layer picture (archive, catalogue, tool) that frames the initiative, the stock-and-flow approach to deposits, the deposit-gate-promote governance, and the access and licensing floor. The IHSN-grammar chapter that follows takes up the folder convention in detail; the datalib API and conformance chapter takes up the cross-language contract and its oracle test suite.
Scope today is deliberately narrow. The archive covers household surveys for global child monitoring (MICS, DHS, LSMS, including the MICS Harmonized Database) now; other survey types next; anonymized public-use microdata later. Nothing in Part V assumes more than that.
The reproducibility floor is a guarantee you inherit rather than a feature you remember to switch on. For the aggregate warehouse, the toolkit builds that floor from provenance sidecars, a replayable frozen deposit, and uniqueness checks. For survey microdata the failure modes are different, but the promise is the same: a number computed from a 2019 survey today must be computable from the same records, read from the same place, by a different analyst in two years.
Three things routinely break that promise for microdata specifically.
datalib’s answer is to make the shelving convention itself executable. A survey’s country, year, survey instrument, and vintage are encoded in a machine-parseable folder name (the IHSN grammar), the untouched source is preserved alongside every derived form, and one library — in R, Python, and Stata — resolves, loads, and merges by reading that convention rather than trusting a human to remember it. Provenance is recorded structurally: the vintage is in the folder name and Data/Original/ is never mutated. That is the same intent as the toolkit’s .provenance.json sidecar, reached by a different mechanism; the provenance-schema appendix carries only a short pointer to this difference, not a second sidecar specification.
crumbs: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
Silent divergence of “the same” survey. Two teams each hold a copy of the same MICS round. One recoded a variable; the other dropped a module. Neither copy records what was done, and there is no shared name that would even reveal the two are meant to be identical. When their indicators disagree, there is nothing to point at.
Folder names that carry no contract. A directory called Tajikistan final v2 USE THIS tells a script nothing. Which country code, which year, which survey, which vintage? The information a loader needs to resolve a file deterministically is exactly the information a hand-typed folder name tends to omit.
Transformations with no reverse. The deposited .dta is three recodes downstream of the original, and the recodes live in a script no one can find. The output cannot be reproduced because its inputs cannot be reconstructed.
crumbs: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
16.2 Two data layers, one office
The single most important thing to hold clear before reading the rest of Part V is that datalib is not part of the data warehouse. The CSO office runs two data layers under one roof. They share a team and an operator config file; they do not share a store, a contract, or a grain.








Dimension
Aggregate / indicator warehouse
Survey microdata archive




Contract prefix
dw_*
datalib_*


Canonical store
Teams 060.DW-MASTER (+ its Z: mirror)
Z:/datalib* trees + a staging area


What lives there
Deposited indicator files (aggregates)
Survey vintages (household / person records)


Grain
one row per indicator × unit × time
one row per household or per person


Documented in
Parts I–IV of this book
Part V (this part)


Team

the same team


Operator config
~/.config/user_config.yml
the same file



State it plainly: microdata deposits NEVER enter 060.DW-MASTER, and indicator deposits never land in the Z:/datalib* trees. The warehouse holds the aggregates a producer blesses and a publisher pushes downstream to Helix and the public pages; the archive holds the survey records those aggregates were computed from. Same office, two contracts, two stores, different data layer. Everything in Part V lives on the microdata side of that line, and the boundary is referenced again in both the IHSN-grammar chapter and the datalib API and conformance chapter.
The one genuinely shared thing is the operator config file. Both contracts are designed to key off the single ~/.config/user_config.yml, datalib reading a datalib: block from its user section for the library root. As the configuration-across-tiers discussion in the architecture chapter notes, the toolkit side of that shared-file coexistence is in place: dw_load_config skips a datalib: block without adopting its keys (v0.7.0, #138). Treat the two contracts as separate namespaces that happen to share a file.

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
16.3 Archive, catalogue, tool
The governance draft frames the initiative as three distinct layers, and confusing them is the most common way to misunderstand the project. datalib the software is only one of the three.









Layer
What it is
What it is not
Status




Microdata archive
the governed store of the data files themselves — the Z:/datalib* trees, the staging area, and the deposit process that fills them
not a website; not a metadata index
this initiative (all of Part V)


Microdata catalogue
the metadata and discovery layer (IHSN / NADA tooling over a DDI model)
not the files themselves
a Phase-2+ product, seeded by the tool’s auto-generated inventories


Tool (datalib)

neither the store nor the catalogue
shipped: contract v1 in datalib v0.7.0



The one-liner is worth memorising: an archive without a catalogue is unfindable; a catalogue without an archive points at silos; both without a tool are manual drudgery. The three depend on each other, and datalib is the leg that exists today — the executable convention that also produces the inventories the future catalogue will index.

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
16.4 Stock and flow
The archive would never fill if conformance were a precondition for deposit — teams hold years of surveys under their own naming, and demanding they rename everything first guarantees they deposit nothing. So the governance draws a sharp line between what already exists and what is created from now on, and treats the two differently.









Stock — existing holdings
Flow — new work




Rule of thumb
“copy it as it is, don’t touch it”
“name it right from day one”


Naming
preserved exactly as-is, folder structure intact so existing scripts keep running
follows the datalib IHSN grammar from the start


Destination
Z:/staging-area/<domain>/<team-folder-as-is>/
promoted into the domain’s canonical tree as masters / adaptations


Conformance
never a precondition; progressive, survey by survey
required at deposit



Depositing stock as-is is not a compromise; it is the point. Preserving the original folder unlocks a four-phase payoff, each phase enabled by the one before:

Preserve and make portable — get the survey off a personal drive and into a governed, backed-up store without breaking the scripts that already read it.
Compare inputs across teams — once two teams’ copies of the same survey sit side by side, their differences become visible for the first time.
Reverse-engineer transformations — with the original preserved next to each derived form, the recodes between them can be reconstructed.
Consolidate — converge on one authoritative file per survey.

Conformance, in other words, is something the archive arrives at survey by survey, not a gate that keeps surveys out.

title: 16  The microdata archive: archive, catalogue, tool
text:
16.5 Deposit, gate, promote
A deposit is not simply a file copy. It passes a seven-item review gate before anything is promoted from staging into a canonical tree. The gate is summarised here; the deposit quickstart and the governance draft in the datalib repository (docs/GOVERNANCE_microdata_deposit.md) carry the operative detail, and this chapter points to them rather than reproducing them.

Inventory logged — the deposit is recorded.
Naming conforms — the IHSN grammar is checked (flow only; stock is exempt).
Reproducibility — a non-author can re-run the deposit’s script from staging.
No breakage outside its staging folder — the deposit touches nothing else.
Licence recorded — MICS as country-owned, DHS per-project, IPUMS per its conditions.
Access tier assigned — one of the tiers below.
De-identification confirmed — de-identified microdata only.

The division of labour mirrors the toolkit’s producer → reviewer → publisher relay, mapped onto an organisational standard rather than a session-level mode: the Core Group decides the gate outcome, and the Data Steward operates the checks and the move. A pass lets the Data Steward promote the conformed vintages into the domain’s canonical tree — never into 060.DW-MASTER.

The toolkit’s three session-level runners (see the roles-and-mode-contract chapter) need no ratifying layer above them because the toolkit’s governance lives elsewhere; the microdata standard, being an office-wide convention, carries that extra scaffolding of Board, Process Lead, and accountable owner.






Promotion targets a thematic domain tree, not one global folder: health → Z:/datalib-hlt (HLT), education → Z:/datalib-edu (EDU), nutrition → Z:/datalib-nut (NUT), child-protection → Z:/datalib-chp (CHP), cross-cutting → Z:/datalib. A domain is the organisational grouping of holdings; a collection is the harmonization code in the folder grammar (the IHSN-grammar chapter covers collections). The two are aligned but not identical — and as of v0.7.0 / contract v1 only HLT (and IPUMS) is registered in datalib’s merge registry; EDU, NUT, and CHP become first-class as their module lists and keys are verified in later phases.
