text:
B.3 A real example (R / Python)
A write such as:
dw_save(edu_sdg_uis,
        name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"),
        vintage = "2026-05",
        metadata = list(
          title    = "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
          producer = "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
          sources  = c("UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"),
          contact  = "@karavan88"
        ))
produces a sidecar of this shape:
{
  "path": "C:/Users/.../teamsWrkData/ed/dw_ed_edu.csv",
  "format": "csv",
  "written_at": "2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000",
  "user": "jpazevedo",
  "dw_mode": "producer",
  "vintage": "2026-05",
  "sha256": "9f2c1a7b4e0d8c5f3a6b2e1d9c0f4a7b8e3d2c1f0a9b8c7d6e5f4a3b2c1d0e9f",
  "isid": ["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "TIME_PERIOD"],
  "schema": {
    "rows": 48213,
    "cols": 9,
    "columns": ["DATAFLOW", "REF_AREA", "INDICATOR", "SEX",
                "WEALTH_QUINTILE", "RESIDENCE", "TIME_PERIOD",
                "OBS_VALUE", "DATA_SOURCE"]
  },
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
    "producer": "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
    "sources": ["UIS bulk SDG_092025", "WPP 2024"],
    "contact": "@karavan88"
  }
}
The Python sidecar is the same shape: the helper builds the identical key set, serialises with json.dump(..., indent=2), and computes sha256 by streaming the file in 64-KiB blocks. R serialises with jsonlite::write_json(..., auto_unbox = TRUE, pretty = TRUE). The two pretty-printers differ in whitespace, and auto_unbox means a single-key isid in R collapses to a bare string rather than a one-element array — but the keys, types, and values otherwise match.

title: Appendix B — Provenance sidecar schema
text:
B.4 Multi-producer lineage fields
In a project whose cso_project.yml sets collaboration: multi-producer (see the roles and mode-contract chapter), every R, Python, or Stata write adds lineage fields (R/Python after schema and before metadata; Stata after sha256). Single-producer sidecars, including every sidecar written in a repository without cso_project.yml, keep exactly the key set in the core schema above.









Key
Type
Meaning
Languages




collaboration
string
Always "multi-producer"; marks a sidecar written under the multi-producer rules.
R / Py / Stata


previous_sha256
string | null
SHA-256 of the file this write replaced, computed from its bytes just before the write (so after a takeover over an out-of-band change it is the hash of the bytes actually replaced). null when the output is new.
R / Py / Stata


previous_user
string | null
user of the replaced file’s sidecar; null when there was none.
R / Py / Stata


previous_written_at
string | null
written_at of the replaced file’s sidecar; null when there was none.
R / Py / Stata


git_branch
string | null
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD in the output’s folder, best effort; null outside a repository or without git.
R / Py / Stata


git_commit
string | null
git rev-parse HEAD, likewise.
R / Py / Stata


takeover
object
Present only when the write passed takeover = TRUE: user, at (ISO-8601 UTC) and overrode, the guards it overrode ("out_of_band", "concurrent", or an empty array when none fired).
R / Py / Stata



previous_sha256 chains the sidecars: each one names the bytes its write replaced, so the history of an output can be walked back without the earlier files. The guards in dw_save() read the same sidecar: a file whose bytes no longer match its sidecar’s sha256 was changed outside dw_save(), and a sidecar whose written_at is later than the session start and whose user is someone else records a concurrent write.
An API-cache write made with refresh = TRUE over a cache fetched by another user also records metadata.previous_fetch (sha256, user, fetched_at of the replaced fetch).

B.4.1 The baseline object
dw_set_collaboration() adds one object to every sidecar that existed when the project switched, as its last key:
"baseline": {
  "collaboration": "multi-producer",
  "at": "2026-11-20T10:02:17+0000",
  "by": "jpazevedo"
}








Key
Type
Meaning




baseline.collaboration
string
The model the project switched to.


baseline.at
string
When the switch ran (ISO-8601 UTC).


baseline.by
string
Who ran it.



The object is inserted as text, before the sidecar’s closing brace, so sha256 and every other field keep their bytes and the out-of-band check still holds. It marks the artefact as project-owned: the first multi-producer write over it does not report a change of producer, and that write’s previous_sha256 is the baselined hash, so the lineage chain starts from the last single-producer state. Sidecars that already carry a baseline, or that were written under the multi-producer rules (they have collaboration), are left alone, which is what makes the call idempotent. A new multi-producer sidecar never carries a baseline. Stata sidecars receive the object too, since it is added to every *.provenance.json. Stata writes the lineage fields too and runs the guards through its Python integration (#168); without Python a multi-producer Stata write stops unless takeover is passed, and its takeover.overrode is then ["unguarded"].

title: Appendix B — Provenance sidecar schema
section: B.5 The Stata sidecar: same shape, one difference that matters
text:
B.5 The Stata sidecar: same shape, one difference that matters
Stata emits a sidecar built to interoperate with the R and Python siblings — the comment in dw_save.ado states the intent plainly: “Write a sibling .provenance.json sidecar with the same shape the R helpers emit, so reviewer-mode integrity checks work across both languages.” Two fields nonetheless cannot be identical, for reasons rooted in the Stata environment:
{
  "format": "dw_save.provenance/1",
  "path": "C:\\Users\\...\\teamsWrkData\\ed\\dw_ed_edu.dta",
  "written_at": "2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000",
  "user": "jpazevedo",
  "dw_mode": "producer",
  "datasignature": "9:9(12345):1234567890:0987654321",
  "sha256": "4b7e0c9d2a…",
  "schema": { "rows": 48213, "cols": 9 },
  "idvars": "DATAFLOW REF_AREA INDICATOR TIME_PERIOD",
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Education indicators — UNICEF DW format",
    "producer": "01_dw_prep/012_codes/ed/02_aggregate_uis_sdg.R",
    "vintage": "2026-05",
    "_end": "true"
  }
}
The datasignature value above — "9:9(12345):..." — is a colon-delimited string of variable count, observation count, and two checksums, opaque by design. It is written alongside sha256, and is the only hash when Stata runs without Python: such a session writes no sha256 key and a local written_at (28 Jun 2026 14:03:51).






Warningdatasignature is not comparable to sha256



With Stata’s Python integration (Stata 16+) a Stata sidecar records the file’s sha256 — a hash of the file’s bytes — as R and Python do (#191), so byte-level checks such as dw_verify_z(compare = "sha256") and dw_provenance_diff() work across all three languages. datasignature is extra and Stata-only: a hash of the dataset’s variables and values, computed by Stata’s built-in datasignature command. It is not comparable to sha256: a .dta and a .csv of the same logical table have different bytes (so different sha256) but could share a datasignature; conversely the same datasignature says nothing about file-byte equality. datasignature is Stata-native, needs no external dependency, and survives the UNICEF-laptop AppLocker restrictions that would block a third-party hashing binary. Without Python, Stata records only datasignature, and that file’s integrity can be checked only inside Stata, against its own datasignature.


The other differences are smaller but worth cataloguing:

written_at format. R/Python emit ISO-8601 UTC (2026-06-28T14:03:51+0000). Stata emits the same through its Python integration; without it, its local human-readable clock (28 Jun 2026 14:03:51). A parser that wants a single timestamp type must normalise.
Key name for the uniqueness columns. R/Python use isid (an array). Stata uses idvars (a single space-separated string).
format field meaning. In R/Python format is the file’s dispatch format ("csv", "parquet", …). In Stata format is a literal schema-version tag, "dw_save.provenance/1". The same key carries different semantics — do not assume format tells you the file type across all three languages.
schema.columns. Present in R/Python, absent in Stata (which records only rows and cols).
vintage placement. A top-level field in R/Python; nested inside metadata in Stata.
_end sentinel. Stata appends "_end": "true" as the final key of the metadata block — a harmless artifact of hand-writing JSON one line at a time to avoid a dangling comma. Consumers should ignore it.

title: Appendix B — Provenance sidecar schema
section: B.6 A note on the remote-URL freeze sidecar
text:
B.6 A note on the remote-URL freeze sidecar
dw_save() is not the only producer of .provenance.json files. dw_use() called with an allowlisted http(s) URL (the remote-URL freeze) downloads the file once and writes its own sidecar with a different shape — url, sha256, bytes, fetched_at, fetched_by, dw_mode (which falls back to the literal "unknown" when no mode is set). API caches written by dw_api_fetch() are not of this kind: they go through dw_save() and carry the standard write sidecar, with the fetch details in its metadata block. The remote-URL variant records the provenance of a network fetch rather than a local write. It shares the .provenance.json extension and the dw_mode / hashing conventions, but its key set is distinct; do not parse it with the same reader you use for the write sidecar. This appendix documents only the dw_save() write sidecar. Its fetched_at is UTC in both languages but spelled differently: R writes 2026-11-24T13:34:49Z, Python 2026-11-24T13:34:49+0000; a reader comparing the two should parse the timestamp rather than compare strings.

title: Appendix B — Provenance sidecar schema
text:
B.7 Consuming the sidecar
A reviewer or a CI check typically does three things with a sidecar: read it, confirm the recorded sha256 still matches the file on disk, and inspect dw_mode / metadata for lineage. Reading is plain JSON; in R and Python, dw_read_provenance() does it for you (output path or sidecar path; NULL / None when there is no sidecar):

RPythonStata


prov <- dw_read_provenance("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv")
identical(prov$sha256, digest::digest(file = "ed/dw_ed_edu.csv",
                                      algo = "sha256"))


import hashlib
from cso_toolkit import dw_read_provenance
prov = dw_read_provenance("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv")
h = hashlib.sha256(open("ed/dw_ed_edu.csv", "rb").read()).hexdigest()
prov["sha256"] == h


* Stata has no JSON reader in the toolkit; verify via the native signature
use "ed/dw_ed_edu.dta", clear
datasignature
* compare r(datasignature) against the sidecar's "datasignature" value by eye
* or with a small text-parsing do-file



A FALSE / False result here means the file changed since it was written — the lineage record no longer describes the bytes on disk, so the sidecar can no longer vouch for the artifact. R and Python can run this byte-integrity check directly because the sidecar records a byte hash, which a Stata sidecar also carries when Stata’s Python integration is available. Inside Stata itself, verification uses datasignature: re-open the dataset, recompute it, and compare against the value in the sidecar. There is no toolkit-provided JSON reader on the Stata side — a real coverage gap, consistent with Stata’s lack of an API wrapper and parquet support documented in the cross-language coverage matrix appendix.

B.7.1 Comparing the sidecars of two runs
Two sidecars of the same output answer a fourth question: did the new run reproduce the previous one? In R and Python, dw_provenance_diff(previous, current) compares the metadata.inputs records (inputs) and the sha256 fields (outputs) and returns reproduced, inputs_changed (with the input files added, removed, and changed), output_changed (same inputs, different output; warns), first_run, or no_input_record. Read the previous sidecar with dw_read_provenance() before the new run overwrites the output. Stata has no sibling (#152, closed: Stata routes through R or Python).

title: Appendix B — Provenance sidecar schema
text:
B.8 Summary
Across R and Python the sidecar is effectively identical — same keys, same types, a byte-level sha256, ISO-8601 UTC timestamps, an isid array, and a full schema.columns list. Stata emits a parallel file with the same intent and most of the same keys, but adds datasignature (and, without Python, has it in place of sha256, with a local timestamp in place of the UTC one), uses idvars for isid and a version tag for format, and omits schema.columns. A cross-language consumer must therefore check whether a Stata sidecar carries sha256, normalise the timestamp when it does not, and never compare datasignature with an R or Python sha256.
Relevant source files (paths relative to the repository root):

r/R/dw_io.R — .write_provenance() (R write sidecar) and .write_remote_provenance() (remote-URL freeze sidecar)
r/R/dw_io.R — also the multi-producer guards and lineage fields (.dw_collab_preflight()) and dw_collaboration()
r/R/dw_project.R — dw_set_collaboration() (writes cso_project.yml, inserts the baseline object)
python/src/dw_project.py — the Python siblings of both
r/R/dw_provenance.R — dw_read_provenance() and dw_provenance_diff() (read a sidecar; compare two runs)
r/R/dw_deposit.R — dw_fetch_inputs() (returns the input manifest recorded as metadata.inputs)
python/src/dw_io.py — _write_provenance(), _sha256_file(), _utc_now_iso() (Python write sidecar); _write_remote_provenance() (remote-URL freeze sidecar)
python/src/dw_provenance.py and python/src/dw_deposit.py — the Python siblings of dw_read_provenance(), dw_provenance_diff() and dw_fetch_inputs()
stata/src/dw_save.ado — Stata sidecar emission (datasignature, idvars, format: dw_save.provenance/1)
stata/src/dw_stata_helpers.py — the Python helpers Stata calls for sha256, the UTC written_at and the multi-producer guards
docs/dw_io_reference.md — sidecar field overview







NoteMicrodata records provenance structurally, not in a sidecar



The survey-microdata archive — datalib’s Z:/datalib* trees, a different data layer from the aggregate warehouse this sidecar serves — records provenance structurally rather than in a .provenance.json companion: the vintage is encoded in the IHSN folder name (<CCC>_<YYYY>_<SSSS>_v<MM>_M and its adaptation extension), and Data/Original/ is kept untouched so the raw deposit is its own lineage record. Different mechanism, same intent as the sidecar — there is no datalib sidecar to document here. See the IHSN convention chapter.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.1 The five categories at a glance
Every error the toolkit raises shares one shape. Wherever a dw_* helper calls stop() (R), raise (Python), or aborts a Stata command, the message follows a three-part error envelope: a WHAT line, a Why line, and a numbered Fix: block.
The leading [cso_toolkit.<func>] prefix is the load-bearing convention. It separates library messages from your own code’s errors, and — because it is a stable literal — it lets you grep a whole consumer project for every site that hits a given error class. The R testthat suite holds raises to this shape through a custom expect_envelope() matcher (it asserts the ^[cso_toolkit.<func>] prefix on the raised condition), and a manual Python script, python/tests/manual/error_envelope_test.py (run by hand, not in CI), checks 33 raise-paths. The WHAT / Why / Fix structure is therefore a tested invariant, not a stylistic suggestion.
This appendix is a debugging quick-reference. It groups the toolkit’s errors into five categories, gives the actual envelope text for each, explains the contract the envelope defends, and tells you how to fix it. For the full per-function reference see the function reference appendix and the IO and external-API contract chapters; for the sidecar fields named below, see the provenance sidecar schema appendix.
Two terms anchor everything that follows. An error envelope is the three-part message above. A session’s role is one of three: a producer may write canonical data and reach the network; a reviewer is read-only and offline; a publisher submits to the upstream warehouse. The roles and mode-contract chapter is the full treatment; this appendix leans only on the producer-versus-reviewer split.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.2 1. Mode-contract violation
The toolkit enforces the producer / reviewer / publisher mode contract at every wrapped call site, not by convention (see the roles and mode-contract chapter). A reviewer session is physically prevented from two things: writing under canonical paths, and reaching the network. When a reviewer-mode session attempts either, the toolkit stops before any side effect occurs.

C.2.1 Reviewer writing under canonical
This is the canonical example of the whole envelope convention. A dw_save() whose resolved destination lies under teamsWrkDataCanonical, teamsRawDataCanonical, or the configured Z: drive root (dwZDrive) stops in reviewer mode. R and Python also guard teamsFolderCanonical, and R additionally matches the OneDrive-synced 060.DW-MASTER path; Stata guards only the two *Canonical roots and dwZDrive. The R text:
[cso_toolkit.dw_save] Reviewer mode forbids writes to <root>: <path>
  Reviewer sessions must keep canonical / Z: deposits read-only to preserve
  vintage permanence; writes go to the local repo sandbox.
  Fix:
    1. Resolve a sandbox path instead (the profile's `teamsWrkData` should
       point there in reviewer mode), OR
    2. If this is a deliberate Database Manager bootstrap, pass
       `allow_canonical_write = TRUE`.
The Z: branch of this check arrived in v0.4.0 (issue #14); v0.3.0 refused only Teams-canonical writes. The fix is to point the write at your sandbox — in reviewer mode the profile’s teamsWrkData should already resolve there, so the artefact lands outside the deposit. The escape hatch exists for one case only: you genuinely are the Database Manager seeding a one-time cache into the canonical store. Then pass the explicit flag:

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        allow_canonical_write = TRUE)


dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        allow_canonical_write=True)


* Stata's dw_save guards canonical + Z: writes via $dw_mode and accepts
* the same escape hatch as a flag (DBM bootstraps only):
dw_save, filename("dw_ed_edu.dta") path("$teamsWrkDataCanonical/ed") ///
    idvars(REF_AREA INDICATOR) allow_canonical_write





C.2.2 Reviewer fetching from the network (frozen remote)
dw_use() accepts HTTPS URLs since v0.4.0: a producer downloads once and freezes the response under a frozen root with a sidecar, and the reviewer reads only the frozen copy. If the frozen copy is missing, the reviewer cannot fetch it live, so the call stops. Since v0.4.x the envelope also names the resolution tier it chose — so you can tell whether the path is wrong or the file is genuinely absent:
[cso_toolkit.dw_use:remote] Reviewer mode forbids fetching from the network.
  Missing frozen copy: <path>
  URL: <url>
  Frozen-root resolution: <chosen-root> (<tier-name>)
  Fix:
    1. If the path above is wrong, set `dw_frozen_root <- '<your-canonical-frozen-path>'` in your profile.
    2. Otherwise, a producer must call dw_use('<url>') once and commit the frozen file + sidecar before the reviewer pipeline can read it.
The tier line was added after a costly miss: a reviewer-mode audit spent three runs (75+ minutes on a slow network) tracing a fallback that resolved to <githubFolder>/_frozen instead of the project’s expected _frozen path. The envelope now surfaces that mismatch at the point of failure. The frozen root resolves in tiers — an explicit dw_frozen_root global first, a githubFolder fallback next, then <working dir>/_frozen — and R notes the fallback once per session whenever it falls back past the first tier (a warning for the last tier). The envelope above is R’s; the Python envelope omits the Frozen-root resolution line and the once-per-session notice.


C.2.3 Reviewer reaching a live API
The external-API wrapper carries the same lock. When dw_apis_allowed is false and the requested cache is absent, dw_api_fetch() stops. In Python it raises a PermissionError with the full envelope:
[cso_toolkit.dw_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls.
  Call:   dw_api_fetch('sdmx_codelist', cache_key='sdmx_codelist_UNICEF_CL_RESIDENCE_1_0')
  Reason: cache missing at /data/raw-canonical/_apis/sdmx_codelist/sdmx_codelist_UNICEF_CL_RESIDENCE_1_0.csv
  Fix:
    1. The expected workflow is that a Database Manager has already populated
       the cache under teamsRawDataCanonical/_apis/. Verify the cache file exists at the path above.
    2. If you ARE the producer, switch modes:
       from cso_toolkit import _state
       _state.configure(dw_mode="producer", dw_apis_allowed=True)
The fix for a reviewer is to confirm the producer has deposited the cache — most often, nobody populated it. The cross-language way to assert the mode you expect appears in the external-API contract chapter; do it once at profile-load time, never per call.






The Fix: block here is genuinely the expected remedy for a reviewer: verify the cache exists, not “switch to producer.” Switching modes is the producer’s path. A reviewer who flips dw_apis_allowed = TRUE to make this stop go away has silently left the reproducibility floor.



R raises the same [cso_toolkit.dw_api] envelope from dw_api_fetch() (its fix step 2 says to set dw_mode: producer in user_config.yml and re-source the profile). Stata, which has no fetcher, enforces the lock through a dw_require_no_api guard that aborts with Stata error 459 and its own prefix:
[cso_toolkit.dw_require_no_api] Reviewer mode forbids live API calls.
  Why: reviewer sessions must read frozen producer caches to preserve
  vintage permanence; any live API call breaks provenance.
A repo profile may also define its own dw_require_no_api() for scripts that call the network directly; its exact text depends on that profile, so match on the dw_require_no_api token rather than on a fixed string.






Coverage note: Stata ships the guard (dw_require_no_api.ado) but not the fetcher. dw_api_fetch / dw_api_cached / dw_api_inventory are R + Python only. A Stata pipeline that needs live data routes the fetch through R or Python on the producer side, then reads the cached .dta. See the coverage matrix appendix.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.3 2. Unsupported / mismatched format
The R and Python IO helpers auto-dispatch on the file extension, covering CSV / TSV / TXT, XLSX (single and multi-sheet), DTA, Parquet, JSON, and YAML (plus RDS / RData in R, pickle in Python), with optional .csv.gz compression. An extension outside that set raises from dw_save() / dw_use() in the same envelope shape. The R text:
[cso_toolkit.dw_save] Unsupported file extension '<ext>' (path: <path>).
  Supported extensions: csv, tsv, txt, xlsx, rds, RData, rda, dta, parquet, json, yml, yaml
  Fix: rename the output so it has one of the supported extensions.
In Python the list reads csv, tsv, txt, xlsx, pkl, dta, parquet, json, yml, yaml, and dw_save’s fix adds “or extend dw_save’s dispatch table.”
The real gap, though, is coverage asymmetry across siblings (see the coverage matrix appendix). The format you can write in R is not always the format you can write in Stata or Python:

Stata dw_save writes .dta only. It does not dispatch on extension — it always saves a Stata dataset, so there is no Parquet, RDS, or CSV write path on the Stata side. Pipelines that need those formats produce them in R or Python and let Stata consume the .dta.
Stata dw_use reads .dta, .csv, and .xlsx only. Parquet, RDS, and RData reads are out of scope on the Stata side; route them through R or Python.
dw_merge, dw_verify_z, dw_stage, and the standalone dw_isid are R + Python only. Calling a name that exists in R but not in Stata fails as an unknown command, not as a toolkit envelope — so a “command not found” from Stata is itself a coverage signal, not a bug.
dw_fetch_inputs, dw_check_deposit, dw_read_provenance, and dw_provenance_diff are R and Python (#152, closed: Stata routes through R or Python). Python raises the same envelopes: FileNotFoundError (no deposit reachable, no input anywhere, no current sidecar), ValueError (a path outside local_root, a failed check, Teams and Z: disagreeing, an invalid sidecar), OSError (a copy that cannot be verified), and a UserWarning for output_changed. Stata routes via R or Python, so the names are undefined there.
.RData / .rda writes skip the provenance sidecar — not an error, but expect it: the write succeeds silently, with no .provenance.json companion.

The fix is to choose an extension the target sibling supports, or move the step to the language whose sibling implements the format. The contract is identical where the format is implemented; the gaps are in coverage, not in semantics. When in doubt, the coverage matrix appendix is the authoritative source for what each sibling can read and write.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.4 3. API failure / blocked
Two distinct failure modes wear the [cso_toolkit.dw_api] prefix; separate them when debugging.
Blocked (policy): the reviewer-mode lockout from category 1. The network was never attempted; the toolkit refused on principle. The Reason line will say cache missing.
Failed (transport): a live call was attempted (you are in producer mode, the cache absent or refresh = TRUE) and the upstream HTTP call itself failed. In Python, every fetcher routes through a single internal HTTP layer (_http_call) that translates timeouts, connection errors, and non-2xx statuses into the same three-part envelope, annotated with the method, URL, status code, a truncated body snippet, and a fix hint:
[cso_toolkit.dw_api] HTTP GET <url> returned status 403.
  Body (truncated): '...'
  Fix: check the API's docs for that status code; common causes are bad
  query parameters (400), missing auth (401/403), missing cache_key (404),
  or rate limiting (429).






This wrapped transport envelope is a Python feature. The R fetchers call httr::stop_for_status(), so an R transport failure surfaces as a raw httr condition without the [cso_toolkit.*] prefix. Don’t grep for the prefix on the R side of a transport error; match on the function and the HTTP status instead.



Which path you are on depends on your role and the cache state:








Session
Cache state
Action




Producer
cache present, refresh = FALSE
reads cache


Producer
cache missing OR refresh = TRUE
hits live API, writes cache, returns


Reviewer
cache present
reads cache


Reviewer
cache missing
STOPS (blocked — category 1)



So if you see a transport failure at all, you are necessarily a producer: a reviewer never reaches the transport layer. The toolkit cannot retry upstream availability for you. Re-run once the source is reachable; the producer-side cache then absorbs the result so the reviewer never depends on upstream uptime. (UNICEF SDMX, in particular, is prone to multi-hour 403 bursts — the cache is exactly the buffer that decouples reviewers from those bursts.) Use dw_api_inventory() to confirm what is already cached before re-fetching:

RPythonStata


dw_api_inventory("wb")    # what's cached for the World Bank source?


dw_api_inventory("wb")    # DataFrame: api / cache_key / ext / size_bytes / mtime / fetched_at


* No API wrapper in the Stata sibling — dw_api_fetch / dw_api_cached /
* dw_api_inventory are R + Python only (see the coverage matrix appendix).









On the Python side, the toolkit redacts secrets (tokens, keys) from caller keyword arguments before writing them to the provenance sidecar — a <redacted> placeholder replaces the value (the _redact_sensitive helper, added after a Copilot finding on PR #7). If a persisted sidecar’s fetch_args look scrubbed, that is the redaction layer working as intended. This redaction is implemented in the Python sibling; do not assume an R-side equivalent.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.5 4. Integrity / isid failure
This category protects the content of an artefact, not the permission to write it. Three sub-cases.

C.5.1 isid uniqueness failure
isid is Stata’s is-identifier check: does this set of columns uniquely identify each row? dw_save(..., isid = ...) runs that assertion on the declared key columns before writing. If duplicate rows exist on those keys, the call stops, prints the duplicate count and the first offending rows, and writes nothing:
[cso_toolkit.dw_isid] (<path>) <N> duplicate row(s) on key (<keys>).
  First duplicates:
  <sample rows>
  Fix: deduplicate before saving (`df <- dplyr::distinct(df, <keys>, .keep_all = TRUE)`)
  or extend the key set so the rows become unique.

RPythonStata


dw_save(df, name = "dw_ed_edu.csv", sector = "ed", kind = "wrk",
        isid = c("DATAFLOW","REF_AREA","INDICATOR","SEX",
                 "WEALTH_QUINTILE","RESIDENCE","TIME_PERIOD"))


dw_save(df, name="dw_ed_edu.csv", sector="ed", kind="wrk",
        isid=["DATAFLOW","REF_AREA","INDICATOR","SEX",
              "WEALTH_QUINTILE","RESIDENCE","TIME_PERIOD"])


dw_save, filename("dw_ed_edu.dta") path("$teamsWrkData/ed") ///
    idvars(DATAFLOW REF_AREA INDICATOR SEX WEALTH_QUINTILE RESIDENCE TIME_PERIOD)



In Stata the uniqueness check is embedded in dw_save (the idvars() option), not exposed as a standalone command. The Stata message carries the same prefix and envelope:
[cso_toolkit.dw_save] idvars [<keys>] do not uniquely identify the dataset (or contain missing). No file written.
  Why: every output must be unique on its id variables, so a later merge or dw_compare is well defined.
  Fix: find the duplicates with -duplicates report <keys>-, then drop them or add the variable that tells them apart.
In R and Python, dw_isid(df, keys) is also callable on its own as a pre-flight check, and that standalone path raises the full [cso_toolkit.dw_isid] envelope above. Either way the fix is the same: the duplicates are real — collapse, de-duplicate, or widen the key set so the declared keys truly identify a row. The printed sample tells you which keys collide.


C.5.2 Frozen-copy / staging integrity (dw_stage)
The staging lifecycle copies a canonical artefact into the reviewer’s sandbox and hashes it, so a reviewer reruns against a byte-verified local copy. Several integrity stops live here, each with its own WHAT token:

[cso_toolkit.dw_stage] COPY INTEGRITY — the freshly staged copy’s hash does not match the source hash after a retry. The copy is corrupt; the staged file and sidecar are not trusted.
[cso_toolkit.dw_stage] SANDBOX DRIFT — the sandbox file’s hash no longer matches the hash archived in its .staged.json sidecar. Something altered the sandbox copy out of band. Fix: re-stage with overwrite = TRUE.
[cso_toolkit.dw_stage] CANONICAL INTEGRITY — both the Z: and Teams mirrors hold the file but disagree by hash. Neither is used as a source; nothing is written. Fix: this is a genuine deposit inconsistency — escalate to the producer to reconcile the two mirrors before any reviewer run can proceed.

An upstream-changed condition (the sandbox still matches its own archive, but the Z:/Teams source has since changed) is a warning, not a stop (UPSTREAM CHANGED): the sandbox is never auto-refreshed, because re-staging is the reviewer’s explicit decision.


C.5.3 Z: mirror integrity (dw_verify_z)
On any read that resolves to a canonical file while Z: is available (producer or reviewer mode), dw_use() compares the Teams and Z: copies (by file size by default; verify_z = "sha256" for a deep check). A mismatch emits a warning and the read still completes — this is intentionally non-fatal, because a size difference is often a benign line-ending artefact rather than a content divergence. Pass verify_z = FALSE to skip the check, or verify_z = "sha256" when you need certainty. (dw_verify_z is R + Python only; the Stata dw_use runs an equivalent non-blocking size/datasignature check inline.)


C.5.4 Input-deposit integrity (dw_fetch_inputs, dw_check_deposit)
For pipelines whose inputs are kept out of Git, the deposit on Teams / Z: is the source of truth, and every local input must have an identical copy there. The stops (R and Python; Python raises the exception types listed in category 2):

[cso_toolkit.dw_fetch_inputs] No input files … were found locally or in the deposit. — nothing matches the pattern in the local folder, on Teams, or on Z:. Fix: deposit the inputs in the Teams folder named in the message (same relative layout) and rerun; if the deposit is unreachable too, source the consumer profile, sync Teams, or connect to Z:.
[cso_toolkit.dw_fetch_inputs] Teams and Z: hold different versions of '<file>'. — a canonical-integrity stop, as in dw_stage: nothing is copied. Fix: decide which version is correct and replace the other.
[cso_toolkit.dw_fetch_inputs] Could not copy '<file>' from the deposit. — the copy failed or its SHA-256 did not match the source, twice; the temporary <file>.dw_fetch.tmp is removed. Fix: make sure the source is fully synced (OneDrive) or Z: is reachable, and that the local folder is writable.
[cso_toolkit.dw_check_deposit] Deposit check failed for N of M input file(s). — the message tabulates each file’s Teams and Z: status. missing: copy the file to the Teams deposit (same relative path) and let OneDrive sync. differs: the local file and the deposited copy are not the same; decide which is correct and replace the other.
[cso_toolkit.dw_check_deposit] Cannot verify the inputs: neither the Teams deposit nor Z: is available. — Fix: source the consumer profile (it sets teamsFolderCanonical, dwZDrive, dw_z_available), sync Teams, or connect to Z:.
[cso_toolkit.dw_check_deposit] N path(s) are not under local_root … — a caller error: the deposit location of such a path is undefined.

dw_check_deposit(..., stop_on_fail = FALSE) returns the per-file report instead of stopping on missing or differing files.


C.5.5 Run comparison (dw_read_provenance, dw_provenance_diff)
Run comparison is informational: a difference between two runs is a status, not an error. Only these conditions raise (R and Python):

[cso_toolkit.dw_read_provenance] The provenance sidecar is not valid JSON — Fix: rewrite the output with dw_save() to regenerate its sidecar, or restore the sidecar from version control. A missing sidecar is not an error: dw_read_provenance returns NULL.
[cso_toolkit.dw_provenance_diff] The current output has no provenance sidecar. — Fix: write the output with dw_save() (provenance = TRUE, the default) before comparing runs.
[cso_toolkit.dw_provenance_diff] Same inputs as the previous run but a different output — a warning (status output_changed): the code or the environment changed between two runs on identical inputs. Fix: if intended, record the change; otherwise run dw_compare() on the two outputs. Pass warn = FALSE to silence it.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
text:
C.6 5. Vendor drift
The toolkit is vendored, not installed over the network: consumers copy the helpers into their own 00_functions/ and pin a version in .toolkit_manifest.yml (see Vendoring and updates). Drift is the gap between that pinned version and the upstream latest tag.
cso_toolkit_check() reads the local manifest and compares the pinned version with two references (v0.10.0):

The latest upstream tag (producer mode only; it calls the GitHub API). A newer tag is informational: with quiet = FALSE a boxed notice names the versions and the exact cso_toolkit_diff() / cso_toolkit_sync() commands, but nothing is raised.
A target version (the target_version argument, or the manifest’s target_version: key). The comparison is offline and runs in both modes. Being behind the target raises a warning in envelope shape, even with quiet on:

[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_check] The vendored cso-toolkit (v0.9.0) is behind its target version v0.9.1 (from the manifest's target_version key).
 Reviewer mode: no network call was made and nothing was changed; ask the producer to re-vendor.
 Fix: in producer mode, run cso_toolkit_sync(target_version = "v0.9.1"): it prints the release notes, then updates the vendored copy and re-pins the manifest. (Re-vendoring v0.9.1 by hand also means updating pulled_version in .toolkit_manifest.yml.)
In producer mode the second line reads Pipelines run on the older helpers until the re-vendor. instead. When the pin is at or above both references, the log reads (up to date).

RPythonStata


cso_toolkit_check()       # warns if behind the target; logs if behind upstream
cso_toolkit_sync()        # release notes, per-file diff, then pull (producer only)
cso_toolkit_diff()        # or step by step: what changed between pinned and latest
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.10.0") # refresh the vendored copy to a tag


cso_toolkit_check()
cso_toolkit_sync()
cso_toolkit_diff()
cso_toolkit_pull("v0.10.0")


* The vintage-sync family (cso_toolkit_check / _diff / _pull / _sync) is R + Python
* only; the Stata sibling has no manifest-sync helper (coverage matrix appendix).



Two limits to note:

Drift detection is tag-level, not file-level. cso_toolkit_check() compares the pinned manifest version against the upstream latest tag; per-file hash drift (catching a hand-edited vendored copy that claims a clean version) is planned, not shipped. A consumer that locally edited dw_io.R but kept the manifest pin is not flagged.
The upstream poll needs the network. cso_toolkit_check() calls the GitHub API only in producer mode; in reviewer mode it skips the poll with a notice. The target-version comparison needs no network, so set target_version: in the manifest to have reviewer sessions warn when they run below it. cso_toolkit_pull() and cso_toolkit_sync() go further and stop in reviewer mode (a diff against a local clone, cso_toolkit_diff(toolkit_source = ...), still works offline):

[cso_toolkit.cso_toolkit_pull] Forbidden in reviewer mode.
 Why: an update changes the vendored helpers and re-pins the manifest, a
 producer's decision (and reading a release from GitHub is a network call,
 which reviewer mode forbids).
 Fix: switch the profile to producer mode (set dw_mode: producer in
 user_config.yml) before re-running; to inspect only, use
 cso_toolkit_diff(toolkit_source = "<a local clone>").
The pull also stops, with the same envelope, when the vendored folder has uncommitted changes (commit or stash first), for a downgrade without allow_downgrade = TRUE, for a tag that does not exist (for a local clone the fix is git -C <clone> fetch --tags), and with confirm = TRUE in a non-interactive session (the fix is confirm = FALSE).
When behind, run cso_toolkit_sync(): it prints the release notes since the pin, the per-file diff, and then refreshes the vendored copy and re-pins the manifest (or run cso_toolkit_diff() and cso_toolkit_pull() yourself). Because vendoring exists precisely to guarantee vintage permanence, treat a pull as a deliberate version bump in the consumer repo — review the diff, do not auto-pull on every session.

title: Appendix C — Error taxonomy
section: C.7 Reading any envelope: a debugging recipe
text:
C.7 Reading any envelope: a debugging recipe
When you hit a [cso_toolkit.*] stop and are not sure which category it is:

Read the <func> token — it tells you the contract layer: dw_save / dw_use (IO), dw_api / dw_require_no_api (external API), dw_isid / dw_stage / dw_verify_z (integrity), cso_toolkit_pull / cso_toolkit_sync (drift).
Read the second word of the WHAT line. Reviewer mode forbids → category 1. COPY INTEGRITY / SANDBOX DRIFT / CANONICAL INTEGRITY → category 4. duplicate row(s) → category 4 (isid). HTTP ... returned status → category 3. is behind its target version (a warning), or the informational notice A newer cso-toolkit release is available → category 5.
Check your dw_mode first. A large share of these stops dissolve once you confirm whether the session is a producer or a reviewer and whether that role is correct for the step you are running.
Grep the consumer project for the prefix (for example [cso_toolkit.dw_save]) to find every other site that can hit the same class — useful when one fix should be applied repo-wide. Remember the R transport errors (category 3) do not carry the prefix.
Do what the Fix: block says, in order. The numbered options are ranked: option 1 is the expected remedy; option 2 is usually the deliberate escape hatch reserved for the Database Manager.

For the precise arguments and return values behind each helper named above, see the function reference appendix; for the sidecar fields the integrity checks compare, see the provenance sidecar schema appendix.

The two are complementary, not interchangeable; do not merge them into one table.

title: Appendix D — Function reference
text:
D.1 Where the per-function reference lives
This appendix is a directory, not a manual. It lists every public function of the toolkit with a one-line description, the languages that have it, and the chapter that explains it. The table is generated from the code by sh tools/docs-tables: the description is the function’s R help title (or, for a Stata-only command, its Stata help title), and a new function without one fails the check. For the argument-by-argument reference, use each language’s own help, described next. For what a function’s note in another language says (a route, a reason), see the coverage matrix.
R — help pages. Every exported R function has a roxygen2-generated help page: ?dw_save after installing the package or devtools::load_all("r"). They are the most complete reference of the three, and worth reading even if you work in Python or Stata, because the behaviour is shared. r/_pkgdown.yml groups the pages into families through each function’s roxygen @family tag, ready for a pkgdown site; none is published yet.
Python — docstrings. Every public function has a docstring and type hints (the package ships py.typed): help(dw_save) after from cso_toolkit import dw_save. There is no generated site. docs/dw_io_python_reference.md and docs/dw_api_python_reference.md are hand-written references for the IO and external-API functions.
Stata — help files. Each command has a .sthlp file next to its .ado in stata/src/: help dw_save. Two internal files sit beside them: _dw_py.ado and dw_stata_helpers.py, the Python helpers that dw_save and dw_collaboration call through Stata’s Python integration.

D.2 Names
Several helpers have two names in both R and Python: a short historical name and a dw_-prefixed alias of the same function (aggregate_data_v2 and dw_aggregate_data_v2, create_profile and dw_create_profile, test_scripts and dw_test_scripts, and so on). The aliases are the same objects, so either spelling works; the table lists each function once, under its short name.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.1 Adaptation (vintage)
This glossary defines the terms the handbook uses with a precise meaning, as of cso-toolkit v0.12.0 (2026-11-24). Some carry contractual weight: a canonical deposit, for instance, is a status that depends on which role is acting, not just a place on disk. Entries are alphabetical; each links to the chapter or appendix that owns the detail. Which languages implement what is in the coverage matrix.
A harmonised derivative of a master vintage, built for one collection and named by a further token block, …_v<MM>_M_v<AA>_A_<HHHH>, where v<AA>_A numbers the adaptation and <HHHH> names the collection. “Latest adaptation” is the numeric maximum for the requested collection. See The IHSN convention and the folder grammar.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.2 Aggregation contract
The capability family that turns country-level observations into regional and global figures while accounting for the share of population the data cover. Its core is aggregate_data_v2(), with helpers for time windows, coverage footnotes and survey weights. See Aggregation.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.3 Cache key
The short snake_case name under which dw_api_fetch() stores a response, chosen to encode what makes it distinct; it becomes the file name <cache_key>.<ext> in the frozen cache, so a reviewer can find the exact response a producer fetched. See The external-API contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.4 Canonical deposit
The single authoritative copy of a project’s deposited outputs and their sidecars: for the indicator warehouse, the Teams folder 060.DW-MASTER/ and its Z: mirror. The producer writes it, the reviewer only reads it, the publisher publishes from it. The microdata archive’s Z:/datalib* trees are canonical in a separate sense, and nothing passes between the two stores. See Why a toolkit, and how it fits together.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.5 Check record
A small file, .checks/<content-hash>.json, that sh tools/check --record commits when every local check passes on committed content, so a pull request can show its checks were run without re-running them on GitHub. See Checks and CI.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.6 Collaboration model
The project setting, single-producer or multi-producer, that says how many people may produce results. It lives in the committed cso_project.yml (no file means single-producer) and is separate from each person’s dw_mode; in a multi-producer project dw_save() guards outputs against concurrent or unrecorded replacement. See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.7 Collection
The harmonisation code in the last token of an adaptation folder name (for example HLT), naming the modules and merge keys a vintage conforms to in datalib’s registry. A domain says where a survey is shelved; a collection says how a vintage is harmonised and merged. See The IHSN convention and the folder grammar.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.8 Contract auditor
The static check, test_scripts(), that flags direct calls to the raw file-IO and API functions the toolkit wraps, so a repository does not drift back to unwrapped IO. A trailing # cso-allow: <rule-id> comment exempts a deliberate exception. See Checks and CI.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.9 Coverage threshold
The minimum population share, a fraction in [0, 1], that countries with data must cover for an aggregate to be reported; below it aggregate_data_v2() returns a missing value instead. The default is no threshold; 0.5 is the common UNICEF choice. See Aggregation.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.10 Cross-language parity
The commitment that an operation has the same name and behaviour in R, Python and Stata, with one sidecar schema, the same mode-aware routing and one error shape. A parity certificate, written by sh tools/certify --record, records the shared test cases’ results in all three languages for one state of the code. See How the three languages stay in step.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.11 Data Steward
In the draft microdata governance model, the role that operates the archive: it runs the review-gate checks, promotes conformed vintages into the canonical trees and keeps the logs, while the Microdata Core Group decides gate outcomes. The post is not yet filled. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.12 DBM / DBR / DBP
The role acronyms: Database Manager (producer), Database Reviewer (reviewer) and Database Publisher (publisher, formerly INGESTOR). See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.13 Deposit check
The rule, enforced by dw_check_deposit(), that every input a pipeline keeps out of Git has an identical copy (same SHA-256) at the same relative path in the deposit on Teams or Z:; a missing or differing file stops the run. See The IO contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.14 Domain
A thematic grouping of microdata holdings, each shelved under its own library root (health under Z:/datalib-hlt, for example). The domain list is still a draft. Contrast Collection. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.15 dw_apis_allowed
The session flag that gates external network calls: TRUE in producer mode, FALSE in reviewer mode, derived from dw_mode when the profile loads. When dw_api_fetch() finds no cached response and the flag is not TRUE, it stops before any request. See Profiles and the mode switch.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.16 dw_mode
The session property, "producer" or "reviewer", that decides which side of the mode contract a session is on. The profile reads it once from the user’s block in ~/.config/user_config.yml, where a dw_mode_by_project entry takes precedence; there is no default, and it is never a per-call argument. See Profiles and the mode switch.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.17 Error envelope
The shape of every deliberate error and warning in the toolkit: a [cso_toolkit.<function>] prefix naming the function that raised it, a line saying why the rule exists, and a Fix: block of numbered remedies. See Provenance sidecars and the error envelope and Appendix C.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.18 External-API contract
The capability family that puts external data sources behind one mode-aware function, dw_api_fetch(), with the source chosen by api =. A producer fetches live and caches the response; a reviewer reads only the cache. See The external-API contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.19 Frozen cache
The store of upstream API responses, <rawdata>/_apis/<api>/<cache_key>.<ext> with a sidecar each, that a reviewer re-runs against without the network; a missing response stops a reviewer’s call. “Frozen” means the response does not change under the reviewer, so a published figure can be reproduced later. See The external-API contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.20 HTTPS-URL freeze
dw_use() accepting an HTTPS URL in place of a path: a producer’s first read saves the file as <host>/<path> under the frozen-cache root, with a sidecar, and later reads use that copy. Only URLs matching the profile’s dw_url_allowlist (empty by default) are accepted; a reviewer never downloads. See The IO contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.21 IHSN convention
The folder-naming grammar datalib encodes, after the International Household Survey Network’s shelving pattern: country, survey, master and adaptation vintages, each vintage holding Data/, Doc/ and Programs/. Because the path names the vintage, the microdata archive records provenance in folder names rather than sidecars. See The IHSN convention and the folder grammar.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.22 Input manifest
The table dw_fetch_inputs() returns, one row per input with its path, SHA-256 and origin. Stored in an output’s sidecar as metadata.inputs, it lets two runs be compared. See The IO contract and Appendix B.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.23 IO contract
The capability family that gives every read and write one shape: dw_save() and dw_use() choose the format from the extension, route paths by mode, check uniqueness, write sidecars, mirror canonical writes and check canonical reads. See The IO contract and Appendix D.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.24 isid
A uniqueness check named after the Stata command: it asserts that a set of columns identifies rows uniquely. The toolkit offers it as dw_isid() and as the isid = argument of dw_save(), where a failure blocks the write. See The IO contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.25 Manifest (.toolkit_manifest.yml)
The committed YAML file in 00_functions/ that records which toolkit release a repository has vendored: the upstream repository, the pinned tag and the copied files, among other fields. See Vendoring and updates.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.26 Master vintage
A numbered release of a survey’s cleaned data, the block _v<MM>_M after the survey stem. Vintages are integers, and “latest” is the numeric maximum, never the alphabetical one (v10 is later than v09). See The IHSN convention and the folder grammar.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.27 Microdata archive
The governed store of survey data files: datalib’s Z:/datalib* trees, a staging area and the deposit process. It is a different data layer from the indicator warehouse in 060.DW-MASTER, and distinct from the catalogue and from datalib, the software. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.28 Microdata catalogue
The planned metadata and discovery layer over the microdata archive, an IHSN/NADA-style index on the DDI model, to be seeded by datalib’s inventories. It is not yet built. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.29 Mode contract
The rules for what each mode may do at every wrapped call: a producer may call APIs and write canonical paths; a reviewer may do neither, so its writes go to the sandbox and its API calls stop. The code enforces it, at each dw_save(), dw_use() and dw_api_fetch(). See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.30 Module
A single survey data file within a vintage (household, for example), stored under Data/Stata/ as <vintage-folder>_<module>.dta. The collection’s registry gives each module’s level and merge keys. See The IHSN convention and the folder grammar.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.31 Producer
The role (DBM) that owns the deposit: it refreshes API caches, runs the pipeline and writes the canonical outputs, and is the only role allowed live network access. Set with dw_mode: producer. See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.32 Provenance sidecar
The <file>.provenance.json written next to each output, recording when, by whom and in which mode it was written, its SHA-256 and shape, and any caller-supplied metadata. It is what makes a deposit auditable. See Provenance sidecars and the error envelope and Appendix B.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.33 Publisher
The role (DBP) that pushes deposits the producer has signed off and the reviewer has checked to downstream platforms such as Helix. It reads canonical and writes only outside the deposit; dw_publish() so far supports only a dry run. See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.34 Review gate
The seven-item checklist a microdata deposit must pass before promotion from staging into a canonical tree, covering naming, reproducibility, licence, access and de-identification among others. The Core Group decides; the Data Steward runs the checks. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.35 Reviewer
The role (DBR) that re-runs the pipeline from the canonical deposit, writing only to its sandbox, and compares its outputs with the deposit. It cannot write canonical paths or call external APIs; the vendored helpers and the frozen cache let it work offline. Set with dw_mode: reviewer and a sandboxRoot. See Roles and the mode contract.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.36 Sandbox / sandboxRoot
The per-user folder a reviewer session writes into instead of the canonical deposit, set as sandboxRoot in ~/.config/user_config.yml. A profile that derives the write paths points them there in reviewer mode, so pipeline code needs no edits. See Profiles and the mode switch.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.37 Scaffolding
The capability family that writes a project’s standard parts: a profile (create_profile()), a sector script, or a whole repository with its checks, hooks and agent files (create_official_stats_project(), create_research_project()). See Starting a repository.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.38 Sentinel object
The variable a generated profile sets last, profile_<repo> <- TRUE, to show it loaded completely; a sector script can test it and refuse to run without it. See Profiles and the mode switch.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.39 Staging area
The waypoint tree Z:/staging-area/<domain>/<team-folder-as-is>/ where a microdata deposit waits for review, readable by default only by the depositing unit, the Data Steward and the Core Group. It is not an archive: each deposit is promoted or turned down within a quarter. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.40 Stock and flow
The two microdata deposit modes. Stock is existing holdings, deposited exactly as they are so current scripts keep running; flow is new work, named by the IHSN grammar from the start. See The microdata archive.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.41 Vendoring
The toolkit’s production adoption model: a consumer repository copies the helper files into itself and pins the release in .toolkit_manifest.yml, instead of installing them or sourcing them over the network. A re-run then uses the helpers as they stood at release, offline if need be. See Vendoring and updates.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.42 Vintage
A dated snapshot of data or code: the data vintage in a deposit’s provenance metadata, or the toolkit vintage pinned in the manifest. Vintage permanence is the guarantee that a published vintage never changes, which frozen caches and vendoring exist to keep. See Why a toolkit, and how it fits together.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.43 Vintage sync
The capability family that keeps a vendored copy from falling silently behind: cso_toolkit_check() warns when the pin is behind, and other helpers show the differences and refresh the copies. Updating is a producer’s step; reviewer mode makes no network call and refuses updates. See Vendoring and updates.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
E.44 Z: mirror
The copy of the canonical deposit on the UNICEF Azure file share, the Z: drive. A producer’s canonical write is copied there automatically, and a failed copy warns rather than undoing the write; canonical reads compare the Z: copy with Teams by size, or by SHA-256 on request. See The IO contract.

title: Appendix F — Curated third-party functions
text:
F.1 Inclusion rules
CSO production pipelines use a small number of functions the toolkit does not provide and UNICEF does not maintain — community Stata commands, CRAN and PyPI utilities. This appendix is the honest register of that third tier of the ecosystem (the architecture chapter defines the tiers): what these functions are, which versions were verified, by whom, and when.
Two things this appendix is not. It is not an endorsement — UNICEF curates this list, never the code behind it. And it is not a conformance claim: nothing here follows the toolkit’s mode contract, error envelope, or provenance sidecar unless the caveat column says otherwise. The book’s assertion for every row is exactly this: the named version behaved as described, on the stated date, in the stated pipeline. Nothing more.
The list is derived, not curated by taste. A row enters this table only when all of the following hold:

title: Appendix F — Curated third-party functions
text:
Production use — the function is called in at least one production pipeline (a DW-Production sector script or an equivalent vendored consumer). No speculative or “might be useful” entries.
Verified by its user — the sector lead (or pipeline owner) who actually uses the function stamps the row: version tested, date, and any caveats. The handbook maintainer records the stamp; the user of the code owns the claim.
License compatible — the upstream license permits the production use.
Environment-safe — installable and runnable on the UNICEF laptop baseline (AppLocker: no unsigned binaries; corporate network: no unusual endpoints at runtime).

title: Appendix F — Curated third-party functions
text:
F.2 Staleness policy
Rows are stamped, never re-certified wholesale. A row whose Verified date has aged past the version it names simply displays that age — stale rows are visible, and staleness never blocks a release of the toolkit or this handbook. If an upstream release breaks a pipeline, the fix is a new verification stamp (or the row’s removal), not an emergency edit to this book.

title: Appendix F — Curated third-party functions
text:

This register was introduced with the ecosystem taxonomy (architecture chapter) and starts deliberately empty rather than pre-populated: per inclusion rule 2, every row needs its user’s verification stamp, and importing an unverified list would put the book’s name on claims nobody owns. Candidate entries — functions already visible in production pipelines — are collected by scanning the pipelines’ vendored manifests and dependency loads; each becomes a row when its sector lead verifies it.
